item.title: 350 years ago, Ole Rømer discovered that light has a finite speed
item.description: 267 points, 79 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (sciencenorway.no)

→ HN comments  ·  267 points  ·  79 comments

Top #1 — goache:

I created a web comic based on this measurement! https://randomlyunique.com/plancky/2018/roemers-speed-of-lig...

↳ reply 1 — Modified3019:

Wow, what a wonderful little site. It never occurred to me that optical disks worked via constructive/destructive interference: https://randomlyunique.com/plancky/2018/how-optical-disks-wo...

↳ reply 2 — mkehrt:

Thanks, this is a much clearer explanation than the article.

Top #2 — kstrauser:

I don’t quite understand this. The length of the eclipse would be the same, right? Or was it more like that the eclipse ended 10 minutes earlier on the wall clock than expected? I guess what would surprise me about that is:

1. I didn’t know clocks were that good by then to make that reliably measurable.

2. I didn’t realize clocks of the time could measure the period of the eclipse that accurately. Like say one took 24 hours and 7 minutes. If you’re off by 30 seconds, and you’re making a prediction today of when the eclipse would happen six months from now, you could easily be off 90 minutes just based on cumulative error.

The discovery seems easy enough given today’s widespread access to atomic clocks, but extra freaking impressive with clocks from the 1600s.

↳ reply 1 — adrian_b:

The pendulum clock had been invented by Christiaan Huygens a couple of decades earlier.

It became quickly widespread, especially at astronomical observatories.

It is likely that the recent availability of accurate pendulum clocks was essential for Rømer's measurements, so such a result about the speed of light would have been impossible for the previous generation of astronomers.

Nonetheless, inside a fixed astronomical observatory, where there has been built a meridian circle with a telescope, and if there is available a good catalogue of stars, it is possible to measure the current "sidereal time" and use differences in sidereal times to compute the corresponding differences in time, even without a clock. The sidereal time is not a time, but the angle of rotation of the Earth vs. the stars. The rotation of the Earth vs. the stars is much more uniform than the apparent movement of the Sun on the sky, which determines the days.

So it would have been possible, but in a much more difficult way, to measure accurately the duration of some astronomical events even without clocks, but only with accurate instruments for measuring angles, used to determine the celestial coordinates of the stars, then compute the difference in the transit times of some stars whose transits coincided with the beginning and the end of the duration that must be measured, from the angles between them.

When good clocks are available, it is easier to measure the transit times of the stars and compute the angles between them from the times, than the reverse procedure, which would be needed without good clocks.

↳ reply 2 — canpan:

To measure longer periods count the number of days. We have a built in clock which is relatively exact: The rotation of the earth. You only need a clock that measures time correctly during one day, much easier. Which existed at a time.

For the other point, and how he did, i guess the article is badly written. This should be better: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R%C3%B8mer%27s_determination_o... (he didnt need to measure months/years)

Top #3 — ibizaman:

There was a much better explained video from Physics Explained about this https://youtu.be/8yhk1EZq9tY?is=2BvxUY5HKEWkk2LL

It’s one of my favorite science fact and question to ask at parties. When I ask people when do people think humans thought for the first time light had a finite speed, the earliest date I got was 1950.

Speaking of favorite question, here’s a brain teaser. Give me a spot on earth from which you move south 30km, east 30km then north 30km and you end up in the same spot?

↳ reply 1 — rdtsc:

> Give me a spot on earth from which you move south 30km, east 30km then north 30km and you end up in the same spot?

North Pole, a good one. It's popular brain teaser on non-planar geometry for kids. I usually use: "north 100km, west 100km and south 100km", then ask kids if it's possible to end up in the same place. Most say "no". Then I tell them that it is and ask them where would that place be. If still don't know I tell them "pretend you're penguin" pretty much giving them the answer.

The other one I like to ask is if it's possible to have a triangle with all right angles. (That's called a trirectangular triangle, on earth it would starting and north/south pole, all the way to the equator then a 1/4 way east/south).

↳↳ reply — Someone:

> North Pole, a good one.

There are infinitely many such spots, almost all near the South Pole. Apart from the North Pole, any spot 30km north of a line of latitude whose length is 30km/n for integer n will do.

↳↳↳ reply — terio:

Exactly! It surprises me that almost nobody comes up with this one.

↳ reply 2 — huseyinkeles:

For the brain teaser; isn’t it straight forward that it’s the North Pole or am I missing something?

item.title: Solid 2.0
item.description: 245 points, 69 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (solidjs.com)

→ HN comments  ·  245 points  ·  69 comments

Top #1 — wk_end:

What's amusing and/or interesting is that the stuff under "Built to Be Written by Agents" also would make it easier to write by hand, I imagine. It's just better debug diagnostics; nothing really to do with agentic development specifically.

Maybe that's just marketing, but it's really intriguing how human best practices are also agent best practices; how, maybe, we've reached a point where even devs aren't recognizing agent best practices as human best practices anymore; and how suddenly best practices are being prioritized in a way they often weren't - humans could/would/were expected to suck it up and deal with poor devex, but agents simply can't. A strange sort of victory for us folks who cared about it.

↳ reply 1 — lemming:

A friend of mine who works a lot with AI commented that working with AI was making him develop like a grownup for the first time. Turns out that all the best practices really do carry over, but the consequence of not doing it is greater with agents.

↳↳ reply — gwerbin:

Same here, bigtime.

AI has forced me to write out more planning documents. Not waterfall strategic planning, but tactical planning such as describing the desired behavior of a script before I write it, or pre-registering a data analysis and my expected findings in writing before I start querying data -- that goes in a PLAN.md within whatever folder I'm working on at the moment.

I now keep a systematic todo list that I call TASKS.md, which groups tasks into topical sections and every task has an ID, such as MD3 or EV7.

I also keep an append-only-ish journal of results, findings, unfinished thoughts, rejected ideas, etc.

All of that goes right into my project Git repo. It works great for both AI agents and humans.

But perhaps more interesting than my new workflows, is that I actually learn things from the AI. The idea to start pre-registering all my little analyses, not just the big tasks, was a Claude-ism that I've since adopted even when I'm not using AI.

↳ reply 2 — novacrazy:

Kind of the same reason Rust works very well with agents, good error messages and strict type system. Harder to screw up for humans and bots alike.

↳ reply 3 — phailhaus:

Have you looked at Docker's home page recently? The title is now "Secure Sandboxes for AI Agents". There is some insanity going around, rebranding basic tools as "for agents". Docker is just secure sandboxes for everyone, from that tagline you'd think they were somehow specifically made for agents.

Top #2 — miguel-muniz:

Congrats to Ryan and the team. I never got deep enough into front-end to understand the nuance of these things but I still occasionally tuned into his Friday streams just to listen. You can tell he cares about this subject deeply and I enjoy listening to passionate people talk about their craft.

Top #3 — dmix:

Still waiting for Vue 3.6 Vapor to be released which is supposed to be more competitive with these frameworks like Svelte and Solid in performance. Vue 3.5 came out in Sept 2024 and I've ported a lot of code off Vue since then.

↳ reply — pier25:

Performance of Vapor mode is similar to Solid and Svelte.

https://krausest.github.io/js-framework-benchmark/current.ht...

Between Solid, Vue, and Svelte it's more a matter of features and personal preference than performance at this point.

↳↳ reply — intellix:

Well yeah, unless it's resumable it's just a matter of personal preference on how you like to organise your overhead of hydration.

item.title: MAI Code 2 and Code 2 Flash
item.description: 305 points, 139 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (microsoft.ai)

→ HN comments  ·  305 points  ·  139 comments

Top #1 — pseudosavant:

I'd hate to be OpenAI and Anthropic. They are better than the rest of the available models currently, but only by a few months.

That is a very tenuous lead and doesn't speak to much of a sustainable competitive moat for either company. The have to keep sprinting as fast as possible on the hamster wheel to just stay ahead.

↳ reply 1 — com2kid:

Claude has pushed hard on productization. Day to day I use codex for everything, I went to watch my wife use Claude and the way it works is so different. I was shocked when she was modifying an artifact through the Claude website and it was able to make changes to a local file on her desktop.

Microsoft didn't win spreadsheets by having the most advanced or releasing the most often. They made a really good, easy to use product, and got it in front of everyone. (Though Office's p-code was a huge advantage to portability)

↳↳ reply — abixb:

I started using Claude in Chrome three weeks ago (after switching to Chrome after almost a decade) and I've been bloody impressed. It's able to invoke the desktop app for desktop stuff, use my browser for browser tools related stuff, and finally, uses MCP for all the apps I've given it gated access to using 'connectors.'

Anthropic's productization is an order of magnitude better than OpenAI, imo, even if OpenAI has nearly the same, if not better, raw model performance. UX wins every time.

↳↳↳ reply — ls612:

Now if only they could have one of their innumerable agents make a Firefox version.

↳ reply 2 — AnotherGoodName:

The worst thing for them would be if someone made reasonably priced hardware that could run the ‘near enough’ models like kimi or glm 5.3 or whatever the equivalent is in the future that the home user could buy.

I think it’s inevitable. Hardware manufacturing will ramp up to meet a demand and the demand from consumers is there. The big providers can’t monopolize a commodity forever.

The biggest hope is HBF (high bandwidth flash) which has the bandwidth of HBM with the density of flash. It has much more latency but when you’re repeatedly pumping weights through a compute unit it’s not a blocker.

↳ reply 3 — giancarlostoro:

I think Google and Microsoft have the benefit of time as you say, and already being profitable without AI.

Honestly, this line up is impressive, I wanted to try MAI since v1 came out, but Microsoft locked down Copilot subscriptions. If they gave me a comparable plan to Claude Max I'd consider it.

Top #2 — chopete3:

Github Copilot offered MAI Code 2 at 50% today.

I switched it to that model and it was able to resolve tricky python build issues within Windows WSL/ubuntu and also generated a good number of test cases and ensured all of them pass.

It resolved all the Azure deploy (bicep) issues as well. Didn't feel the difference from Claude Opus.

Top #3 — SillyUsername:

Whatever happened to the Microsoft Phi series?

I felt that the training data and behaviours for this at the time were very OpenAI like, due to responses similar in structure to ChatGPT (like how ChatGPT now usually has a section at the end "Why this matters")

Top #1 — cjbconnor:

↳ reply 1 — SilentM68:

Oh, so that's why I could not login and had to reset my password. Ok, now I know it wasn't me.

↳ reply 2 — itopaloglu83:

Honestly I was surprised Apple stayed up during the Microsoft outage as it affected so many interconnected services and infrastructure. I presume that the Cloud providers are shifting some of the workload around and caused other critical services of their customers to fail.

↳ reply 3 — N19PEDL2:

> new iPhones that people bought weren't able to be activated

Bricked from the very beginning.

Top #2 — blop:

what a world we built in less than a generation... everything and everyone dependent on a few cloud services, we're very far from the original vision of a decentralised internet :'(

The only chance we have for a more reliable world is if these outages and hacks become more and more common. Institutions and people will be forced to wake up and find more local and diverse alternatives...

↳ reply 1 — lukeify:

If only big tech wasn't actively hampering attempts to allow decentralisation to even function. Microsoft has _always_ abused their position of power to make it very difficult for people running their own email services to even get reliable mail delivery.

↳↳ reply — The-Bus:

"We are also seeing a lot of noise in the computer industry that the solution to reducing complexity is a simplistic approach, that is, running all software on the server, and giving users nothing but dumb terminals. It generally is not the customer's desire to throw away the billions of dollars they have invested in their current computing environment, turn all their currently productive PCs into dumb terminals and run all of their software on expensive new servers. Customers soundly rejected this model of computing when the Unix vendors tried to convince them to buy network computers."

"Putting everything on a server (and asking the world to rewrite all of its software along the way) may seem attractive if you build servers, but it ignores the real concerns and needs of many customers."

These were quotes from Paul Maritz (a VP at Microsoft) made about 27 years ago to the WSJ[1] in a back-and-forth discussion with a Sun executive (Pat Sueltz). Some of the comments were quite prescient, others aren't.

1 = https://www.wsj.com/articles/SB942104638509774099

↳↳↳ reply — linguae:

"It generally is not the customer's desire to throw away the billions of dollars they have invested in their current computing environment...."

This is true. However:

1. We now have tens of millions, maybe even hundreds of millions, of users who have little experience with traditional desktop computing. They grew up on Web services that they access primarily using smartphones, Chromebooks, or web browsers on desktop computers. There are many people with little-to-no experience with desktop applications like Microsoft Office and the Adobe Creative Suite, but they do their work on Web applications such as Office 365 and Google's suite.

2. Even for traditional desktop computer users, they often spend considerable amounts of money updating their environments once every few years. Windows has excellent backwards compatibility, but most people aren't interested in running Office 97 and Photoshop 5.5 on Windows 11 even if those programs can run on Windows 11. I like Office 97, but I need to deal with modern Office documents, plus I want the improved multi-language support and extra features that have been added in newer versions of Office. The Mac is much more aggressive about cutting off support for old programs; my PowerPC Mac OS X software can't run on my Apple Silicon Macs, and even support for Intel Mac programs will be dropped soon.

Because so many computer users these days didn't start off with traditional desktops, and also because of upgrade churn, this is how we ended up with the current situation, where many people rely on centralized solutions.

↳ reply 2 — AceJohnny2:

Efficiency and resilience are often in competition.

Price is vaguely related to efficiency, so that's what the private sector optimizes for. Think about that next time people complain about Government efficiency.

As one NASA chief said: "if we could blow up rockets as much as SpaceX did, yeah we'd be much faster and cheaper"

Top #3 — NoPicklez:

My theory with all of this is that AI vulnerability detection has risen significantly, as well as AI tools that can exploit them such as ARTEX (which the FBI has put a briefing out for).

These interruptions are potentially a combination of companies racing to patch faster to keep up, or a large exploit has been found, or importantly AI exploit tools like ARTEX are being used in the wild.

I have nothing else to go on

↳ reply — octoberfranklin:

Yeah my bet is on ARTEX too.

item.title: GPT‑6.2 Astra and Sol
item.description: 1133 points, 714 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (openai.com)

→ HN comments  ·  1133 points  ·  714 comments

★ Comments from: simonw, tedsanders

Top #1 — chriddyp:

Pretty incredible cost reductions. In our data analytics exam [1], Astra went from ~$20 (V6) to ~$4 (V6.2) and Sol went from $2.6 (V6.1) to $1.2 (V6.2).

Similar accuracy in both. It's cheaper both because of token reduction (20%) but it also took less tool calls to answer the questions. In some cases, it "finished early" and didn't find the answer we were looking for.

Also very fast. Both Astra & Sol are the 2 fastest models I've tested that got at least an A in the exam.

[1] https://plotly.com/blog/gpt-6-2-sol-plotly-data-analytics-be...

↳ reply 1 — andai:

>In some cases, it "finished early" and didn't find the answer we were looking for.

I just tried out Codex for the first time in a few months, using GPT-5.6-Sol. It keeps doing work in small chunks and stopping. So far it feels pretty different from last time, when it would just persist to absurd lengths and do way more than I asked for. Now it's not even doing what I asked and just keeps stopping.

I'm doing a RE task now (x86-64 ELF to C++) which I haven't tested before (mostly did features and greenfield stuff) so maybe behavior is different there, but it's a bit annoying.

The models in Codex go all the way back to GPT-5.6-* so I'll have to do some more tests with different models and tasks.

EDIT: I even asked it why it keeps stopping, and clarified that I want it to continue, and it keeps stopping anyway. What the hell. I hope the older models aren't like that.

↳↳ reply — skybrian:

Does increasing "effort" help?

↳ reply 2 — maxnevermind:

> ... Sol went from $2.6 (V6.1) to $1.2 (V6.2). Similar accuracy in both. ....

The accuracy according to your link dropped from 100%(Sol v6.1) to 93%(Sol v6.2), not sure if that can be called similar.

↳ reply 3 — chr15m:

It's like they are trying to find the balance point between a model that persists too hard, making it do crazy things, and one that knows when to stop.

Maybe that point is a large overlap though, depending on the task

Top #2 — Topfi:

Office work has never been OpenAIs strength, no shame in that by itself, but these Slideshow examples look particularly awful, far worse than what I myself got out of GPT-5.6 Sol about two weeks ago in a single prompt.

Same for Workbooks and memos, those examples read inferior to some pre Opus 4.5 and Kimi K2 Thinking docs I have kept around. It's ok for a model not to be great at these, but these are some very poor examples. I am really confused what is going on at OpenAI in this regard.

I remember the same with their frontend blog post a few months ago that they proudly shared while filled with visual glitches, bugs and issues. Also, the vibe charts from a bit before that. Please, get someone with fresh eyes to look at your communications before you publish, these leave a very bad first impression.

Regardless of office work, I can't wait to find out whether these models finally adhere to a prompt or are still willing to carry out explicitly disallowed, irrecoverably destructive tasks, just because those might (but don't even always) get the model to a result more quickly along with some of the other regressions that have been present since the release of GPT-5.5. GPT-5 to GPT-5.4 were truly groundbreaking, but since then there have been regressions in what made those models so useful and reliable.

Edit after the first, incredible simple test prompt using GPT-6.2 Astra on High using Codex, this was the response to me sharing a screenshot of the very much not in scope result and asking how that happened:

"[...] I added controls and reconstructed interface chrome that weren’t authorized [...] visuals often failed to show the feature [...]"

Great, so it's one of those releases again. Will still run the full evals of course, maybe I'll get surprised by end of week when those are done, but not a good initial experience. New idea, besides the existing destructive git tasks, have something similar using Mercurial based projects and see which models just decide to port that over to git without permission or request cause it feels like the right thing to do, is easier to work with or whatever justification one wants to employ.

Please OpenAI, get it together, we need actual competition. I am an unashamed Haiku enjoyer, it doesn't even take much to excite me.

6.2 seems optimized for benchmarks. Not creative.

After a couple hours of testing, we reverted back to 6.1 for basic document generation, proposals, marketing content.

I also wonder if this is a disconnect of tech workers from other users? Inversely all the improvement examples on slides looked directionally like things coming out of a big finance shop. In the tech groups I am part of I constantly see ai slop images, charts and similar. I wonder if it’s simply a taste difference if users.

↳↳↳ reply — ★ tedsanders:

One nuance to be aware of is that the AA version uses the mini-swe-agent harness, which can understate performance of models trained to use particular harnesses. Implementations also can differ in terms of timeouts on tasks and memory/etc. resources given to the agent, which affect scores on longer running, resource-intensive tasks. I believe these differences are why we chose not to use AA scores on this comparison, but I’ll double check when I get back to my computer.

item.title: Nvidia stopped disclosing Singapore sales as revenues hit $104B
item.description: 423 points, 206 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (ft.com)

→ HN comments  ·  423 points  ·  206 comments

Top #1 — Pwntastic:

https://wallhop.io/https://www.ft.com/content/dbde7a30-548c-...

Top #2 — alangibson:

Half of their revenue was booked through Singapore? I suspected that Jensen was fired for helping evade sanctions, but now I'm sure.

I dont believe the board fired the founder and only CEO they ever had over a series of affairs. They fired him because one of the affairs was with a lady pretty clearly helping import chips from Singapore to China.

↳ reply 1 — areoform:

Singapore is essentially the Delaware / Ireland of Asia. Revenue gets booked through there because Singaporean laws are well defined, there are tax treaties with multiple jursidictions, and there isn't onerous regulatory overhead.

https://www.irishexaminer.com/business/companies/arid-418199...

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple%E2%80%93EU_tax_dispute

Apple and Singapore, https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/articles/singapore-...

https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/08/singapore-ove...

↳↳ reply — GIFtheory:

It’s still kinda surprising that half of Nvidia’s revenue comes from Asia/Pacific, given the (apparently laxly enforced) export restrictions to the largest market in that region.

↳ reply 2 — theseamusjames:

One thing that hasn't been established is if they were actually evading export restrictions.

It wasn't illegal to sell GPUs to china. It depends on _which_ GPUs they were selling, and I haven't seen any reporting that identifies specifically which models were found in Megaspeed's possession. If the had 600,000 H200s in their closet, it wasn't illegal.

And while the US was allowing certain chips to be exported, China wasn't allowing their companies to buy them (although they definitely trained on them in data centers outside of China). That could account for why they're in storage and not deployed.

Also, it's entirely possible that the board didn't fire him and he resigned because there are a bunch of other women and he doesn't want his family to suffer the embarassment of more of them being revealed.

Top #3 — mlmonkey:

> US authorities are investigating whether the Singapore business, Megaspeed, was involved in smuggling Nvidia chips to China

I don't understand one thing. Why does the end user (China) need the physical chips?? I train my models on machines sitting in some datacenter on the East Coast, or sometimes even Finland. I have never seen an NVidia GPU in my life, and probably never will; as is the case with most developers.

As I see it, Chinese developers don't need physical access either. So why does it matter that Singapore ordered the chips, or Finland? If you have enough money, you can access the latest and greatest NVidia chips in however much quantities you want!

↳ reply 1 — aperrien:

If you have physical possession, it's much harder to deny access later.

↳ reply 2 — kube-system:

For the use cases that are of national security concerns, you’d need physical possession of the chips and the networks they run on.

item.title: What is the best harness for each model?
item.description: 343 points, 119 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (runta.com)

→ HN comments  ·  343 points  ·  119 comments

Top #1 — seizethecheese:

The headline here is confusing. They ran a bunch of harness and agent combinations on terminal bench tasks, and 64% of the spending was on tasks that didn’t pass terminal bench verifiers.

It’s unclear whether that’s supposed to be surprising against the selected models for the benchmark. I suspect it’s not and the headline is written to pander to “wasting money on AI” upvotes.

Edit: they changed the title. The one used to get to the front page was something like "Across N agent runs 64% of agent cost went to failing runs".

Edit2: since the link is poor quality, I tried to answer some of these questions myself using 927k agent runs vs. this blog post's 27k: https://micjm.com/blog/on-model-harness-interactions/. The upshot: there's not a lot of harness x model interactions. OpenAI models do seem to have a preference.

↳ reply 1 — seizethecheese:

Okay, I wanted to know “which tasks” and dig into the methodology, and its documented nowhere!

A serious effort here would use a specific set of terminal bench questions. Instead these look like cherry picked questions. How were they picked and why? Without an answer we should assume they were picked to produce some result.

↳↳ reply — jzemeocala:

For real, i remember setting up advanced Linux configurations back before the 3.0 kernel and I'm pretty sure I had a higher failure rate.

The biggest difference is that I, as a human, get mentally exhausted. but modern AI (when given unlimited tokens and tools) is like if Stephen hawking had a meth habit and the tenacity of Sisyphus with a bad case of syphilis after being told he can be cured if he can get that boulder over the hill

And even if they did try to test them on a lot of gotcha tasks; I'm perennially reminded of the ever-relevant quote about AI and other tech: "this is the worst it will ever be"

↳↳↳ reply — dotancohen:

That quote is outdated. My phone nags me now twice daily to update, and the update removes features I use so I'm careful to tread around it.

My Windows work desktop has two orders of magnitude more memory and more processing power than the last time I used Windows, yet boots slower and is laggier than any Windows I've ever used.

Almost all useful information online is concentrated into YouTube and Reddit, everything is advertising and trying to steal attention. I'm not even welcome on Reddit anymore due to the media campaigns against my country and race.

We've definitely passed the point where the derivative has gone negative.

↳ reply 2 — onlyrealcuzzo:

There's thousands of benchmarks, and nobody can agree on what the best models are if you run all of the benchmarks which costs tens of thousands of dollars for frontier models.

Then, somebody runs a small subset of benchmarks - with not enough data to have any statistical significance - and makes further claims.

How are we supposed to derive value from this?

↳ reply 3 — plufz:

Yeah exactly, compared to what baseline? People here will probably be stunned when I say this, but my pre-agent code was usually not bug free on my first attempts either.

Top #2 — Zigurd:

I find myself pulled in two directions by the performance of coding agents: First, keeping them on a short leash seems sensible. I don't get failed results very often. When I first started using coding agents, this seemed not just sensible but required in order to not deal with a lot of hallucinated weirdness. Secondly though, it's pretty cool to vaguely wave your hands in a certain direction and get both user interface and business logic that's objectively nicer than I would've gotten from the effort I would've put into manually coding. Whenever I cautiously use a coding agent, I wonder what I am missing by not letting it cook.

↳ reply 1 — nolok:

I don't understand why that idea was adopted that IA had to be that "give one command have a perfect run and correct answer" thing when it's clearly not how it works and an eternal "the last % is worth 99%" issue.

I know why the US frontier labs push it of course, you can't push a trillion dollar plus idea if you also say it should be a cheap commodity and the best and latest are now the answer, a bazillion mid levels are.

But most work of value I do is with a swarm of "not the latest nor the brightest" models, with a smart one controlling the dance. Most decisions or review is better done through consensus. The myth that "if we keep going it will reach a point where it's always correct" seems so obvious to me, it doesn't work like that, for that matter we don't work like that.

This is not a jab at it. I work with it. I love it. But I think the story imperative are a mismatch for the actual needs of most companies, and it's hiding between the "frontier needs" of special research & co, or the governemental needs.

On the same line of thought: it's pretty obvious as great as these things are, no they're not going to "replace all employee", and no employee without them won't be able to compete either. They're a supercharger, a self multiplying smart assistant with capabilities in any field, and it feels so wrong to me that they've been presented in a complelty different way.

↳↳ reply — krrrh:

> it doesn't work like that, for that matter we don't work like that.

The parallels with self-driving cars are interesting. We demand that agents don’t just produce better code than most humans (which the frontier models do), but that they perform much much much better.

↳ reply 2 — contravariant:

I think Conway's law applies. In an ideal situation your code mimics your organisational structure.

The places where you let an agent do its thing is bound by the (implicit) interface your prompt creates. In an ideal situation this interface is a simple isolated thing in your application.

If you just let it do its thing, expect a monolith. You shouldn't rely on it coming up with interfaces that mesh well with what you had in mind, and each of those interfaces represents a decision that it took, restricting future iterations of the code. So a monolith is not only what you can expect, but also the best you can hope for.

If you want to let it cook, create more places for code that does a thing and you don't care how.

Top #3 — xyzzy_plugh:

I don't like this framing.

For a given model, the best harness depends on the problem. As models become increasingly capable, the harness appears to matter more than the model. This is perhaps controversial but allow me to explain.

Most of my problems are in a single domain, using specific tools and programming languages. I give whatever model de jour the specific tools it needs to solve the problem. I don't let it execute arbitrary scripts or programs (though it can, if it really tries). I give it a restricted number of calls and I feed that information back into it (budget). I let it farm out work to other models, using the same harness. I give everything a budget, which is tracked and enforced, but it's not real, and refills at different times.

This bespoke, specialized harness absolutely smokes any other mainstream harness for these tasks. Significantly faster, cheaper, more correct.

But I can't build a mobile app with this harness, or make a movie.

These tests are doing the same thing. They measure a handful of scenarios. I can't easily tell if those map to my needs or not. In my experience, very few of them do.

Can these general purpose harnesses solve my problems? Yes, if I'm willing to let the model churn for a long time and burn a lot of tokens. But that doesn't feel like a sustainable practice.

Maybe I'm too early, maybe it's premature to optimize the harness this way, but I'm spending fewer tokens than my peers and getting a lot more done, and that matters.

↳ reply — botanrice:

hey! would you be so kind as to share your method or point me in the direction towards resources on how to setup a harness as you describe?

I've been tinkering with harnesses recently but have mostly used github copilot on vscode mostly thus far as my ai tool and feel like the harness setup on there is lacking (or really confusing...). many thanks if so :)

just trying to learn without googling "how to setup a harness" and get bombarded by a trillion yt vids or competing harness providers lol

↳↳ reply — xyzzy_plugh:

Just ask one to write the other.

"Write me a harness in $LANGUAGE that uses the $MODEL API and has tools for X Y and Z" etc etc

I added remote management and web console over tailscale in about 20 minutes last week.

item.title: We don't need more apps, we need better open source
item.description: 345 points, 234 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (jordankrueger.com)

→ HN comments  ·  345 points  ·  234 comments

Top #1 — joshdata:

> Pick one open source tool you use. Find the most annoying thing about installing or running it. Spend a weekend fixing it, with the people who maintain it. Then tell me about it.

My open source projects were barely sustainable when the few PRs that came in would fix actual, non-hypothetical, serious logic problems.

Now I've been seeing PRs like that, fixing annoyances, performance edge cases, or hypotheticals, across my open source repositories, and I don't have time for them. I especially don't have time to fix problems that probably nobody will ever experience, and yet they keep coming. I have not organized my life around triaging annoyances (let alone fixing them).

If the trend continues, I'll soon be forced to close repositories to contributions, or just stop maintaining the projects entirely. And I imagine that's the point a lot of maintainers are at.

↳ reply 1 — chasd00:

rejecting a PR saying "i don't have the time to deal with this" is 100% valid thing to do. Don't let yourself be taken advantage of, it's your project. If the submitter doesn't like the answer then they an fork and go on their merry way, that's also a 100% valid thing to do and is the backbone of open source.

↳↳ reply — ravenstine:

PRs should be rejected by simply not enabling PRs in the first place. If PRs are needed for development, then that should be done in a private repo that is mirrored to a public one. I wouldn't even be surprised if that person'a readme says the project is open to contributions and that pull requests are welcome. I've found this contradiction to be very common, yet it seems like I'm in the minority for believing it's rude.

↳ reply 2 — athrowaway3z:

I've had my AI contribute to a bunch of open source so i'm on the other side of this.

For me they're real issues. Half of which i'd found before but never had the time to submit something for, the other half its things the AI will have encountered - and i check to confirm its a real issue.

The AI will follow guidance you leave in a repository. One of them said "no ai", so it reported that to me and I just forked and went on with my life.

There might be people farming for gh contribution i dontk now — but I can assure you the trend will continue, and afaict it is improving software; at least most of my contributions have been merged.

↳ reply 3 — verst:

I don't accept PRs anymore for which there isn't an open issue where either maintainers discussed the issue or it has significant discussion among users. I'm trying to use issue labels to indicate if something is ready to accept PRs.

I see a lot of unsolicited PRs (and my case not from actual users but instead university students trying to pad their resume with random open source contributions but while clearly using AI exclusively)

Top #2 — timbert:

I think we need a new model of software delivery.

Here's my most-recent real-world problem: I wanted to plug in my midi controller keyboard and just play a piano, so I can practice my choral music. Very basic.

This turned into many hours over several days trying multiple DAWs, trying to get tehm to install, get them to run at all, get them to recognize my controller, get them to play a VST plugin...changing system settings, completely jacking up my sound, restoring it all again.

It was a nightmare.

So instead I fired up Claude, worked with it for about 3 hours, and now I have an *8-channel* VST player that supports all my hardware, and includes a snappy UI, with outstanding performance and sound. It's amazing!

I literally spent less time creating a custom solution than I did trying to get the off-the-shelf stuff to work. I could make my player OSS too, but the effort to do that is huge, for all the reasons this forum would understand.

Bespoke software avoids all of that and allows me to do what I want, with the environment I have. I don't have all the features of an FL Studio, but I have what I need, and that works for me, beautifully, at low cost and effort. What's not to like?

So maybe we should share OSS "templates" instead of full products, projects that are the barebones of a solution that you can clone, and have your LLM modify to suit your needs, on your platform of choice.

For example, perhaps my barebones VST player is mostly good enough for you, but you also want to play sound fonts? Cool, clone my project, instruct your LLM to add sound font support, and add support for your controller or your output device. Or convert it from Gnome to KDE.

The time and cost of doing this is so little now, why not? I'm getting more out of my computer than ever, and I'm happy about that :)

↳ reply 1 — nayroclade:

Yes, right now this is absolutely the best way to build bespoke software, but it is also very wasteful. Think of all the time and the billions of tokens being burned to repeatedly reimplement apps and features. LLMS code fast, but not yet instantaneously or perfectly for complex features.

What we need is more than just OSS templates. We need fully LLM-managed "software libraries". These would be like package managers on steroids. They would be a huge hierarchy of LLM-coded modules. When you ask for an app, your LLM assembles it from the modules that already exist. If you ask for a novel feature, it codes it up and places it into the library.

So, for your VST player example. You would ask for a barebones version with just the features you need, and your LLM would assemble it for you from preexisting library modules. Then you ask for sound font support. If there is an existing sound font module, it would download it and add it into your app. If there wasn't, it would create one and put it into the library, so the next time someone asks, they can quickly get a VST player with sound font support.

↳↳ reply — jhloa2:

I have a similar experience where I’ve been learning the keyboard but didn’t like the available free options and the good paid apps had really expensive subscription plans so I had Claude build me something that runs natively on my iPad, with midi and microphone support and generates custom learning plans for midi pieces that I import.

I’m an engineer but not a software engineer and it’s been pretty interesting trying out vibe coding and seeing the barriers of entry being blown apart.

I’ve been progressing at learning the piano quite a lot faster than I expected with this. I’ve been debating open sourcing it but I’m not sure I want to take on the work of managing it

↳↳↳ reply — compacct27:

Oh wow, just did the exact same thing on my end. If I’m struggling with some fundamentals I’ll just have Claude scour the internet for the best instruction and throw it into a lesson

↳ reply 2 — montenegrohugo:

Fully aligned, i echo the above experience strongly.

However, it seems to me like there must be some middle ground, between sharing architecture "ideas" and full on code PRs.

I myself maintain various FOSS projects; and incoming PRs are marginally useful. generally i just close, and copy with claude following my own & project taste (crediting initial contributor).

Top #3 — linsomniac:

> Pick one open source tool you use. [...] Spend a weekend fixing it

Beware: Your best path forward there may be, contrary to part of the thesis in this post, be to vibe code a replacement. There are a couple reasons why:

Expect to encounter significant push-back due to AI contribution. For example, I've had bug fixes to significant problems be rejected because "we are in the future going to be adopting a no-AI policy". Annoying because I spent my time working on it because they did not have a no-AI policy. Amusing to have another contributor contribute the exact same fix, like character for character, under a new PR (referencing my issue, so not done in isolation) and get it accepted.

There may also need to be sweeping changes to the project you are fixing -- which are going to be a burden to the maintainer and likely wouldn't be accepted because of that. A fork may be the way to go here, but also "vibe coding" a replacement might be the best option.

Earlier this year I build a replacement apt cache called apt-cacher-ultra. Part of it was because the existing apt-cachers had reliability issues, but a bigger part was I wanted something that would survive ubuntu.com being under a DDoS for a week or two. apt-cacher-ng was totally useless at that. The path I wanted to try was to have verified known good snapshots of the upstream, background refreshes, pre-fetching of known "hot" packages when the upstream refreshed. HUGE changes.

I've put 100 hours or more into this "vibe coded" alternative (mostly enhancements and fixes for other users use cases). I'm pretty confident that this wouldn't have been something the apt-cacher-ng or apt-cacher maintainers would have been interested in accepting.

item.title: Loopholes Are for Assholes
item.description: 169 points, 206 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (actsofvolition.com)

→ HN comments  ·  169 points  ·  206 comments

Top #1 — vehemenz:

The example cited--parking in a no-parking zone--isn't an example of a loophole. A loophole is usually understood as an act that honors that letter of the law but violates the spirit of the law.

↳ reply 1 — skeeter2020:

OK - we could keep it in the same analogy ballpark: driver behaviour in heavy traffic. A very small minority do legal but antisocial (and very dangerous) things to improve their experience marginally at the cost of the entire population. If everyone followed their lead we'd shift the same traffic problems to some other permutation, lose any consistency we currently get and have more accidents. ex: zooming up the exit lane and then bullying your way back into through traffic makes you an asshole.

↳ reply 2 — mungoman2:

What is it called when breaking the letter of the law, but not the spirit of it?

↳ reply 3 — dieselgate:

I’m surprised it’s not mentioned in the article because the real loophole in parking in a no parking zone is utilizing the “park anywhere lights” aka hazards.

Top #2 — JumpCrisscross:

Consistently using loopholes makes you an asshole.

Loopholes are social slack. You can speed to the hospital, usually, in an emergency. If you’re running late to pick up your kid, sure, double park or streetside with hazards.

But if you turn this into a lifestyle, you’re broken. (Every person tweeting with religious zeal for Jensen falls into that camp.)

↳ reply 1 — jcranmer:

Those aren't loopholes. Those are just plain breaking the law, relying on the violation either not being caught or being dismissed as not worth prosecuting, or in the extreme case, relying on sympathy getting you off of the hook.

↳↳ reply — bryanlarsen:

People engaging in this behavior should not be doing so expecting to being let off the hook, they should be doing so when willing to pay the consequences.

If I'm speeding on the way to the hospital and have to pay a fine for doing so, so be it. If your reason for speeding isn't good enough that you're not willing to pay the fine, you shouldn't be speeding.

↳ reply 2 — nadis:

I would more consider loopholes to be something where there's not normally social slack (it's weird or frowned upon to exploit a loophole so most people don't do it) versus something like speeding to the hospital in an emergency is rule-breaking, but socially accepted because it's for an exceptional and valid reason (and something most people would probably do in the circumstance).

I was trying to find a good example of a loophole and found this which was bizarre but sort of meets my imagined criteria:

"The Pudding Frequent Flyer Loophole: In the late 1990s, Healthy Choice ran a promotion giving away frequent flyer miles for buying their food products. A civil engineer named David Phillips realized that buying thousands of individual cups of pudding was the cheapest way to accumulate over 1.25 million airline miles, which he used for free travel while donating the pudding to charity for a tax write-off."

So a loophole is legal but not really "normal" behavior like the pudding example, while the speeding to the hospital example is rulebreaking (illegal) technically but is more accepted as "normal" due to the circumstances.

Top #3 — fwlr:

When applying the categorical imperative (“what if everyone acted in accordance with this belief?”) I have found it useful to look at it game-theoretically (is everyone acting this way a stable equilibrium? where does the equilibrium end up?) and also examine the counterfactual causal consistency (if everyone had been acting this way previously, would we have arrived at the current scenario? when thinking of exploiting a commons before others do, consider that the commons could not have accumulated into existence in the presence of others’ exploitation; the fact that you have the opportunity is evidence that you are not in a race to use that opportunity).

↳ reply — legacynl:

Ultimately it is about following (unstated) rules. Whatever you tell yourself is just justification. OP is right. Society demands us to adjust ourselves to others, and this is a good thing.

item.title: Baidu, Xiaomi CEOs warn of growing gap between AI hype and returns
item.description: 185 points, 243 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (scmp.com)

→ HN comments  ·  185 points  ·  243 comments

Top #1 — jnwatson:

Given the Hacker News bias towards tech, it is easy to focus on just the challenges of exploiting AI for software development.

The problem is, to justify the substantial investment in data centers and the eye-watering valuations of Anthropic and OpenAI, AI has to successfully reach into essentially every niche of the economy. It can't just be a tool to code faster. It must make most jobs faster period. From daycare to farming, we need relatively short-term ways of integrating this technology.

AI will survive the hype cycle, but the AI companies very well may end up like railroad companies or Iridium, where the shareholders got zeroed out and then someone comes in, buys the assets for 10 cents on the dollar, and builds something useful out of it.

↳ reply — ralph84:

It is going to require new companies that organize themselves around AI. Existing companies have too much inertia to adapt. Sears was selling virtually anything through the mail 100 years before Amazon. But it required a new company in Amazon to truly take advantage of the Internet. The same will be true with AI.

↳↳ reply — ryanSrich:

Having seen this firsthand. I agree. The inability of many to think in an AI-forward or AI-first way is puzzling. There's a fundamental disconnect many have that they may not be able to get around. If you're working in a company that primarily does business on a computer, you need to fundamentally rethink your staffing. Every new and existing role needs to be justified. Does this need to be a human or can an agent do it? I would much rather manage an agent than a human. I can easily train an agent to do better. I can give it more context. I can have it act like a human. I can give it a script. I can give it autonomy when it makes sense.

↳↳↳ reply — therealdrag0:

I think the challenge is it’s usually not a one-to-one relationship. Often what can be done by AI is a fraction of each person’s individual role so it’s hard to replace a single headcount purely with AI. On the other hand, they do seem to be examples of companies going balls to the wall, but that is a much larger restructuring and as you said it’s entirely Greenfield company organization structure.. for example I just read an article by a company of 10 people who spend 30x headcount on AI. I think most companies can’t imagine spending multiples of their labor costs on AI and what that may or may not do for them.

Top #2 — tyleo:

The tools are good and even getting better but the gap is real. If the tools made people 2x faster AI CEOs would say 5x faster, if they made people 5x faster they’d say 10x faster.

I feel like expectations of a gap should be built in.

↳ reply 1 — JeremyNT:

I think a part of it is that AI companies are software companies, and of course software development is the field that (so far) has been most revolutionized by language models.

So AI CEOs are seeing around them, everywhere, the absolute best case scenario for how a field can be transformed - in their own organizations. It's pretty easy to drink that kool-aid and extrapolate out from there.

Investors don't seem to mind, and all of these companies are all-in thinking that what happened to software is going to happen to every field, but you have to wonder how long the expectations vs reality "gap" will be tolerated.

↳ reply 2 — runarberg:

Corollary: If AI actually made your job slower, worse, less efficient, etc. AI CEO would still say they’d make it 2x faster, or 5x faster, or even 10x faster.

Worse, AI CEOs would fund biased research to show that it made your job 2x faster while claiming it makes it 10x faster.

That the tools “are good and getting better” may not be true at all.

Top #3 — SecretDreams:

The tools are good, but the ideas are not. These tools basically see many people building the same things independently, rapidly, and over and over again.

I'm not seeing a lot of unique applications. I am seeing some optimization, plenty of rehashing the same crap. Lots of thought outsourcing.

Honestly, I'm mixed as someone who also uses these tools. Is it really efficient for 100s of people to be spending tokens and electricity to all make, effectively, the same bad app from their shower thought/idea? I love that we've democratized coding so that it's more accessible to laypeople - but it is mostly all slop and lack of creativity being produced. And, in the rare instances where someone genuinely makes something good, 100x people will then spin their own AI to rip off the same idea.

Where does this all go at the end of the day for humanity when nothing is new or creative and we are going backwards in critical thinking along the journey? Especially since the journey IS the thing for humanity - not the end product of the journey.

↳ reply 1 — schnevets:

> The tools are good, but the ideas are not. These tools basically see many people building the same things independently, rapidly, and over and over again.

Isn't this just every bubble technology since the 80s? I remember being at parties in the early 2010s and hearing awful web site ideas that were certainly feasible with an RoR stack but had a <1% survival rate. The only difference now is less engineers acting as gatekeepers.

I'm certain it was the same way with static HTML webstores in the 90s, social media since early blogs, and other industries that received funding spikes that eliminated financial barriers (construction, film, video games, restaurant chains, etc)

Eventually the Gartner Hype Cycle proves true and the hysteria dies down, but out of those promised elevators of progress come a few incremental steps upward.

↳↳ reply — hnlmorg:

I don’t think there was enough money in the web in the static HTML days to have the same bubble. But I do recall domain squatting being a lot more prevalent then than it is now.

More recently was blockchain hype.

↳ reply 2 — guyomes:

Whether great or not, it seems to follow the birth of home videos with youtube, tiktok, etc. The video industry went:

- from highly founded centralized creations (TV, movies, series),

- to highly founded centralized creations (TV, movies, series) plus public home made videos (influencers, etc.) plus private home made videos (vlog for friends, etc.).

I can imagine the same with software, where big highly funded software remain, on top of home made software. Some home made software on neglected areas might be exchanged on some social platform (for example, apps to help women track their period was neglected for a long time), and some will just be for friends and family (like a personalized educative video game with a kid's favorite plush).

item.title: New Evidence Shows School Phone Bans Are Gradually Improving Test Scores
item.description: 1186 points, 589 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (nytimes.com)

→ HN comments  ·  1186 points  ·  589 comments  ·  comments as of 15h

Top #1 — 40four:

http://archive.today/pbZQw

Top #2 — yorwba:

The study https://cepr.harvard.edu/sites/g/files/omnuum9881/files/2026... finds a ≈0.01 standard-deviation difference in test scores the year lockable phone pouches are adopted, with no detectable additional difference in the following year. Certainly nothing to sneeze at from a system-wide perspective, but easily overwhelmed by other factors for any individual student.

↳ reply 1 — rahimnathwani:

That ≈0.01 SD effect is actually 0.0087 +/- 0.0043 (standard error), giving a 95% confidence interval of roughly 0.0003 to 0.0171 standard deviations.

So the effect could be tiny.

Worse, the report says it excludes observations outside the 0.5th and 99.5th percentiles of the 2021–22 fall-to-spring score-change distribution. I'm not sure how this is defensible. Either you trust your measurement instrument or you don't.

If you're using a difference-in-differences design, excluding observations can change what you're measuring, particularly if the exclusions differ between treatment and control groups or over time. Without trimming those observations, the estimated effect drops from 0.0087 SD to 0.0058 SD (and is no longer statistically significant).

The authors preregistered their study, but there's nothing in the report indicating that the trimming of 'extreme' values was part of that preregistration...

↳↳ reply — oofbey:

Sounds like they noticed a few extreme outliers were pulling the difference down and hacked it out. Methodologically that’s really sus to do this after the study is done. But generally I think it’s okay to exclude extreme outliers - we generally assume Gaussian distributions, but the real world happens and messes things up. Having a few kids that are 5 or 6 sigma out pulling your averages - I can believe the rules are different for them. But this should have been decided ahead of time.

↳↳↳ reply — rahimnathwani:

I emailed the authors and received a reply. That part of the study was not preregistered.

My message to them:

  Dear Dr. Burland and Professor Kane,
  I was reading your November 2026 report, Phone-Free Schools and Achievement Growth, and saw that the study was preregistered on the Open Science Framework. I haven’t been able to locate the registration.
  Could you please share a link to the preregistration or let me know where I can find it? I’m particularly interested in checking whether the exclusion of extreme fall-to-spring score changes was specified in the original analysis plan.
  Thank you for your time and for making the research available.
  Best regards
Their reply:

  Rahim:  That part of the study was not pre-registered.   We have used the NWEA data from earlier years, but had not encountered such extreme outliers.  The magnitude of gains or losses we dropped were clearly errors—multiple standard deviation gains in a single year, also inconsistent with the midyear measurement.   I’m ccing our colleague, Samantha Cullum, who can provide the link to the pre-registration.   Tom Kane

↳ reply 2 — seizethecheese:

Contrast that with all the anecdotes in this thread from parents about how great banning phones is, I'm left with two possible conclusions:

- Trust the anecdotes and this effect can't be fully captured by the study

- Trust the study and assume the parents are projecting their desire for banning phones to be a good thing.

I'm leaning towards #2, since I also have a strong desire to ban phones around my kids (they're 3 and 1(x2) so yes, around them not for them). I'd personally be really prone to confirmation bias myself around phone bans.

Top #3 — vezycash:

Everyone in the US knew phones were destroying attention spans years ago, but educational bodies and school boards punted the burden down to individual schools, teachers, and parents. Of course it failed: no single teacher or parent wants to be the bad guy and face social friction.

China just banned them outright. It's the same with companies - weak committee vs. a founder who just makes the hard call.

↳ reply 1 — japhyr:

Absolutely. I was a high school teacher in the 2010s, and it was such a hard aspect of teaching to navigate.

For any reasonable phone policy to be implemented well, it has to come from the highest level of administration. It has to be enforced consistently across all levels from the district/principals down to individual classroom teachers. That requires a lot of people to understand the issue well, come to agreement, and be capable of enforcing difficult policies.

There are so many factors that make it difficult for this to happen. Parents who disagree with policies, often for valid reasons. Staff turnover makes consistency difficult. If one teacher lets students use phones, it makes it harder for everyone around them to manage the policy effectively. If groups of teachers don't adhere, it gets even harder.

This is no different than the impact of AirBnB on housing availability, especially in tourist destination towns. Tech companies create a situation that's really hard to manage, and then leave it to individuals and small organizations to manage something that really needs to be figured out at a societal level.

↳ reply 2 — tootie:

It's really not obvious and genuinely feels like moral panic to me. The data here are so weak for something that is supposedly so harmful. It doesn't stand up to scrutiny. I don't think phone bans are worth the cost of the pouches. In some small ways it's actually hurting kids. They used to take pictures of the board or check google classroom assignments and now they can't. Mine are more likely to miss assignments now than before the ban and I don't see any change whatsoever in kids behavior.

item.title: If an App Asks for Full Disk Access or System and App Protection Override
item.description: 237 points, 121 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (support.apple.com)

→ HN comments  ·  237 points  ·  121 comments  ·  comments as of 19h

Top #1 — gbdubs:

This is a very poorly conceived API. If developers' use cases don't fit cleanly into Apple's (narrow) idea about how a hypothetical app should work, developers will continue to feel like they need to request these expansive permissions. A good filesystem permission API could include any of these which would make users WAY safer and enable developers to request far smaller scopes:

- Allow the developer to specify the common location(s) that they need access to. Rather than having to have the user select the folder they want to grant access to, have the developer say "this app uses data in these 5 folders, do you want to grant that access" - so much clearer, and useful in cases where an app has to integrate with other apps through the filesystem. - Readonly access. Allow an app to read your files but prevent writes or deletes. - Time limited access. Allow some kind of access and allow the user to auto-expire it rather than having to remember it exists. - Allow for negative access (i.e. allow labels or tags on directories to mark them as sensitive and prevent access by default - browsers could do this for their cookie stores, `~/.ssh` could ship with it as a default, etc.)

Apple could have used this opportunity to think through the question of "why do developers ask for filesystem access, and how can we allow legitimate usage through well scoped access controls", but instead they built a bad API that will (I would guess) not actually allow developers to be more judicious or achieve any of the user-safety benefits.

Apple needs to learn to talk to (and listen to) developers.

↳ reply 1 — geocar:

> This is a very poorly conceived API.

However users are very happy with it.

> developers will continue to feel like they need to request these expansive permissions

And users will continue to seek alternatives, or risk denying said permission.

I don't use any apps that require this permission, and would never use any app that required this permission without an extremely good explanation of why it was needed.

Until that happens, no.

> Allow the developer to specify the common location(s) that they need access to.

Why not just back up: How does the developer know the location. What's common about it?

I'm so not sure they need access to anything yet.

I use Spotify, Slack, Zoom, and WhatsApp: All of them have asked for it, but they all seem to work fine if I deny them access to full-disk access. So I am confident your issue is a non-issue for me and millions of people like me.

I don't have any apps that need this, so I do not want you to blow past this so quickly with the prior that just because you are a developer who has a use case that requires this, it is still my computer and you don't get any time on it while you're asking for this.

> Readonly access. Allow an app to read your files but prevent writes or deletes

Again: Absolutely not. There are no files I want your app to have access to without an explanation.

> Allow for negative access (i.e. allow labels or tags on directories to mark them as sensitive and prevent access by default - browsers could do this for their cookie stores, `~/.ssh` could ship with it as a default, etc.)

I know Linux works this way, and it only ever works for stuff that the integrator ships (i.e. on Red Hat, they are called seLinux labels), so it's not something that independent publishers have ever done, and to my knowledge, despite it being so easy, not one independent developer has ever used them in the way you say, despite such a thing being possible for more than 25 years.

> Apple needs to learn to talk to (and listen to) developers.

That sounds like your opinion. I think developers need to explain better what they actually want and why.

You have what you ask for on other platforms, so I think if your ideas were so right you would have simply ignored Apple, so I think Apple doesn't need to do shit for you, and you have some explaining to do.

↳↳ reply — dvdkon:

All the apps you listed probably work the same on your Mac as they do on an iPhone. If that's the kind of software you're using, then it makes sense you're happy with macOS' current permissions.

MacOS is also used by power users, though. The kind of people who were drawn to it being a user-friendly UNIX and then stayed. I think it's reasonable for them to ask for a more granular permission system that actually supports their usecases.

↳↳↳ reply — smilespray:

Sure, and power users can grant access.

Regular users need a way of giving informed consent.

The existing system reminds me of Windows; poorly dialogs designed without any thought for regular users whatsoever, which causes everybody to grant access to everything, as a knee jerk response.

↳ reply 2 — simondotau:

Developers are important, but Apple understands that it must ultimately prioritise non-technical end users as their highest priority. Apple's approach puts control in users' hands rather than allowing developers to define the scope of access. Moving from Full Disk Access to user-selected folders is a significant security improvement, even if the API doesn't accommodate every developer use case.

It's also critical to recognise that data exfiltration is just as serious a risk as data manipulation. Read-only access doesn't prevent data theft, and time-limited access can't undo it.

↳ reply 3 — comex:

Apple tried the first thing first. That was App Sandbox, and you can grant access to specific folders through the open dialog (or better yet, use the open/save dialog to access individual files so that no broad permissions are needed at all). But nobody adopted App Sandbox unless forced to.

Negative access is what came next, applied to all apps. By default, an unsandboxed program can access everything except specific protected directories, and can request access to those directories too, e.g. Documents, Desktop, Photos, other apps' data.

Full Disk Access is the last resort that turns all of that off. Or, well, was.

It's also the only way to access Messages, which might be why certain AI apps request it.

Top #2 — vbezhenar:

For me more important would be to exclude specific folders from that full disk access (like ~/.ssh), rather than selecting one directory.

For example I've used Daisy Disk app to visualize directory size. It's best used with full disk access. But I know that my `.ssh` is tiny and I'd prefer for this app not to be able to access it at all.

↳ reply 1 — hosteur:

Yeah. And being able to see that a file exists and its metadata like size, modified date, etc. should be possible to grant without granting access to reading the contents of files let alone writing files.

↳ reply 2 — eviks:

What "you'd prefer" is for that app to have full access to metadata instead of the current dumb system that's not granular enough to block reading secrets

Top #3 — kinabalu76:

I think Apple is being smart here and people are blowing this way out of proportion for views. The truth is that we've seen people who know how to run secops get hacked, so putting controls to ensure we scare the shit out of people who think giving claude access to their entire disk is no big deal is a great idea.

item.title: Running coding agents without handing them my credentials
item.description: 126 points, 110 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (blog.antonio.cx)

→ HN comments  ·  126 points  ·  110 comments

Top #1 — saagarjha:

I just don’t think I agree with these designs at all. Everyone seems to be super laser focused on “not allowing their AI to have keys” when basically giving their AI direct access to what the keys enable, optionally adding a layer of ceremony in front where you tap “approve”. I’m looking at the alert that is shown there and I don’t see anything that makes me feel like it allows for an informed choice at the time of it popping up. So then, what’s the benefit?

↳ reply 1 — fractorial:

As much as I wanted to say you’re wrong, you’re right. After reading TFA, the security boundary is not sound.

Wanting agents to act like you is wrong. You need to own that trust boundary. Build whatever tooling satisfies the contract that agents should have a “not”+<you> (or <you>+”-agent”) identity, and you actuate across that boundary explicitly.

For example, I have a second agent GitHub account that points at my human one. That allows me to write a trusted proxy that ACLs its identity tightly.

It cannot write to public repos ever. In the worst possible case, it externalizes to a private repo’s issue tracker. (Still has never happened in ~4 months)

Once you have this, you can let agents run free. But, it isn’t trivial to set up. Moreover, people don’t want to “do the work.”

All this assumes you abide by “never run untrusted agents on trusted hardware.”

↳↳ reply — thayne:

I would certainly prefer having separate credentials with permissions limited to what I want to allow the agent to do. However I have run into two problems with that.

The first, and bigger, issue is that some services either don't have have suffiently fine control over permissions, so in order to grant permission to do useful things, I also have to allow it to do dangerous things, or I don't have a way to create a more limited access token at all. I wish that it was more common to allow creating short-lived, limited accces personal access tokens for services.

The smaller issue is that sometimes I do want the agent to do something more risky with my approval, and provide me with sufficient context to make an informed decision. That can sort of be worked around though by telling it to just give me the command to run, then I can audit and run it myself.

↳↳↳ reply — tsergiu:

This is exactly what https://keycontain.com is for! It wraps services to give ultra-fine-grained ACLs. They can be arbitrarily granular, and much more granular than the underlying API.

↳ reply 2 — binsquare:

Basically these designs are meant to protect the key from leaking i.e. if agent holds key, prompt injections can happen.

If agent never holds the key, then the risk profile changes.

But you're right that it's a different problem to what access the key has and that's a different problem usually solved by having narrower keys or etc.

disclaimer: I work on smolvm which does this at the networking layer and argued with myself on this too.

↳ reply 3 — recursivedoubts:

I'm trying to address this w/ clank.talk: a self-discoverable scripting language for agents that replaces bash with a controlled sandbox environment and strives to be easy for humans to read:

https://clank.talk

I'm designing this for the student AI infrastructure here at Montana State, to avoid rolling out the current wild-west of local agents to our student body.

Top #2 — ryanczak:

Docker sandboxes support secret injection. https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/sbx/secret/set/

↳ reply 1 — adverbly:

From https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/sbx/secret/set-custom/

> Custom secrets work via a placeholder: the sandbox sees the placeholder value instead of the real secret. When the sandbox makes an outbound request to the target host, the proxy replaces the placeholder with the real secret in the request headers — the secret never enters the sandbox directly.

↳ reply 2 — zmmmmm:

exactly, i don't know why everyone is ignoring this. It's the obvious solution to at least 80% of what most posters here are complaining about and comes built in already in multiple existing solutions.

Top #3 — __MatrixMan__:

My solution to this is two laptops. No SSH between them, just a custom http API. Agents can run amok on the laptop without the secrets, but if they want to act as me, they have to use the API. If they need to do something not already in the API, they can add commits to the server, but I'm going to review those before I deploy that server on the laptop with the keys. This way I don't have to rely on the downstream services to have sufficiently granular permissions.

I guess I could do the same thing with VM's, but for reasons I can't fully explain it's just easier to stay vigilant with separate hardware.
