item.title: Why 3dfx 1 cards had such a washed out color output?
item.description: 275 points, 102 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (twitter.com)

→ HN comments  ·  275 points  ·  102 comments  ·  comments as of 21h

Top #1 — AkBKukU:

I have two alternate observations, because VGA is an analog signal there are standards for what the voltages should be. But they were not always followed. Keep in mind that the first two Voodoo cards were also video switchers with a chip to output either the 2D passthrough or the internally generated 3D chip signal created by its own GENDAC.

1. I have a Voodoo 2 paired with an S3 Virge/DX, the Voodoo 2 output level is lower. On a CRT I always have to make the image brighter when running a 3DFX game. Additionally, the V-Sync pulse is not the same as the Virge/DX and the Voodoo 2 image is shifted up.

2. I have a Voodoo Rush which is the maligned hybrid model of 2D and 3D chipsets on a single card. It still uses the internal switching though. On this card the voltage issues are the opposite, the 2D output is significantly dimmer than the 3D which makes the 3D game clip badly when running something until the image is adjusted again.

These problems are voltage level issues with the signal, not gamma. Adjusting gamma will not change the black or white voltage level of the signal. But a lower voltage signal may seem brighter as gamma is raised and the dynamic range is compressed.

> we were so enthralled by the absolute performance of 3DFX that the color fidelity didn’t get as much attention as it should have.

I would say it's more likely that they just didn't notice and the varying outputs from different 3DFX cards, with different GENDAC's, on differently calibrated CRTs just made it a total mess to try and and dial in something as imperceptible as a gamma level. Also keep in mind that around 1995-1996 adjusting the brightness of a CRT was as easy as twisting a few knobs on the front of it.

↳ reply — seritools:

the S3 Trio3D/Virge also have a raised the black level, which can be turned off with a VBIOS patch: https://bitsundbolts.com/2026/04/23/fixing-the-s3-brightness...

or some register poking after startup, e.g. https://github.com/RetroLoom/S3ctl

Top #2 — hmstx:

One other aspect of 3dfx looking a bit washed out beyond the gamma problem is the trickery performed in the RAMDAC before it blasted those cool pixels to the VGA port.

If you remember, 3dfx screenshots were just as dithered as, say, an ATI Rage, but on screen it looked smoother (although a bit blurry) while the others looked visibly dithered still (see some 3dfx screenshots https://www.vogons.org/viewtopic.php?f=46&t=36548 )

Part of it is the gamma shenanigans mentioned, and also the blur filtering pass taking place in the DAC which "upgrades" the image (eventually claimed to be so-called 22 bit precision for Voodoo3), introducing some quite visible smudging and hints of unexpected colors as a result.

This has been approximated in shaders you can apply to most games with ReShade etc., take a look (https://www.vogons.org/viewtopic.php?t=36470)

Top #3 — herodoturtle:

It's pretty cool that someone can ask an interesting graphics-related question, and John Carmack of all people steps in to answer it. And then even Eric S. Raymond adds a comment further below.

↳ reply 1 — Sharlin:

Yeah, Carmack isn’t super surprising especially as it’s Sanglard who’s asking, but ESR I haven’t really spotted anywhere in a long while. Just some time ago I was thinking that he’s probably a nobody to a lot of the younger folk, or at the very least known only for some of his more terrible political opinions.

↳ reply 2 — parasti:

Fabien Sanglard isn't just someone.

item.title: Optimizely compromised, served malware on Zoom, GitLab
item.description: 651 points, 257 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (blog.report-uri.com)

→ HN comments  ·  651 points  ·  257 comments  ·  comments as of 22h

Top #1 — stickfigure:

The whole concept of Google Tag Manager was that you could give marketing departments the ability to add "tags" to the website without having to involve engineering. That's how we got 10MB of javascript with every news article.

I hope folks are re-evaluating that now.

↳ reply 1 — CM30:

Client side A/B testing through services like Optimizely and VWO and Adobe Target is a massive security nightmare in of itself. You're giving anyone with access to a third party service the ability to run any code they like on your website, and change any and all interface elements as they see fit.

Even one of these accounts being compromised would be a massive security incident that would potentially put millions of people's data at risk.

↳↳ reply — MontgomeryPy:

Just pointing out that these testing solutions can also be deployed server-side instead of via client-side tags. I suspect that is the route a lot of their customers will take now.

↳↳↳ reply — mankins:

And even at the edge via things like edge side includes or their modern worker versions.

↳ reply 2 — goalieca:

It also makes adding csp a nightmare. Your marketing department is putting in 30 trackers, changing monthly. And then there’s different countries for end clients with different TLDs for connect-src. You can’t possibly get anything locked down enough. That’s bad for security when you rely on csp for mitigating other factors.

↳ reply 3 — jeswin:

> I hope folks are re-evaluating that now.

Not going to happen. Most decisions in tech do not factor in risk, only cost. Risk mitigation usually requires considerable spend, and very few people/companies are willing to spend on low-probability events.

Top #2 — mcoliver:

This stuff is so avoidable but unless we implement meaningful reprocussions things aren't going to change. There is no accountability.

In this case optimizely should have had better systems to spot a release like this (internal cool downs, check and balances, phased rolouts, automatic security checks). And sites that have massive user bases (cnn, bbc, etc..) have zero excuse to not have the same.

I would go so far as to say those sites should not be serving from vendors but should be vendoring their own scripts that they also are passing through security audits and serving them selves with cool downs.

How do these companies not have better dedication to protecting their users is beyond me.

↳ reply 1 — noir_lord:

> How do these companies not have better dedication to protecting their users is beyond me.

It doesn't cost them anything but a "whoops" post when they fuck up, so the incentive is misaligned (as you noted under repercussions).

The cost is externalised onto everyone else not them so it's not going to change.

↳↳ reply — geetee:

This is the only answer

↳ reply 2 — Havoc:

Accountability is incompatible with tech sector as it currently exists. The entire ethos of move fast and break things is incompatible with it never mind the shady adtech part of the sector.

Top #3 — ano-ther:

Maybe I overlooked it, but is this something persistent that I should take care of on my phone and computer or was it confined to a browser session?

And would uBlock origin have prevented it?

↳ reply 1 — Groxx:

Somewhat anyway. It's on the BadBlock lists, which are kinda common: https://github.com/celenityy/BadBlock/blob/ab58b46ad48893c91...

For anyone unaware, this also works on Firefox on Android, as it has support for almost all extensions.

↳ reply 2 — _ks3e:

Based on a brief skim: not persistent on computers, persistent on phones for certain old iOS versions (18 and below, 26 would only be fingerprinted).

Some ublock lists (e.g. Peter Lowe's server list) block everything from optimizely.com, so if you enabled those you're good.

item.title: Windows 11 is collecting data on which coding agents and developer tools you use
item.description: 702 points, 580 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (xusheng.dev)

→ HN comments  ·  702 points  ·  580 comments  ·  comments as of 22h

Top #1 — s_dev:

Just as AI has advanced massively in the past two years, I think a lot of gamers would be shocked at how viable Linux is as a genuine gaming platform in 2026. I already have plans to switch from Windows to Linux, I even have Linux running from an external drive to play with it.

The vast vast majority of single player games are 100% perfect on Linux. Multiplayer still has lots of hiccups.

↳ reply 1 — SOLAR_FIELDS:

Praise Gabe. No seriously, you would not be saying this in 2026 had it not been for a singular person named Gabe Newell. Valve’s Proton initiative almost single handedly brought us this. I don’t use Steam, or really any Valve products or games, just as some observing third party it’s really hard to say that this would have happened had Valve not done the whole Proton thing

↳↳ reply — Gigachad:

Before Valve gaming on Linux was limited to Super Tux Kart and a small number of ported games. Once steam came to Linux around 2013 you had a selection of indie games mostly Unity stuff that could export to Linux for free. But still almost all major games did not work.

Proton was the turning point where you went from specifically looking for Linux games to just assuming everything works.

↳↳↳ reply — Scaevolus:

Wine existed long before Valve poured money into it. It was nowhere near as reliable before DXVK existed, but you could play many commercial Windows games well-- you just couldn't expect nearly universal support.

↳ reply 2 — eastof:

I'm an avid gamer, fully made he switch earlier this year to CachyOS. Dota 2 is my main game, I get better FPS on Linux than I ever did on Windows. I play other games like PEAK, Risk of Rain 2, and Enshrouded no problem with my friends. I have been enjoying STALKER 2 on Linux as well, runs just fine.

The biggest barrier is kernel anti cheat, so no Call of Duty, Battlefield, etc. Luckily my friends don't play those AAA multiplayer games, protondb is a good resource to check which games can't run due to their anti cheat.

↳ reply 3 — accrual:

Yes, I switched to Fedora in January and have been playing all sorts of games on an RTX 4080 via Steam, Heroic Games (Epic Games alternative launcher), Modrinth, emulators, etc. The only one I haven't tried is GTA V: Online as I've read it's not compatible due to anti-cheat.

Claude Code/Codex is very helpful for overcoming any transitions hurdles - pop open a shell, describe the problem, and a few moments later it's fixed up. I recommend maintaining a doc as one gets the new system setup so it can be easily reproduced and referenced later. Anytime I change a setting or install an app I find useful, it goes in the doc.

Top #2 — dannyw:

So does Intel, AMD, and NVIDIA drivers; they collect what executable name and paths you run; unless you opt out.

Most Chrome configs end up persisting full browser history and clickstreams inside a Google account.

If you use Debian and opt-in to popularity contest; it may collect and send similar info depending on how you installed these coding agents.

↳ reply 1 — graemep:

The Debian example is not comparable. Its opt in, verifiably anonymous, its only their own packagers.

↳ reply 2 — Cthulhu_:

This one seems to specifically target coding agents, but then, I'm sure they did targeted metrics gathering of specific categories of apps for years so I'm sure this is a nothingburger.

Top #3 — ashton314:

I've been a heavy macOS user for dev work since early adolescence. Before that I used FreeBSD, so I'm comfortable with the command line. (Yes, you read that right.) But it's been a while since I used anything other than macOS for serious development work. A lot of the shenanigans around macOS Tahoe made me seriously consider switching to Linux. Last month I finally got the gumption and set up a Linux desktop how I like it.

I see no reason why any developer, other than someone writing something for the Windows platform specifically, should not be using Linux over Windows. MacOS has a ton of polish in so many places—but then there are all these little paper cuts that keep coming: funny little bugs that interrupt work or make you scratch your head. Peeking over the garden wall into Windows' garden only seems worse. Linux by comparison is awesome! I look forward to spending my day on my Linux desktop.

Seriously, if you do dev work, do yourself a favor and boot up—I dunno, maybe Fedora Silverblue—on a separate partition and force yourself to work on it for a day or two. Use an LLM to diagnose issues as they come up. (I had some serious stability issues; Claude suggested it was a memory issue; running memtest86 told me I had bad RAM—fixing that and all problems went away.) You'll find that your system is quieter and less distracting.

I still don't think Linux is for "average users"—even though most people probably only need a web browser. But if you have gone anywhere near a command line in your life, it will be worth the switch.

↳ reply 1 — benrutter:

> I see no reason why any developer, other than someone writing something for the Windows platform specifically, should not be using Linux over Windows.

I agree, but I think there's a big reason they do use windows. A lot of companies choose Windows for corporate IT. That's a decent enough choice if most of your company are non-devs working in email, excel and word etc.

In a big company, that often leaves developer using windows.

That's been the story whenever I've had to use windows professionally in the past anyway.

↳ reply 2 — alerighi:

> I still don't think Linux is for "average users"—even though most people probably only need a web browser. But if you have gone anywhere near a command line in your life, it will be worth the switch.

There are Linux distros like Ubuntu that are far simpler to use for the average user than Windows, especially nowadays that the average user is used to smartphones, where you go to a store and install an app with one click.

Windows is much more complex to use to me, I've installed Ubuntu to a lot of average users and the feedback they gave me was always that it was so simple to use compared to Windows, install programs with one click (yes, now Microsoft has its store but for most software you still need to go on the internet, download the installer, answer questions the average user has no clue what to respond, and hope to have downloaded the official installer and not a virus), there are no automatic updates that start without your consempt that will break your PC (you don't know how many people computer break after a Windows update), there are no viruses, no need to create an account just to be able to start using your computer, usually the stuff you connect (e.g. printers) doesn't require you to install a dedicated driver, and you can keep using your 15 years old PC just fine, no need to buy a new hardware every 4 or so years because Windows 11 needs 16Gb of RAM just to boot.

Unless you have the need to use particular proprietary software (which most user don't, since nowadays practically everything is web based and 99% of the stuff they use is the browser) there is no sense in using Windows.

item.title: Spamhaus new email sender requirements in November
item.description: 141 points, 139 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (spamhaus.org)

→ HN comments  ·  141 points  ·  139 comments

Top #1 — BLKNSLVR:

> Publish forward-confirmed reverse DNS for every sending IP

> Every sending IP must have a reverse DNS entry pointing to a fully qualified domain name (FQDN). That hostname must, in turn, resolve back to the same sending IP address. This is known as forward-confirmed reverse DNS (FCrDNS). An IP with missing or mismatched reverse DNS is treated as suspicious and is one of the most common reasons for an IP to be considered for listing.

I self-host an email server behind my ISPs connection, and so I do not own the IP address that I send mail from, therefore I can't satisfy the reverse DNS requirement.

↳ reply 1 — elric:

It's a stupid policy that will lead to many false positives among small installations, while having zero impact on actual spammers.

A lot of modern spam policing is just protectionism of a duopoly masking as security theatre.

↳↳ reply — seb1204:

Agree, Like airport security theater.

↳ reply 2 — rafram:

I’m surprised your emails have ever gotten through if they’re coming from a residential IP. That’s definitely not considered good practice.

↳ reply 3 — kbenson:

Which is exactly where a lot of spam comes from, exploited systems that don't have correct reverse DNS. The checks are stringent because to allow exceptions is to allow people to abuse those exceptions.

FWIW you could probably get yourself a $5 VPS to use as the public portion of your mail setup that just forwards to your local mail server, which can in turn smart host through that VPS, and you'll have most the same features but with a dedicated IP that you can control both forward and reverse DNS through (depending on provider).

Depending on your ISP they may also allow for options for setting reverse DNS depending on your service. It's a bit niche these days unless you're paying for a business class service, but it really does depend on the ISP, as some offer it fairly cheap and some don't (independent ISPs may be more likely).

Top #2 — albertgoeswoof:

These techniques rely on it being hard (or at least long winded) to setup a domain and server properly, such that spammers (who are self selected to be lazy) won’t do it right and give up quickly.

But with AI, it’s easy to get DKIM, DMARC, HELO etc. set up perfectly for almost no effort (maybe fcrdns is a bit more complex as it’s a manual process at most ISPs)

I think we are in the end going to go back to it just being based on IP (v4) reputation, and this is all theatre.

↳ reply 1 — 2000UltraDeluxe:

DMARC, DKIM and SPF are not hard to deal with. HELO/PTR is considered basics.

If you need an AI to set these things up for you then you shold honestly consider having someone else run your email for you. Most hosters handle things like authentication out of the box.

↳ reply 2 — 0x1ch:

Even before AI, was DKIM and DMARC hard to setup? It's been a streamlined process for at least four years now (as long as I've had to professionally enter records in a registrar), and even longer before that in my homelab setups.

Top #3 — computer23:

Anyone else having their email blocked by Microsoft and Spamhaus?

Microsoft Office 365 relies on Spamhaus and was blocking my email because the HELO on the mail server was mydomain.com instead of mailserver.mydomain.com.

Once the problem was fixed, it took time for Spamhaus to re-scan the mail server and take the mail server off the block list. And it took more time for Microsoft to stop blocking mail.

https://check.spamhaus.org/

↳ reply — Sebguer:

Make sure to register on their SNDS and you might be able to find the issue? https://substrate.office.com/ip-domain-management-snds/snds

You can also reach out to sender support through the same, and they are ~reasonably responsive (though very clearly outsourced / limited power). If it's a lingering MS block they should be able to override it. I've had luck in the past (though this was on behalf of a notable tech company, I don't know that the support people cared at all about that fact).

↳↳ reply — dclaw:

SNDS is a complete joke. 2-3 times a year some or all of one of my subnets gets blocked by MS email services, outlook, hotmail, etc... SNDS never shows a single issue with any of verified subnets. It takes on average 1-2 weeks playing email tag with their support (who tell us to sign up for SNDS!) and them refusing to provide any evidence, before it magically just works again. It's happened so many times now I've begun to just not bother, and usually it still resolves itself. Meaning the support ticket is basically doing nothing. :-(

item.title: OpenCode Browse
item.description: 323 points, 208 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (opencode.ai)

→ HN comments  ·  323 points  ·  208 comments  ·  comments as of 24h

Top #1 — eatfish:

I keep asking my own agents if prompt injection is a solved problem. By and large the answer seems to be ‘no, anything a model sees can be used to steer it and enters the context’.

I know you can forward raw output through subagents to summarize content and mitigate the risk - but most projects don’t do that.

↳ reply 1 — christkv:

Yeah I'm a big fan of the Playwright MCP server I use it a ton.

↳ reply 2 — cyanydeez:

I implemented this hard forking paseo.

It's deferent; with a plugin in firefox, edge, chrome, chromium; I can bring an agent into it. Secure contexts like outlook I can have the agent scroll through my messages.

Playwright won't (safely) get you these things.

Top #3 — SillyUsername:

MCP servers to me seems like a dead man walking technology and I don't understand the point of it.

It adds security but...

- adds a single service which is another attack surface that can be compromised.

- adds another system that requires maintenance and securing to prevent compromise.

- takes machine resources

- duplicates a subset of what can easily be harness functionality

- duplicates services and security (usually) of existing APIs, or adds another layer on top.

Whereas ultimately an AI harness

- will improve and optimise its own skills performing the same MCP functions

- can use plugins

- can have harness centralised (common) security controls and behaviours

MCP becomes a false economy for our current AI implementations, it's real purpose seems to be a crutch for small models that struggle to write their own skills that use existing APIs. The thing is this is a problem that is rapidly disappearing, but could also be performed by secured harness plugins.

↳ reply 1 — mickeyp:

Harness developer here.

I am going to push back on this a bit as someone who also has scepticism (bloated spec, concepts deprecated already, etc.) but ultimately think it solves a few gnarly problems whilst admittedly -- it's early days -- creating a few more.

The first argument in favour of MCP is that large enterprises like it. It's a controlled surface to give access to things that may never have had an API before. Yeah, OK, that feels like a "loser takes all" moment but it does at least give you access to something you did not have before.

It also resolves a problem: monolithic apps without a CLI/server infrastructure can now expose a simple MCP endpoint and immediately get it to work locally with their own agents. That has value too.

The second is that it tries to solve thorny things like letting the server ask for information by way of a form-like construct. That is actually quite handy for servers that do asynchronous or slow work, and that may require feedback from you over time. Doing this with start-stopping a tool harness can also work, but it's fiddly because a context compaction event can happen which might lose state; not all harnesses handle this well; LLMs may get confused; etc.

Finally you can inject, in a good harness anyway, some or all of these tools into your system so they become part of the fabric. You can build your own little cut-down surface area so by removing shell access you let your AI call Foo and Bar MCP calls and nothing else. That also is useful.

But yes: you're right fundamentally. It's SOAP/RPC all over again, and CLI+skill should be the default for your own tooling if you can get away with it.

↳ reply 2 — jgilias:

You forgot the main one:

- they necessarily work through the context window and therefore don’t compose;

Meaning, if your agent has a skill that needs to run five MCP tools in a certain way, it can’t just script that away the first time it sees this, and have that flow be fast and token efficient from then on.

MCPs are a 2025 tech meant to solve 2025 AI problems.

item.title: Comcast's "fiber-powered Wi-Fi" is cable, AT&T says in false advertising case
item.description: 164 points, 144 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (arstechnica.com)

→ HN comments  ·  164 points  ·  144 comments

Top #1 — bob1029:

Fiber is so much better than cable in an emergency. The equipment consumes significantly less power and is likely to stay up longer during a power outage. You get way more customers on each battery / generator.

I had an FTTH provider with 100% of their network on natural gas standby generators. Went through a week long power outage without losing a single packet. You can support something like 100k households with well under 50kW of power. There are homes with larger generators than this. Docsis 4 would put you somewhere around half a megawatt.

↳ reply 1 — dmurray:

> You can support something like 100k households with well under 50kW of power. There are homes with larger generators than this.

There are what? I can't imagine what a single-family home would do with 50kW of power.

↳↳ reply — DannyBee:

I have a large woodworking and metalworking shop behind my single family home.

I have a transformer that serves only my shop :)

I use 800 amps of single phase inverted into 200 amps of 480v 3 phase (the rest of the single phase is for the house and apartment above the shop)

I have 200kwh of battery as well.

This is definitely on the extreme side, but most woodworkers (and metalworkers) i know use 50kw total easily within their single family home garages. Once you get past portable tools, they really don't make tools with less than a 5hp motor because it would be more expensive and annoying.

↳ reply 2 — delta_p_delta_x:

> You can support something like 100k households with well under 50kW of power

I feel like there's something wrong here; you're three orders of magnitude off. Many typical household appliances easily cross multiple kilowatts. For some scale: running a kettle, a washing machine at max temperature, a dishwasher, a microwave, a high-end gaming PC, and a conventional oven, all simultaneously, approaches a power draw of about 25 kW.

Top #2 — userbinator:

While Comcast has deployed plenty of fiber throughout the US, its cable Internet service makes the final connection to homes with coaxial cable. This results in upload speeds being far slower than download speeds. In contrast, fiber-to-the-home service can provide symmetrical upload and download speeds.

You can get symmetric DOCSIS, and apparently Comcast do offer that service[1]. Likewise, FTTH can be asymmetric if they set the traffic shaping that way. IMHO the only things that matter to the average user about an Internet connection are bandwidth, volume, and availability. As long as it terminates in WiFi or a standard Ethernet connector and passes IP traffic at the rate I paid for, I personally don't care what the physical infrastructure beyond the demarc is.

In fact, anecdotes from a few people I know have been that service interruptions actually increased after they upgraded to FTTH from DOCSIS.

[1] https://corporate.comcast.com/press/releases/comcast-multi-g...

↳ reply 1 — tialaramex:

Service. What I most value from my service provider is that I can get answers from them without being treated like a baby.

Last time I called my ISP (last year? the year before? I don't remember) I was wondering when I would get service back. The street had exploded, underground power cable threw a tantrum and tore a big hole in the road, the grid company come out and fixed that but then of course my Internet didn't come back once the lights did.

The person who answered my call:

+ Did not waste my time asking that I restart laptops, routers, etc. the diagnostic lights on the router indicate No signal => not a problem I can fix by rebooting things.

+ Without needing me to re-specify where I live went straight to the identified problem (DSLAM offline) and to the fault report (to last mile provider for a failed DSLAM) and told me that in their experience I should expect a fix on Sunday (it was Friday evening). Which is what happened.

↳ reply 2 — RulerOf:

> As long as it terminates in WiFi or a standard Ethernet connector and passes IP traffic at the rate I paid for, I personally don't care what the physical infrastructure beyond the demarc is.

I get that attitude, but coax connections are fragile in a way that fiber is not. Water infiltration, bad crimping jobs, unterminated ends in the neighbor's house all cause signal degradation that is extremely time and labor intensive to identify and fix.

Cable is an excellent solution for distributing broadcast analog radio signals over a private line cheaply and efficiently, but two-way digital signals over the same medium aren't as robust as their fiber-based counterpart.

ISP outages are one thing, but if you ever experience service degradation—and not a full outage, but tear-your-hair-out crap like "my internet goes down for 15 seconds once every 16 hours with no discernible pattern"—and it ends up being some particularly coax-flavored problem, you'll understand what I'm talking about.

Top #3 — ben1040:

Back in the days of rolling out U-Verse (their FTTN service), AT&T's advertising used exactly the same strategy of weasel-words to say "fiber" without making an actionable implication that it was fiber from A to Z. Phrases like "fiber rich network" and "U-Verse uses fiber optic technology."

↳ reply 1 — bearjaws:

I came here to say the same thing, I remember getting an ad for "U-Verse" and being like "omg fiber???" and then did their online check to see that it was basically DSL.

↳ reply 2 — soupfordummies:

Just a few years ago during the industry-wide upgrades to 5G, AT&T branded their 4G service as "5G E (5G Evolution)"

They are terribly slimy.

item.title: Rust changed me as a developer
item.description: 269 points, 170 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (blog.startifact.com)

→ HN comments  ·  269 points  ·  170 comments

Top #1 — bryanlarsen:

A standard piece of advice is that every developer should do a major project in every big language family. A Lisp, an OO language, a functional language, Prolog, VHDL or Verilog, a Forth, et cetera. They'll all make you think differently and teach you lessons you will use outside of the family.

↳ reply 1 — nomel:

> Verilog

My favorite side quest that I definitely recommend. Physical parallelism is so fun to reason about.

I had the advantage of sitting next to a proper professional to bounces questions off of, so I was able to get an SPDIF decoder to work in about a week! It was a very interesting lesson in the costs of abstraction, and why you will never really find abstraction layers in hardware.

↳↳ reply — pastel8739:

> why you will never really find abstraction layers in hardware

This is interesting to me, in the very little HDL I’ve done there were abstractions: you set up modules with inputs and outputs that provided a consistent interface despite complexity inside the model. Is this not what you mean by abstraction layer?

↳ reply 2 — brightball:

100% agree with this.

Elixir was somewhere between my 12th-14th language and nothing changed my perspective so much as understanding why the BEAM works the way it does.

↳ reply 3 — ivanjermakov:

Advent of Code is coming in two weeks, I highly recommend completing 12 challenges in 12 different languages!

Top #2 — dabinat:

One of the things that I think makes Rust unique is that it acknowledges the possibility of human error. I think it’s also one of the most controversial too: there are certain people who get an ego hit at the insinuation that they ever could have written C code with mistakes.

Instead of hoping you remember to check for NULL, Rust forces you to make a decision on how to handle the possibility of failure. Sure, you can still pick a bad decision (unwrap) but that is at least a specific decision and you can’t forget to do it.

You can take it even further with things like the newtype pattern. If you have lots of numeric IDs (project ID, user ID, etc) you can give them distinct types so you don’t mix them up.

So Rust taught me I can program defensively against my own brain, which sometimes gets tired or lazy or distracted.

↳ reply 1 — PaulKeeble:

This was always the same thing that Unit tests were trying to bring, defend against your own errors and try to get the most quality out of the tools as possible. A lot of language progress has been exactly this over the years, from removing goto and introduction of for/if/while to constraining types and everything since. As an industry we could do with more of this mindset in general, just use everything we can to try and catch bugs earlier when they are cheaper to find and fix and avoid them happening at all.

↳↳ reply — bunderbunder:

I have always had a love/hate relationship with unit tests. I love them for all the obvious reasons. I hate them for all the times I read a test suite where 80% of the tests could have been eliminated by just improving the design of the system under test so that error condition wasn’t possible in the first place.

↳ reply 2 — pjmlp:

Most programming languages acknowledges the possibility of human error, even those that predate C, like Fortran, Lisp, JOVIAL, ESPOL, NEWP, ALGOL, COBOL, PL/I.

The ego hit has been mostly a C culture thingie.

Top #3 — edarchis:

I would like to suggest another improvement: stop doing first name, last name. A lot of cultures in the world don't follow that. W3 suggests using the full name and "how should we call you". You only ever address people by their full name or just for casual interactions. It leads to people asking to be called "Captain Foobuzz", but that actually becomes a security feature. If they ever get mail from you and it's calling them by what the script guessed their first name was, it'll raise their suspicion. https://www.w3.org/International/questions/qa-personal-names

↳ reply 1 — nedt:

Exactly this. Here we have a couple of people named "Fullname ." in Outlook because we can't just enter a single word name and are forced to use a dot to fill the second field.

Would have also been a much better example for the enum to have the second type being a human with just a single name instead of a cat which is stretching what a person is.

item.title: Software is breaking down at a systemic level
item.description: 375 points, 233 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (breck-mckye.com)

→ HN comments  ·  375 points  ·  233 comments  ·  comments as of 18h

Top #1 — doug_durham:

This narrative isn't consistent with reality. Cloud computing is much older than 10 years ago. We were doing production grade cloud computing over 16 years ago. The OSS revolution dates to the late 90's. The author seems to think that SWE was in a golden age 10 years ago. Sorry, but it's about the same. We have the same problems in SWE as we had 40 years ago. The scale and ambition of the problems we are solving have increased as compute capabilities have increased.

↳ reply 1 — swatcoder:

The timeline is very confused, but the arc is mostly right.

1. Consolidating internet-dependent projects to a few winning cloud vendors and a dozen winning SaaS providers, made all of those project have coincident failure points. Which is great for corporate accountability ("it's Amazon's issue, not ours!") but bad for end users ("shit, EVERYTHING is down today")

2. The movement to migrate fat local-first projects towards thin internet-dependent or server-hosted ones made almost all software share those same coincident failure paths. This was good for entrenching a subscription business model and brought some end user conveniences, but meant everything being down meant everything being down.

3. Anxious and lazy dependency-first development culture ("you could never write that as well as some github rando") meant projects now had an order of magnitude more contributors but only reviewed and owned code for a surface level, making all these projects extremely vulnerable to supply chain failures and subject to constant maintenance churn.

4. Employment and team tenure continually fell so that most projects no longer have experienced owners and instead just temporary custodians.

You can find the seeds of many those problems in the 1990's and earlier and you can even argue that some of them were inevitable (and even worthwhile) destinations for the industry as it evolved without an engineering guild to slow it down and insist on rigor or evidenced safety.

But anybody who's been around for a few decades can attest to how these risky patterns rapidly grew into norms over the past 20 years and shifted the industry from one where any given software had some idiosyncratic bugs that users could learn to work around to one where all software had lots of bugs, many of them correlated across apps, whete failures would wash through and shut down (or make vulnerable) whole industries for hours or days, with effecrively nobody in particular to hold to account for any of it.

Software has never been in a pristine "golden age", but the last 20 years built almost everything on one giant, shared house of cards that's now teetering on the brink of collapse. Better or wose, it's indisputably different than it was before.

↳↳ reply — dathinab:

> Anxious and lazy dependency-first development culture

I think this is the completely wrong takeaway.

Ober the last ~15 years I have probably used around ~10 web frameworks/libraries

_not a single one was even close to being complete or mostly correct, even just for standard HTTP ~1.1 handling_!!! (The routing, path, header handling. Not any of the complex stuff in HTTP2, Quick etc.)

the problem isn't using dependencies, that is the solution (not reinventing the wheel again).

And preferring reusing solutions which are more complete, practical testet and have more resources to maintain/improve basic functionality is (in most situations) not "anxious" development, but (should be) common sense.

The amount of hidden complexity in even somewhat basic stuff like HTTP is enourmous, rewriting everything all the time is wasting billions across the industry all the time and (in general) increases the chance for bugs.

The problem isn't "using dependencies" or small dependencies, but:

- availability (or lack) of high quality well maintained dependencies

- "no one" wanting to pay for software dependencies

- misguided tendencies for 'clever' & overengineered solution in one extreme (e.g. the stuff which lead to log4shell)

- misguided obsession with deceptive simplicity in artificial examples which lead to 1001 incomplete solutions because of the obsessiv simplicity doesn't stop at cutting out over-engineering but also cuts out fundamental parts

- lack of widely adopted, effective, tooling & infrastructure to trust dependencies.

- lack of tooling to more efficient reuse and compose working parts, the way we do programming seems just very fundamental broken.

- also a lot of legacy tech we are stuck with making many things unnecessary complicated

Also as a side note, number of packages != number of entities to trust. Weather you use 10 or 1 package from the same source, maintained and published in the same way often makes little to no difference for supply chain security.

↳↳↳ reply — narnarpapadaddy:

That’s a long list of issues that go away or you gain control over if you choose not to take a dependency…

↳ reply 2 — cmiles74:

AWS is 20 years old, before that people did rent machines from places like Rackspace. Maven Central (Java) is 25 years old, RubyGems is 22 years old, CPAN (Perl) is 31.

I find the arguments about decoherence and the sort of snowball-of-complexity more compelling than this timeline.

↳ reply 3 — paldepind2:

I get the impression that when the author says "open source" they mean "rampant use of dependencies". And while the terminology is confusing and the time frame maybe not quite right, there certainly has been a shift where many projects went from depending on none or a few big reputable open source project (MySQL, Apache, Linux, etc.) into depending on hundreds of language packages made by random people.

Top #2 — CharlieDigital:

It doesn't have to be this way.

AI is great at following patterns. AI is great at writing tests. AI is great at doing work that humans would consider drudgery and then applying "enough" judgement to it.

The problem is that most software teams and most engineers are very, very bad at the thing that AI needs to succeed: technical writing. Documenting the patterns, the rules, the heuristics, the SOP, the judgement; developers could barely be bothered to write comments before (which in the AI age are free, infrastructure-less memory that is always "line-of-sight" for the agent and can be used to enrich with keywords).

It's not that AI is the problem, it's that we humans are good at resolving these constraints in the real world at a human pace. AI makes that pace impossible for a human to keep up as a trailing activity. Rather teams need to invest more in technical writing and producing the corpus that AI relies on to learn the operational constraints and rules.

↳ reply 1 — asdfman123:

I'm actually quite good at building robust systems, cleaning up messes, documenting things well.

As a result I get:

1) The enmity of my lead dev who prefers to do things more fast and loose.

2) Not promoted, due to the first reason and due to the fact that I don't have "impactful" metrics.

I'm not saying I'm perfect, there are definitely things I could have done better. But the fact still remains that the industry grossly undervalues maintenance and optimization that doesn't lead to easily measurable numbers that impact the bottom line.

That in turn is because it's hard to tell if SWEs are actually paying down critical debt or just wasting time. But that's the core problem, not that we're not good at it.

The good news is I can get AI agents to do this kind of work so I can now chase after metrics.

↳↳ reply — sushisource:

I think this thinking misses the forest for the trees a lot of the time. Assuming you're as good as you say you are at this, you need to ask how much building robust maintainable systems _actually helps the business_. The number of products where being super duper robust actually matters is probably less than you think. It can be painful as an engineer to accept, but it's often true.

I actually happen to work on a product where reliability _is_ our #1 most critical thing, and even then in certain features and certain situations it is perfectly reasonable to prefer time-to-market over quality as long as we are clear about that to our users.

So, I'd encourage you to think from a product perspective.

↳ reply 2 — cmiles74:

The urge to one-shot everything isn't helping. Getting people to push back on assumptions the model is making, and to have an actual conversation with it about the solution, would lead to more maintainable output.

Maybe part of it is laziness but for sure part of is low morale and hopelessness.

Top #3 — ljm:

Software wasn't exactly hard 12 years ago either, the barriers to entry were being lowered at a rapid pace. 2014 was the dawn of the software bootcamp where JS became more and more pronounced in web architecture.

I feel this piece is either more alarmist than it deserves to be, or it is late to the party.

It uses various incidents in 2026 to prove a point while dismissing those that did take place in the decade or so previous. For example, heartbleed, the log4j RCE, Rails' mass assignment DOS, Cloudflare updating a WAF rule and breaking the internet, Atlassian deleting almost 1000 of its customers' accounts and data, the Ashley Madison breach, Crowdstrike bricking their customers computers, Okta getting owned multiple times, etc.

My own point is that software became like this when we started becoming pragmatic. Nothing to do with AI or management really, we just realised, especially with web tech, that you can release something and then fix it. In the old age of getting CDs or floppies printed and distributed, that was not even remotely feasible. A similar incident in the 90s would involve a product recall or a way to get updated media from a retailer with the fix. Very expensive.

Standards have dropped and continue to do so, because we can also fix fast. It's not suddenly breaking down. If anything, it's just too centralised.

↳ reply — throwawayffffas:

↳↳ reply — ljm:

XKCD - the random number is 4. That came from Sony IIRC.

item.title: Strengthening the fight against online child sexual abuse
item.description: 125 points, 312 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (openai.com)

→ HN comments  ·  125 points  ·  312 comments

Top #1 — maxgee:

Our account was recently banned from OpenAI for a CSAM violation. We had an autonomous agent using an image classifier switch to OpenAI (instead of a local model it should have been using) which was classifying user-uploaded content. After classifying over 100,000 images, OpenAI banned our account.

We asked for further information so we could report the uploader to the NCMEC and remove the content from our systems. They refused to give us any information about this incident, denied our appeal, and have so far, illegally refused our privacy requests for data about our account.

OpenAI does not care about fighting child sexual abuse, this is completely performative.

EDIT: These image uploads are up to 20+ years old, and are being served through Cloudflare with their CSAM scanning product enabled. We've received no notification of any problems from Cloudflare. Something on OpenAI's system thinks that an image we sent to them for classification is CSAM, and they aren't willing to elaborate or communicate about it at all. For reference, our website is https://ytmnd.com

↳ reply 1 — Jimmc414:

I had the same experience with OAI. We were all-in with OpenAI as our primary provider. We used it exclusively for python and go programming requests. Received a ban for "inciting violence". Appeal denied, no refund, no human response or explanation, 3 years of data lost (privacy requests for data denied). We're on team Anthropic now. Still stings when I think about it.

↳↳ reply — techpression:

Anthropic acts the same way (from experience), so take the learning of backing up your data from this, if nothing else.

↳ reply 2 — mattmaroon:

I’m sorry that happened to you, but I would read this more as they are an organization not prepared for this. Why would they be? One minute you’re trying to make computers pass the turning test, the next minute child porn is getting involved.

The fact that they did not previously have proper procedures in place for something like this is not proof that they don’t care. They are one of the fastest growing companies of all time, it’s hard to get disparate parts of an organization aligned on something. Their organization has more than doubled in size in the last nine months.

↳ reply 3 — nonethewiser:

> OpenAI does not care about fighting child sexual abuse, this is completely performative.

That doesn’t really follow from your experience.

OpenAI could care about child sexual abuse and not respond to your appeal, even wrongfully.

Top #2 — gwd:

So I've been working on having Claude using GPT images to illustrate various fairy tales. At some point there was a Russian one of a girl left in the forest, but in the first cut she looked peaceful and happy. I told Claude I didn't think that was realistic, and it said that it had already asked GPT images to show the girl "scared", and it refused 12/12 times. It also refused to have Frost (who in the fairy tale ends up giving her a coat and a chest of gold) standing over her; he had to be at her level, an arm's length away. (Showing the girl as "brave" and then "nervous" had better results.)

Gave me quite a funny feeling, tripping innocently over the empty shape that they've had to carve out. They wouldn't have spent the effort to do that if it wasn't pretty bad.

↳ reply — Aeolun:

ChatGPT is only too happy to generate really messed up images of ambiguously aged characters though.

Top #3 — nolist_policy:

Relatedly, Openrouter now does CSAM scanning and retention on so called "Zero Data Retention" endpoints as well.

https://openrouter.ai/blog/announcements/csam-screening/

↳ reply 1 — AlanYx:

Every mainstream vendor with a US presence does this on their ZDR/MAM AI endpoints. This also includes AWS and Azure. It's explained directly in the AWS ZDR docs, and it falls under the "synchronous" scanning pipeline in Azure with full MAM.

At least with AWS they're clear that this is the only type of proactive scanning they do on their ZDR AI endpoints. With Azure it's actually unclear exactly how much more falls into the synchronous scanning pipeline, though I may be missing some docs.

The way this was explained to me is although there is no legal requirement to do this, vendors are concerned that AI processing constitutes "actual knowledge" of the content unlike a lot of traditional cloud-based workloads, which would expose them to legal liability. Seems like a weird argument in a ZDR context, but anyway, there's also a public optics element too I'm sure.

↳↳ reply — nwlieb:

I'm personally hopeful that as an industry we can move towards E2EE and attested secure enclave pipelines to remove the "actual knowledge" argument. NEAR AI and Tinfoil are the only publicly available providers in this area but I would be excited to hear about more advancements in this area because I personally think that these NCMEC integrated "ZDR" systems are major privacy violations and deceptive marketing.

↳↳↳ reply — AlanYx:

Azure does offer nVidia's secure enclave architecture via "Azure Confidential GPU", but it's limited to a single GPU and a little less than 90GB after overhead, so basically maxes out at Mistral-Large-2 with 4 bit quantization.

This whole thing kind of puts the industry in a bind. On one hand, the big labs do have an incentive to get this kind of thing rolled out so as to avoid open weight on-prem AI gaining traction, and to remove remaining roadblocks to corporate adoption in regulated industries. But rolling it out risks attracting even stronger regulatory responses for them as well (that's even setting aside likely national security/law enforcement pushback), as well as likely being strongly opposed by the AI safety people. There's no one way to square the circle that will please everyone. My guess is the labs will take a third route: continue to lobby against open weight models, thus killing the possibility of on-prem, and then drag their heels on E2EE/secure enclave models except perhaps for military customers.

↳ reply 2 — itake:

How are these companies able to legally train these models? Are the employees citizens of countries that this material is illegal to download or possess?

The introduction of solar is something that my rural Appalachian county has dealt with recently.

There was considerable pushback from the 60+ crowd and NIMBY types just like there is for everything new and different, but we got three permitted and are waiting on them to begin construction.

The thing that got me was there was a lot of people that just made whatever argument they could to try and stop it. All kinds of arguments that people either didn't understand or didn't really believe in. They just knew they hated solar. I really couldn't wrap my head around it.

From my perspective. It's a net good for our ranchers. We're mostly small family ranches, 200 head or less and the lease paid by the solar company helps these folks meet the bottom line. Beef prices won't stay up forever so it's a good time to diversify.

Top #2 — thelastgallon:

There are lots of use cases for solar with livestock and livestock + agriculture.

China has fish farms with solar, reflection from water increases efficiency by 5%: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MgQVV0_75j0

Livestock need shade, and grass doesn't need continuous shade grows better in shade in most tropical climates. If its too hot, grass dies off. Livestock also need ACs when temperatures reach 50+ centigrade, which can be powered by solar.

Cows are ruminants, they lie down and ruminate for hours in shade.

Except for goats, solar works with most animals.

Solar can always be used as a fence (zero land use, zero interruption to machinery) and get paid at a higher rate in the mornings and evenings, extending solar production window by ~4 hours.

Farming is tough and low status. All countries support farming with subsidies. The best use of farms is solar+ anything else. Photosynthesis is 6% efficiency (and it goes down to less than 1% when we use it for livestock feed or ethanol with conversion losses), solar is ~25%. Solar has zero opex and can run for 3 - 5 decades, output can be used directly.

This is the sort of geo-engineering which I think we can all get behind. Solar panels are really more like artificial trees than we might initially think, not only absorbing sunlight but also providing shade. Next step is to design in root like foundations, so that they can hold the soil together. Pretty much close-to-nature form of terraforming.

→ HN comments  ·  402 points  ·  88 comments  ·  comments as of 20h

Top #1 — quodlibetor:

I maintained chrono for about half a decade, and the specific reason I took on maintenance was because the API sucked and I hoped I could make it better.

Turns out, the reason people wanted to use it was because the API was stable and every slight step towards improvement was met with... resistance. I stopped maintaining it because the burnout from seeing what it could be and not seeing any path to get there was too much for me.

I'm extremely grateful to burntsushi for writing the datetime library rust deserves. Chrono is stable and is maintained (though semi-deprecated) by an extremely reliable rustacean -- you don't need to leave, but you'll probably be happier if you do.

↳ reply 1 — lifthrasiir:

As the original author of Chrono, thank you so much for your service. It was always a learning experience for me to design and maintain Chrono (that's why the API is not very good, despite my best efforts) and I too had been burnt out from doing so, so it was fortunate that the right people stepped up and kept the torch burning for so long time.

↳↳ reply — quodlibetor:

I shouldn't have used the word sucked -- personal jargon that I use all the time to describe my own code and try not to apply to other people's -- it was created pre-1.0 and we learned a lot as a community in the 10 years you spent building it.

Thank you so much for building something that was obviously good enough to sustain the community for 12 years <3

↳↳↳ reply — hermitdev:

As someone who has worked with implementing date/time functionality before, I'm empathize. Getting APIs "right" is hard, and getting it wrong is easy because there's so many ways to get it wrong. Especially when you start getting into something like handling something like daylight saving time, which is inherently political and changes arbitrarily over time. I've spent most of my career in finance. I distinctly remember near shouting matches over what it meant to add "1 day" to a datetime. Does it mean adding 24 hours? Or, does it mean give me the same time of day tomorrow? What happens if tomorrow is the other side of a DST change? These seems like trivial questions, but matter if you're talking about, say physical delivery of oil or gas at a set rate per hour.

↳ reply 2 — steveklabnik:

Thanks for helping maintain Chrono. Burnout is the worst, I hope you're feeling better these days.

↳ reply 3 — Arch485:

I'm really curious - what makes you say chrono's API sucks?

I've used it in several projects, and to me it seems just fine. Granted, I don't do a lot of cross-time zone work; I exclusively use UTC whenever possible.

Top #2 — Dagonfly:

> When should I use Jiff? Jiff isn’t always the right thing to use.

I really appreciate when a project calmly acknowledges that it's not the right tool for every use case, and is not trying to be. That's professional engineering.

Especially in the AI-age, the crucial skill will be what NOT to implement.

↳ reply — BrandoElFollito:

I always use a time library (in Python and TS). If you work on time intervals in seconds, fine, you can use what is built-in. But I favor consistency and everything time is a time library object for me.

Outside of this not using a timer library is going for a world of pain

↳ reply 2 — ripvanwinkle:

Generals fighting the last war

Top #2 — dhx:

Vantor WV02 imagery of the site at 2024-12-19: https://livingatlas.arcgis.com/wayback/#mapCenter=48.13598%2...

It doesn't look immediately obvious from satellite imagery that the compound is important but it's got a large communications tower and is adjacent to a parking lot for what appears to be 50 tanks (at 2024-12-19), so perhaps got targeted because the tanks give away a military purpose and the mast is an obvious giveaway of something more important, as are all the barriers for stopping vehicles that you'd only bother installing if there were people working in the buildings.

Scrolling about there is (or was) also an air/missile defence battery nearby at: https://livingatlas.arcgis.com/wayback/#mapCenter=48.14840%2...

Seemingly the battery is there to protect the Mina Abdullah Refinery and Mina Al-Ahmadi Refinery which adjoin these sites, which Wikipedia indicates are together just a bit short of 1 million barrels per day capacity. The Kuwaiti government (probably?) has also more recently got the likes of Google, Esri, Vantor, whoever else to blur the refineries in more recent imagery, including the adjoining US military sites.

↳ reply 1 — SV_BubbleTime:

Maybe you are right, but that is nonstop speculation. I don’t think your public scan of photos is anything even remotely comparable to military intelligence, to the point of it being a silly exercise.

↳↳ reply — dhx:

The coordinates are not speculation. You can confirm with the images provided in the related CNN article from March[2]. They've also been attached to the relevant Wikipedia article since it was created on 11th March (+10 days after the attack).[1] The air/missile defence battery nearby is extremely obvious--all of them share approximately the same layout.

What perhaps may forever be speculation is why Iran chose to target this small compound. Maybe they called up Russia and borrowed an ELINT satellite and detected US military transmissions of interest from the communications tower next to this compound. Maybe they hacked the phone of some US military service member or followed them around. Or maybe they just saw in their own imagery that this compound was used over time for storing tanks and other equipment and therefore it was added to their list for this reason alone. item.title: The Active Directory Era Is Finally Over
item.description: 125 points, 80 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (infisical.com)

→ HN comments  ·  125 points  ·  80 comments

Top #1 — bodeadly:

A central point of this article seems to be claiming that adding a device in AD is an administrative bottleneck compared to cloud. If that is the claim, it is false. By default Authenticated Users have an "Add workstations to domain" capability (AKA ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota attribute on their account) that allows a regular user to create up to 10 machine accounts with zero admin intervention.

Machine accounts have limited rights compared to regular users. AD provides fine grained distributed policy and cert managment. After decades of emperical refinement, AD is often superior to what the cloud offers including Entra. In environments with many PCs that require centrally managed policy, AD is still relavant and probably required.

I think it is also true that there are and always will be many companies that simply cannot expose these PCs to the cloud either because they're working with data that cannot be in the cloud like legal files, finanical documents, schematics or they cannot risk being tethered to the Internet. You know that little micro PC attached to the cart in every exam room in a doctors office? There is a 99% chance it is joined to AD.

↳ reply 1 — jiggawatts:

What Linux admins don’t “get” about Active Directory was the superpowers granted by its Group Policy feature.

Everyone loves to harp on about how terrible the Registry is, but that’s missing the forest for a tree.

The registry + GPO engine is a strongly typed and layered settings engine with:

Machine, Machine Policy, User, and User Policy layered on top of each other, consistently, through pretty much every native app!

More importantly, policy would apply or unapply dynamically and cleanly.

You could move a laptop to a different office and soon as it connected the wifi its set of configured printers would change, its outbound proxy could be reconfigured, etc.

More importantly: Microsoft engineers of the era put in the work of writing up thousands of settings in template files that shipped with Windows, with simple checkbox UI controls and paragraphs of descriptions in every language!

If you think your terrible “settings automation” tool is a viable alternative just ask yourself this question: does it “put the work in” or does its user have to?

↳↳ reply — EvanAnderson:

Group Policy is so immensely handy. It was a game-changer feature for provisioning and maintaining Windows clients and servers from its introduction in Windows 2000. When Active Directory (AD) was brand new I became immediately enamored with Group Policy. "Superpowers" is definitely the right way to put it.

I had a hard time getting excited about Ansible, Puppet, Desired State Configuration, etc, because I was provisioning machines with Group Policy in 2001. Load Windows, join the domain, and the machine gets configured (software loaded, settings locked-in, defaults overridden, etc).

Today I'm provisioning tons of Windows VMs this way: PXE boot the VM to an unattended Windows setup that ends up joining the domain and getting all its configuration. It makes disposable VM instances and horizontal scaling Windows VMs a breeze.

The now-defunct Likewise Open product (https://github.com/vmware-archive/likewise-open) extended Group Policy to Linux machines. I'd lost touch with the product but it looks like it got GPL'd. It was handy, albeit I don't have the experience with it like I had with the native Windows Group Policy client. I only encountered it in one environment and, at the time, it was commercially licensed.

I'm not in love w/ the CIFS-based portion of Group Policy, but there's nothing stopping anybody from extending the AD schema and using the AD LDAP server to deliver policy settings (or any other mechanism). Using the filesystem to deliver settings always seemed like a hack born of expedience.

↳ reply 2 — wtch98:

When it comes to friction in corporations it's typically policy based

It starts off easy to get stuff done, then corporate IT starts to lock down (for various reasons), then those on the edge move to new pastures where they can do work (provision a VM on prem? 50 page form passed through 12 departments. Provision the exact same VM in ec2? 3 clicks)

Eventually corporate IT decides that there needs to be governance and the cycle continues.

↳ reply 3 — philamonster:

> You know that little micro PC attached to the cart in every exam room in a doctors office? There is a 99% chance it is joined to AD.

So are the cop cars in my city. Walked by one w/two officers in it in a supermarket parking lot last year and had to explain what a trust relationship issue is, unironically.

Top #2 — sirjaz:

The funny thing is that AD has all the capabilities that are discussed here. Even AWS recommends it for kubernetes as a service account using gmsa: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/...

↳ reply 1 — itintheory:

The document you linked is for Elastic Container Service which is not Kubernetes based. It looks like gMSA is supported for Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) if you're using AD as an iDP but I don't think that's the same as AWS recommending it exactly. Most EKS workloads will use IAM Roles for Service Accounts, or EKS Pod Identity. I'd also wager >99% of EKS workloads aren't Windows based so I don't think this is a very widely used technology in that context.

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/window...

↳ reply 2 — sebazzz:

And you can use gMSA for IIS application pools as well. Completely passwordless.

Top #3 — breakwaterlabs:

> Human approval doesn’t scale to developers creating and deprecating testing databases, Kubernetes clusters, and CI runners at will.

Service (or gMSA) accounts handle this, and auth-integrated reverse proxies can move parts of the problem into a more tractable place.

I feel like the article also conveniently forgets that kerberos/ldap backends for SSO systems are extremely common, and solve this.

> In Kubernetes, each pod gets a service account token, which allows it to assert its identity within the cluster.

How is this qualitatively different than onboarding a new computer object or gMSA entitlement in AD?

The problems that the blog asserts affect AD (how to onboard and delegate access and trust) are inherent in any sufficiently robust identity implementation.

The best thing I did wrt Amazon is kill off my Prime account. It eliminates hundreds of even thousands of dollars of wasteful impulse purchases every year.

Most online retailers (Amazon included) still give free shipping above a certain threshold ($35 per order or whatever) so for things I need, I wait until I reach that threshold to place the order, and often purchase at other retailers or directly from the brand.

Also, everyone does "Black Friday" sales nowadays, in many cases matching the same window as Amazon.

Amazon is the only service that can provide that for the vast majority of products, with Walmart filling in the gaps for the rest (but not as fast as Amazon). Literally no other vendor can compete with those two on shipping speed without paying a huge premium.

At some point, we lost the plot on online shopping. Sometimes physically going to the store to hold an item in your hand and bring it home within the hour is far more convenient than comparing 4-8 items online and waiting several days for it to arrive.

I live in a big city so there is some niche stores were I can go and get actual quality products, but the big stores are all selling the same trash they were selling when I was a kid, and I don't see the point of going there when I can buy quality products on niche websites.

I cancelled my Prime account when they decided I would need to pay $2.99/month on top of my Prime account if I wanted ad-free videos on Prime Video. Being nickel and dimed with a monthly fee when I was already paying a yearly fee for their supposedly premium service was a bridge too far. I was already disillusioned by Amazon from the eruption of the wishlist functionality, the scam 3rd party sellers, and other such degradation of the service.

A couple of years after quitting I downloaded my order data and plotted it to see the impact of quitting Prime. My order volume dropped by 70%. I've been making a point to try and use my local stores more often. Being able to see and try the item in-store, and go home with it, may take more time, but it's faster in elapsed time, and I rarely have to return anything, because I know what I'm actually getting.

Top #2 — akudha:

I've mentally tuned out of words like sale, discount, deal etc when I see them while shopping. It seems most things are on sale most of the time - how is that even possible? As much as I think Apple is arrogant, at least they don't do this crappy "sale" thing. Right now there is a whole page of "deals" on Microsoft https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/store/b/sale

Walk into any store (JC Penny etc) half the items are on sale. Even groceries - go to Safeway, there is a newspaper style coupons - multiple pages. This whole thing is just bizarre and tiring.

If you are willing to delay purchase until they are discounted then you can get additional savings. Often times these discounts are predictable, such as brands often offering Black Friday discounts.

It depends on what you buy, and where you buy it from, but there are legitimate deals out there. I probably save about $1000/yr total in these sales just by asking ChatGPT how frequently a brand has sales and then leaving the items in my shopping cart until the next sale.
