item.title: Microsoft blames monster email outage on software defect introduced in July fix
item.description: 355 points, 266 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (theregister.com)

→ HN comments  ·  355 points  ·  266 comments  ·  comments as of 23h

Top #1 — mike_hearn:

No big surprises here. Big outages at big firms seem to always look like this.

The electricity industry has this notion they call a black start, where they bring the grid online from zero. It's a very difficult operation because you can't start a generator straight into an offline grid otherwise it gets hit with full demand and can't keep frequency in the right range, which can damage equipment. So they have to start by disconnecting all the loads and then bringing load blocks back in sequence, trying to roughly balance available generation with the size of the next block. In practice black starts are extremely rare, but they can happen after a cascading failure in which something causes some generating stations to trip, redirecting load onto the remaining stations which can't handle it causing them to trip in turn. The entire grid can collapse in just 60 seconds or so once that kind of runaway failure starts.

This kind of outage is very analogous to a black start. A few servers get into trouble - maybe they're in a crash loop or maybe their caches are cold - the load balancers shift traffic onto the remainder which then can't handle the load either and so the failure cascades. Once a service is in this state sometimes the only remedy is to disconnect all load, bring the servers back to stability, then bring load blocks back online in small chunks, making sure to never hit anything with the full load immediately to ensure any caches or JIT compilers have time to warm up.

It's the sort of thing that requires a bit of preparation because naive ways of doing it like just randomly dropping 90% of requests will yield a broken service for everyone. Ideally your LB can drop traffic by modulus of the session cookie or similar, so users are let back in atomically.

Black starting a service is obviously quite hard to practice, but is probably something that sufficiently well resourced SRE teams should try once a quarter or so on a test cluster. I used to be an SRE at Google and although we regularly started up new clusters and moved traffic around between them, actually starting an isolated service instance entirely from scratch was never something we practiced. I remember in a few cases teams discovered devs had introduced circular dependencies by accident, i.e. starting service X required service X to already exist, or it depended on service Y that in turn depended on X. Sometimes you can only find these things by practicing.

↳ reply 1 — hwillis:

> and can't keep frequency in the right range, which can damage equipment.

This is one of those beautiful engineer understatements. Rotational speed is fundamentally linked to voltage by the motor velocity constant: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motor_constants

Although it's fundamental for all motors, the actual constant is arbitrary for each motor. Voltage is still proportional to change in field is proportional to speed; at zero voltage you have zero speed.

A large dead AC load has its own speed- zero. It's connecting the engine without a clutch, but the engine makes hundreds of megawatts. The 6' wide generator wants to go from 3600 RPM to a standstill in a few inches. A full speed rotor can have up to 5 gigajoules of rotational inertia; over a ton of TNT.

On a live grid you've got a synchronoscope: https://youtu.be/LVozbX9Mn1c?si=RhRPIkuTVxh4Wseq&t=181

Which is great, because connecting it backwards would cause a slow motion explosion. On a dead grid the only thing saving you is the resistance in the wires; it would be LOUD if you connected to it and you would very likely increase the ventilation through the walls of the plant.

↳↳ reply — jeffreygoesto:

Somebody sent on HN a while ago how a small water power plant is synced to the net [0], I found it super fascinating.

[0] https://youtu.be/xGQxSJmadm0?si=fVdJXtN0bCBX_fyW

↳ reply 2 — nilptr:

There's literally no such thing as "black start" at Microsoft that I am aware of. The way services are brought online initially is through a build out process coordinated through hundreds of Teams. It's an organic, messy, and painful way of doing things. As such, build outs are a human driven process with bits of automation spanning sometimes 20+ years of engineering touches, troubleshooting guide, and some additional tribal knowledge thrown in passed down through the years. There is little consistency across teams and sometimes even within a team as every Azure Cloud is effectively slightly "different".

↳ reply 3 — CobaltFire:

I never worked in civilian power generation, but I can vouch for this on Nuclear Ships.

We had to practice load pickup on a normal start at the pier often, but we likely practiced a full SCRAM to back online (including a FULL load shutdown) more.

Having predefined lists of what gets brought up at various points helps a ton, but it's still not an easy or simple operation.

Top #2 — sinuhe69:

No one has asked the obvious question: how much AI contributed to the epic failure by Microsoft. Was the patch programmed and tested by AI? Not because they are inherently bad but it begs the question of how much do the remaining humans at MS understand the patch? And did using AI contribute to the atrophy of knowledge and skills, especially deep, specific skills such as network failure inspection, load balancing and fail over recovery, that led to a slower response and recovery time?

Without a functioning intuition, discovering the causes to initiate recovery effort in a high-stress, unfamiliar situation with catastrophic dimensions could be significantly hampered.

They are valid questions and of particular interest in the age of AI. Productive, highly specialized skills could degrade faster than one imagine once we start rely too much on external helps.

↳ reply 1 — quikoa:

Microsoft would never admit to AI being at fault. Businesses praise AI if something goes right and blame people if something goes wrong. If the opposite happens to be true then they'll simply won't share what caused it.

↳↳ reply — wrasee:

What’s interesting is what they did admit to, that this was introduced in a change made in July 2026. They didn’t have to mention that specifically, and that date alone is carrying a lot of indirect information.

They’ll also be self-aware if this, and know the conclusions that people will draw.

↳ reply 2 — frereubu:

Sibling comments are right that Microsoft would never admit that publicly, but I do think it's worth asking on HN in case there are MS employees who might be able to create a burner account and respond without revealing their identity. Of course it's difficult to verify whether what a burner account says is true, but I still think it would be of interest.

Top #3 — andix:

There is one thing I don't get with this issue. The problem was basically that their system couldn't handle the normal load. Why couldn't they just reduce the load at some point just by dropping/limiting connections?

For example just accept connections from specific (random) IP ranges. They could even cycle through different ranges every 5 minutes to give clients a chance to sync at least once every hour.

The reduced load could be used to gradually bring up servers again without failing, add additional capacity, and gradually restoring access. Completely without fixing the bug at all. The system managed to handle usual load even with the bug, it just hit some critical point that made it collapse. Adding more resources would also fix that.

↳ reply 1 — mike_hearn:

The issue appears to have been in one of the load balancer layers themselves (the "front door"). So that makes it a lot harder.

Most big cloud services operate several layers of load balancing. The first is a smart DNS server that turns a lookup of mail.outlook.com or whatever into an IP address of a datacenter roughly nearby to where the user is, to a datacenter that's not too overloaded. But because DNS lookups are cached and sometimes cached too long by clients this is a very rough and ready form of LB.

The second layer are routers that spread requests to a single IP address over "hardware" LBs that take raw TCP/IP connections from the internet. Then those machines do some basic health checking and forwarding to the frontend web servers. At that level the machines aren't aware of what service or customer the connections are for, they're just doing some flow hashing to pick a "backend" (another frontend).

Then the cloud/service level machines terminate the TCP/IP connection and often TLS as well. They're reverse proxies that do URL matching and forward traffic on to the app specific servers. This is the first layer at which you can start to intelligently inspect or drop traffic.

No one person in a big org has the ability to limit traffic to a service across every layer of load balancing that exists. If the reverse proxies start dying, reducing traffic would mean changing the configuration of the hardware LBs which is usually a different team.

↳ reply 2 — itopaloglu83:

You mean they should've made disaster recovery plans ahead of time? That requires experience and a certain level of know-how, in a company that has just decided to "voluntarily retire” a quarter of its most experienced workforce. There was a lot of things they could've, should've, and would've done.

item.title: Do Repeat Yourself
item.description: 148 points, 51 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (arcentry.com)

→ HN comments  ·  148 points  ·  51 comments

Top #1 — nitwit005:

My company has a script to set up a repo in an expected pattern. The first thing you have to do is disable a bunch of logging that no one uses, as that can cripple the performance of your app. Then you have to go update a bunch of dependencies with security problems. Then you have to fix their git hooks.

Which is to say, standard does not imply good. A lot of times companies just standardize around how they did things most recently, which means they haven't learned all the problems yet.

Top #2 — pmg101:

Sometimes syntactic duplication can give you a hint to underlying semantic duplication. But it's no more than a hint.

DRY doesn't mean don't repeat a similar looking block of code, it means try to structure your code so that each element of the design has a single representation.

There's no shortcut to good design where no thinking is required, much as a lot of people seem to wish there were.

↳ reply — hansvm:

Absolutely. The rule of thumb is that two things should be abstracted together iff they should change together. The down-sampling constant matching the upweighting factor? Don't repeat yourself. Needing a half-dozen subtly different circular buffer definitions? Circumstances vary, but repetition is probably fine. Two pieces of code which are literally identical? As you said, the syntactic duplication suggests there's an underlying semantic duplication you might want to iron out, but if the two callsites really want the potential for independent behavior then byte-for-byte code duplication can make more sense.

But, like the rest of software, even that's just a guideline. Suppose you've been painted into a corner where code needs to be synced between languages. There are solutions, but especially if it happens rarely then those solutions might be a lot more expensive than just a comment at both locations.

Top #3 — umvi:

Or as the go proverb goes "a little copying is better than a little dependency" (https://go-proverbs.github.io/)

item.title: The Secret ThinkPad Powerbutton Code to Bring Dead Laptops Back to Life (2007)
item.description: 312 points, 125 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (masnick.com)

→ HN comments  ·  312 points  ·  125 comments  ·  comments as of 25h

Top #1 — legacynl:

From a former call-center phone operator, I think the 10 1-sec pushes, is just a way to make sure the customer presses the buttons long enough. In our callcenter we often had to ask customer to hold the reset button on their router for 3 seconds. When the router didn't reboot, I would send replacements, until a colleague advised me to tell customers to hold the button for 10 seconds. Apparently when you ask customers to hold the button for 3 seconds, some will actually only hold it for 1 or 2 seconds. Suddenly most customers were able to reset their routers.

↳ reply 1 — rozularen:

This just saved my Lenovo Legion laptop! :) My gf dropped it a few days ago, and it hadn't booted since. I had already tried the static discharge procedure, but it didn't work for some reason. After reading your comment, I figured I'd give it one more shot, and it finally booted up. Thanks a lot!

↳↳ reply — devsda:

My non lenovo laptop requires holding power button for 10 seconds or more to even charge after an accidental deep discharge(modern standby sucks!). I got a few scares when it didn't power up even after 10 seconds. It did comeback up when checking it later.

↳↳↳ reply — dylan604:

> I guess there are hardware level variances for the time needed or its just variance in perception of time across individuals,

This is something that I've always been good at after being in marching band. Marching bands are pretty much set to 120bpm and that tempo is ingrained in you. To this day, I still subconsciously skip steps to walk in step with the person next to me when in a group. You are correct. item.title: Coffeehouses and the Rise of Science [pdf]
item.description: 179 points, 101 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (monirbounadi.com)

→ HN comments  ·  179 points  ·  101 comments  ·  comments as of 16h

Top #1 — zero_k:

Habermas talks a lot about the coffeehouses in his "The Structural Transformation of the Public Sphere" -- how they changed the way society functioned, and politics was discussed and formed by them.

``` However much the Tischgesellschaften, salons, and coffee houses may have differed in the size and composition of their publics, the style of their proceedings, the climate of their debates, and their topical orientations, they all organized discussion among private people that tended to be ongoing; hence they had a number of institutional criteria in common. First, they preserved a kind of social intercourse that, far from presupposing the equality of status, disregarded status altogether. The tendency replaced the celebration of rank with a tact befitting equals. The parity on whose basis alone the authority of the better argument could assert itself against that of social hierarchy and in the end can carry the day meant, in the thought of the day, the parity of ‘common humanity’ (‘bloss Menschliche‘). Les hommes, private gentlemen, or die Privatleute made up the public not just in the sense that power and prestige of public office were held in suspense; economic dependencies also in principle had no influence. Laws of the market were suspended as were laws of the state. Not that this idea of the public was actually realized in earnest in the coffee houses, the salons, and the societies; but as an idea it had become institutionalized and thereby stated as an objective claim. If not realized, it was at least consequential. ```

↳ reply 1 — Merrill:

Doesn't Habermas associate the coffeehouses with the rise of the bourgeoise to become the dominant class in the 18th and 19th centuries. The coffeehouses enabled the formation of a public that was beyond the control of the church and the nobility, which had been predominant before and after the Peace of Westphalia respectively.

Habermas and his Coffeehouses https://medium.com/whither-news/habermas-and-his-coffeehouse...

↳ reply 2 — jaspa99:

Sounds similar to anonymous internet forums around the mid 2000s until the mid 2010s

Top #2 — jt2190:

Not at all equivalent to today’s coffee shops:

> The social impact of coffeehouse culture shows most clearly when juxtaposed with earlier social norms. As Cowan (2005, pp. 101–105, 112) explains, coffeehouses, rather than alcohol-centered public houses, became key venues for elite exchange. In early seventeenth-century England, the virtuosi (natural philosophers and scholars) tended to gather in aristocratic great houses, where interactions were formal and exclusive. Coffeehouses, by contrast, encouraged informal, cross-class dialogue and, as such, challenged traditional pathways to intellectual recognition. For less wealthy aspiring virtuosi, coffeehouses provided unprecedented access to information and social networks.

> That access mattered more than the drink…

HN itself is probably filling that function to a degree.

Top #3 — zeristor:

So modern day equivalents might be Maker spaces?

There’s also online communities: forums, game boards, HNews itself of course.

But I’m guessing in person is a bigger deal.

There used to be Skillsmatter CodeNode in London, which was such a key focus for years. (Big thanks to Wendy)

But neutral venues for Meet-ups seems to be hard work

↳ reply 1 — gilleain:

Not only in-person, but the smaller population size - and presumably the smaller social circle of those involved I should read the paper!) would mean the patrons of these coffeehouses were less likely to be strangers.

I could go to a coffee shop or bar right now, but I'm unlikely to start a conversation with a stranger about science or philosophy. Might be on me :)

↳↳ reply — zeristor:

Yes, I’m guessing this is third-space territory, recurrent social fixtures.

There’s a whole social ecology to a city, for want of better words.

A city with these structures for people to meet and get to know each other; would one would think be able to have more ferment in new companies and social cohesion.

Sweden has a start-up culture, I’m wondering does it have avenues for people to meetup too. Is it only in certain Swedish cities.

I guess there’s an Francisco too, is a university the key catalyst?

↳↳↳ reply — OkayPhysicist:

San Francisco, as far as tech is concerned, doesn't have a noteworthy university. UCSF is just a medical school, and the other colleges/universities in town are small and unremarkable.

Probably can be explained by being "the city" to a region containing plenty of world-class universities, though.

↳ reply 2 — crimsoneer:

I think the problem with online spaces is they're both very easy to get into, and very hard - so it's easy to stick your head into a massive Discord group, but you're also quite unlikely to just stumble into a conversation that's particularly relevant to your interests.

item.title: Interpreting claims that a theorem is correct because it was checked in Lean
item.description: 291 points, 132 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (xenaproject.wordpress.com)

→ HN comments  ·  291 points  ·  132 comments  ·  comments as of 19h

Top #1 — Legend2440:

Worth pointing out that this article is by Kevin Buzzard, one of the biggest advocates for Lean and automated theorem proving.

It's refreshing to see intellectual honesty about a tool's limitations, from someone still advocating for its strengths.

↳ reply 1 — Isamu:

Seems more about the limitations of the way it was used

>It is worth noting that of the 290 OpenAI theorems which come with Lean code, around 38 of them have the property that the Lean code does not even state, let alone prove, the main theorem of the paper. And OpenAI never claimed that it did! They just said “here is some Lean code which goes with this paper”. Sometimes the code just states and proves some intermediate results — my impression is that OpenAI decided to go live when some of the formalizations were incomplete, so just dumped what they had.

↳ reply 2 — guenthert:

"Worth pointing out that this article is by Kevin Buzzard"

Is it? The site claims that the article is written by the Xena Project. In the comment section it answers on (paraphrasing) "whether proving that a Lean kernel written in Lean and verified by Lean would be a circular proof" with "I’m really sorry, you need to ask these questions elsewhere (e.g. on the Lean Zulip). I am by no means an expert in these matters, all I know is that people who are experts have thought hard about them. "

If that is indeed Kevin Buzzward's writing, it is by no means obvious.

↳ reply 3 — samlinnfer:

He’s currently working on formalising Fermat’s Last Theorem in Lean btw.

Top #2 — wodenokoto:

Isn’t “proof is checked in Lean” kinda similar to assuming your code works just because it compiles.

Sure, the code works, but does it work at doing what you want?

Sure, the proof is valid, but does it prove what you set out to prove?

↳ reply 1 — throwawayffffas:

The gist of the article is that it's worse.

That it's the equivalent of saying "It's full moon tonight because I wrote this program".

And he states that you have to check that:

1. The statement the author is making corresponds to the statement in the lean program.

2. The lean program actually compiles.

3. There is no shenanigans hidden in the lean program to disguise a trivial proof as the one stated.

4. The program does not exploit bugs in lean.

↳↳ reply — csande17:

On the bright side, the article claims Lean has built-in tools to do 2-4 as long as you have enough RAM. In particular, there's a formally verified alternative implementation of Lean's checker that would theoretically rule out 4.

That implementation seems to be vibe-coded/vibe-proven in Lean itself (assuming the "con-leche" that my quick Google search turned up is the one he's talking about), so it's kind of turtles all the way down, but it does decrease the chance that a program could be exploiting both a Lean bug and a con-leche bug.

↳↳↳ reply — lumost:

Saying that a "formally verified" program rules out any bugs is a bit of a reach. Formal verification only checks that the properties you claim are true are actually true in the absence of bugs in the proof logic.

Example bug

A verified network program ensures that "data from two addresses are never commingled", but it does not verify that the NIC can't overwrite control flow memory opening up RCE attacks/other memory reads.

It certainly is harder to make bugs in formally verified software than the alternative, but it is not bug free.

↳ reply 2 — program_whiz:

Reading the friendly article:

It is worth noting that of the 290 OpenAI theorems which come with Lean code, around 38 of them have the property that the Lean code does not even state, let alone prove, the main theorem of the paper.

So even if LEAN is 100% bug-free, its still on the programmer to correctly express the logic and proofs, or they could be proving completely unrelated facts.

Top #3 — trehans:

One thing I'm surprised to see little mention of here is that if you want to use Lean proofs for your code and really want good correspondence between what is proved in Lean and what your code actually does, you need a mathematical model of your programming language embedded in Lean and a deterministic parser converting your code itself into Lean. Otherwise, yes, an AI actually has no checks against hallucination and while writing Lean proofs probably helps AI identify its mistakes it really isn't an end-to-end proof of your code's functionality.

I personally think the future probably involves a combination of unit tests and formal verification to support our confidence in AI-written software, as well as means to align high-level human intent with the low-level intent of individual code pieces, which as this article mentions is the other big piece that can slip with formal proofs: we might not be proving what we think we're proving. For those interested I've written an educational post about this topic here as well: https://kellerai.io/resources/ai-proved-your-code-correct

↳ reply 1 — jeremyjh:

I guess it isn't mentioned here because it is completely off-topic. Lean can make formal proofs of code but TFA is about proofs in pure mathematics.

↳↳ reply — trehans:

To clarify: mentioned "here" meaning mentioned in the comments. HackerNews is presumably majority programmers and the comments section is mostly comments about using proofs for formal verification of code. I agree the article is coming from a mathematics standpoint

↳↳↳ reply — Ar-Curunir:

Why would comments on an article about formal proofs about mathematics discuss formal proofs about code?

↳ reply 2 — fritzo:

You don't need a model of your programming language in Lean, that's overkill.

It's already useful to isolate a DSL in your software and model that in Lean. Sure that only proves that the domain specific code is correct, but now you've factored your proof into proving high-level correctness and low-level correctness.

item.title: How to make almost anything
item.description: 847 points, 144 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (pub.cba.mit.edu)

→ HN comments  ·  847 points  ·  144 comments  ·  comments as of 21h

Top #1 — renehsz:

It seems some people aren't happy about the fact that this course only glosses over each topic, teaching students only superficial knowledge instead of doing a deeper dive on one or a few.

But let's not forget that an overview of what’s even possible is extremely valuable in its own right. When these students are later faced with a problem X, they'll remember that there was this thing called Y which might help. They won't know the details, but at least they'll know where to start looking.

This is especially important if you want to rise to managerial positions, and it might become more relevant now that AI agents are increasingly capable of implementing things: Solving problems is not all about how to do something, but also about knowing what can be done at all. Laypeople often have no idea what's possible, but engineers do, which lets them be creative with their tools.

All of this is not to downplay the value of true in-depth knowledge of a specific subject. But those subject matter experts typically gain their expertise on the job, or at a later stage in their academic life when they conduct proper research. An overview course like this one doesn't hurt even if many students will choose to specialize later on.

↳ reply 1 — tekacs:

A book recommended to us when applying to Trinity College, Cambridge was 'The New Turing Omnibus' by A.K. Dewdney [1].

It's still to this day one of my favorite reads. By the time I read it, I knew about a lot of the possibilities within it already. But it does exactly this: it skims across the top of dozens of topics, and it makes you just aware enough of... all sorts of areas of CS.

If you're curious, you might dig deeper - at worst, you know these all exist.

[1]: https://www.amazon.com/New-Turing-Omnibus-Turning-Excursions...

↳↳ reply — bre1010:

I LOVE this book. I worked through it in 2012 the summer before I went to college and learned so much that my intro CS class didn't really introduce any concepts I hadn't seen in one of the chapters.

I remember that the book uses a basic or python-like pseudo code and that their neural network implementation has a couple of very subtle bugs which prevent a direct translation to python. The surrounding explanation was correct, but the code wasn't, and so it (presumably unintentionally) forced me to really understand what was happening in order to get it working. I forget the bug, something like a dropped negative.

The information density of the book is just so incredible. Each chapter is like 6 pages long and somehow that's enough to go from zero to a working single-layer neural network, or boolean logic circuits, or error-correcting codes, or 50 other things. I remember it being almost addicting to work through.

↳ reply 2 — qalmakka:

A gut feeling I've been having since the start of the LLM era is that horizontal knowledge (aka, knowing that stuff exists, can be done in certain way, being able to understand the details without knowing them intimately and being able to do it with a wide array of things) will start getting more and more important the further we go in, because if you know that stuff exist you can point an LLM at it or get it to go in a specific way that it wouldn't take otherwise. LLM have a very strong tendency to just go from point A to point B, and they're often limited to what you can prompt.

This is basically the opposite of the last 50+ years where vertical knowledge (being a savant in a certain very specific field) was seen as the most important thing to have in a super specialised world.

This of course is just my perception, which needless to say, may be wildly off

↳ reply 3 — pmontra:

I fully agree and I add that this applies to every kind of job. I recently watched a plumber open and clean some pipes. I understood (at least at a superficial level) what he was doing and I've been able to complete the cleaning myself (he couldn't for a number of reasons that don't matter here.) Of course I've been clumsy and I took N times as long as he did but I finally got water again in my kitchen. Without watching him maybe I wouldn't have trusted myself to open some connections or I would have taken hours or days to reason about what was going on and probably do a lot of useless work.

Going back to CS and IT, I found myself talking many times along the years with good software developers coming from a totally different education path (graphics, philosophy, agricultural science, etc) and they had blind spots in areas that I had been exposed to at least a bit at university. Examples: SQL, one of them knew perfectly well how the ORM of the day worked (some JS one 12+ years ago) but not why; networking, one of them knew only to enter the SSID and password and everything else was magic.

Top #2 — zakqwy:

I took and later TA'd this course. The weekly pages that guide lectures are only part of the story; the best way to see what is actually taught is to peruse the sites students make to document their projects. Past experience varies, but in most cases folks come in with minimal knowledge of e.g. electronics, CAD, machining, programming, etc., or are perhaps specialists in just one of the disciplines. HTM(A)A is about the delta between the start and end of the semester for each individual, and is both a life-changing course and a massive time commitment for all involved.

↳ reply — vladoski:

do you think that it would be possible to share the lectures and recitation videos for this year's course when it will finish? I'll be glad to watch them :)

Top #3 — Animats:

That's just one course, not a full load. The pace of that course is insane. It's not clear how much of what they throw at students is intended to be used. The syllabus is huge but the actual projects aren't that complicated. They make students make their own PC board, but that's not all that hard if you have all the right tools. Which they probably do. It's trying to do it in the kitchen sink that's miserable.

I was around for the glory days of TechShop, took about thirteen of their classes, and they covered most of the techniques listed. But making actual stuff took much longer than the classes on machine operation.

I miss having access to CNC mills, laser cutters, and a water jet cutter. The computer-controlled stuff is easy to learn for a programmer. Welding requires endless practice and most people never get very good at it.

↳ reply 1 — WillAdams:

In a recent video on Adams Savage's "Tested" Youtube channel, he put forth that in 10 years or so, desktop CNC machines will be pervasive (ob. discl., I work for a company which makes and sells such machines).

The software has certainly gotten much better --- one of my early projects had me drawing up vectors in Macromedia Freehand/MX, exporting them to make a font, and to import into a CAM program (MakerCAM, it was a Flash file, really), and coordinating the output from that with using the font in F-Engrave to V-carve a dial.

File and image at: https://community.carbide3d.com/t/locking-register-calipers-...

These days of course one could directly make it in any number of free or affordable programs.

↳ reply 2 — bhelkey:

>I was around for the glory days of TechShop

There are still makerspaces around many major cities. It sounds like you are in the Bay Area, Maker Nexus is still around. My understanding is that many of the staff/much of the community from TechShop moved to Maker Nexus.

  [    2.920022] i915 0000:00:02.0: firmware: failed to load i915/kbl_dmc_ver1_04.bin (-2)

  ...

  [    3.818174] r8169 0000:02:00.0: firmware: failed to load rtl_nic/rtl8168h-2.fw (-2)
And a few more, just search for "fail". If NIC doesn't come up that explains why machine unreachable over ssh etc, right?

Might be a filesystem hiccup, and some firmware blobs went missing, or something? Just speculating here. EDIT: links in the article mention some ext4 issues (and maybe ntfs too?).

Might also be handy to save dmesg output from the kernel version that works fine, and lay output side-by-side.

Top #2 — hmm37:

Interesting.. I was suddenly having issues with 6.1 and Manjaro on an old laptop a week ago. It kept randomly freezing, sometimes after an hour, other times 12 hours of uptime, etc. Once I changed the kernel to a different version like 6.18 or 7.3, it worked with no issues. I wonder if it's related.

Top #3 — walrus01:

When people say "this is a VM on xen" I really wish they would provide on essential piece of troubleshooting data. As a domU, is it PV, PVH, full HVM, or HVM with PV drivers? There's a huge difference for how a modern xen dom0 handles the bootloader and kernel boot for those.

At this point trixie is also extremely mature and has been out for a long time, and while I'm not saying this isn't a major issue, if lots of people are seeing it, it's also a solid argument in favor of upgrading those bookworm systems to the latest bookworm and then to trixie to begin following the 13.x stable branch. The 6.12.x kernel in trixie fixes a lot of issues related to both being a hypervisor and running inside a hypervisor.

Qwen4-Max pelicans at four reasoning efforts (none, low, high, xhigh): https://tools.simonwillison.net/markdown-svg-renderer?url=ht...

For comparison, here's one I got from Qwen3.8 Max (at default reasoning effort): https://simonwillison.net/2026/Jul/20/afraid-of-chinese-mode...

This inspired me to re-run pelicans through 3.8 Max - but OpenRouter has qwen3.8-max-prime and qwen3.8-max-0902 - prime is twice the price and faster - so I went with the 0902 one.

Here are those 3.8 Max 0902 pelicans: https://tools.simonwillison.net/markdown-svg-renderer?url=ht... - they're mostly not as good as 4, but I prefer the 3.8 xhigh one.

item.title: Universal XSS in uBlock Origin from website-driven element picker
item.description: 587 points, 165 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (iter.ca)

→ HN comments  ·  587 points  ·  165 comments

Top #1 — ByteOfWood:

I never really loved how extensions have to put their interfaces in the website's DOM if they want to be able to work with the page's elements, like this selector, or a password manager's suggested logins. Especially in the password manager's scenario, it could leak what accounts you have to a given website to that website itself, if the page is looking for new DOM elements. Not exactly a showstopper vulnerability, but it's not a good thing.

↳ reply 1 — esprehn:

I've always regretted we didn't push harder on an extension overlay API. It was supposed to be based on Top Layer, but the primitive version of that API was never added and the things that were added can't be effectively used to attach subtrees for extensions.

https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Glossary/Top_layer

As a fun fact the Devtools also have a separate "Overlay Page" to draw on top of the web page for specifically this reason. The date picker on some platforms similarly uses an overlay page. This machinery was just never exposed to extensions.

↳ reply 2 — btown:

Setting aside data leaks, this also causes bugs in extensions to potentially affect websites en masse. For instance, as recently as this January, 1Password began injecting prism.js globally on all pages, breaking many <code> blocks for at least 20 days: https://mjtsai.com/blog/2026/01/07/1password-browser-extensi...

↳ reply 3 — wtallis:

Did XUL extensions in Firefox prior to WebExtensions have a different way of interacting with the page contents? I know they tended to integrate better with the host browser's UI and inherited more of the host OS's UI conventions as a result, but the web back then didn't require as many CSS-based ad blocking rules (domain/URL-based rules worked for almost everything) so I don't remember what the element picker UI was like on eg. AdBlock Plus or Adblock 0.5.

Top #2 — taylorfinley:

Really love the "I wrote all the prose, gpt wrote the POC" disclaimer, I would love to see more of those kinds of signals on human authored content.

↳ reply — hiccuphippo:

If there's enough of them and AI trains on it, then AI will write that disclaimer itself to make itself more believable.

↳↳ reply — techpression:

Only if it’s part of a benchmark that matters, which is the reason we are where we are today, good writing is not benchmarked enough.

Top #3 — jonhohle:

UBlock (and possily many more) leaks its UUID? So by installing an ad blocker, you’ve just given websites a unique fingerprint to reliably track you?

item.title: Nimony: A New Compiler for Nim
item.description: 172 points, 92 comments. See description for top comments.

→ Article (nimony.org)

→ HN comments  ·  172 points  ·  92 comments

Top #1 — stakhanov:

When I was doing the rounds roughly 10 years ago, trying to find a new programming language to learn, my money for "next big thing" landed on nim. I did some personal projects and absolutely loved it but, unfortunately, opportunities to work "on the clock" in nim never materialised and then rust started eating the world.

Thanks, Andreas Rumpf, for sticking with it for all these years: This seems like a great opportunity for me to get back into nim.

Top #2 — afavour:

I’m curious if this closes the door on Nim’s capability to output C code which you then compile yourself. I first discovered Nim when I was looking for something that could work with Apple’s requirements to embed bitcode in iOS apps, it meant you had to use their specific version of LLVM and that ruled out a lot of languages. It always seemed like a really unique feature (though IIRC Haxe has something similar).

Apple has long since removed that requirement so it doesn’t really matter anyway and I wouldn’t blame the Nim folks if it’s gone, these seem like a great set of improvements.

↳ reply 1 — 15155:

The real win with the compile-to-C strategy is embedded - a million embedded devices only publish vendor-provided (typically GCC) C toolchains.

↳↳ reply — elcritch:

This is a great part of Nim. I started using it with ESP32's for 5+ years or so now. Nimony is even more ideal for embedded.

Great part is that Nim's stdlib networking was easy to port to esp-idf's lwIP based network stack. So you get access to production Nim libraries for lots of networking stuff, or async, etc.

↳ reply 2 — txdv:

A lot of compilers nowadays compile to wasm, when you have wasm, you can compile to C.

Top #3 — Symmetry:

> Nimony is case sensitive like most other modern programming languages. The reason for this is implementation simplicity. This might also be changed in the future.

I've never been too annoyed by Nim's approach but I think this removes a complaint many people have.

↳ reply 1 — aslilac:

it also removes one of nim’s most unique differentiators which seems like a loss to me

↳↳ reply — maplant:

If your unique differentiator for your programming language is that identifiers are case insensitive you need to find a new schtick

↳ reply 2 — shevy-java:

I am not sure. I think Nim is a fine language, but it is a little bit cumbersome as well, due to the typing. People complain just about everything, so this is not a good metric to use as the only metric. Nim has a similar problem as crystal has: too few users. With the rise of AI, this problem has amplified. You can see it if you look at Ruby, how it declined in the last two years. I wonder what young people do these days. Has learning programming languages become worse here?

Reasonable to assume, as a threat-modeling step.

I'm not an expert but I would imagine that's the unfortunate nature of a POW challenge: a few seconds for an individual, a millenia for a zombie army.

Same thing for Anubis, Cloudflare challenges, CAPTCHAs, etc.

They're still directed at competitors, it's just every node not compromised by whatever state actor is doing this is treated as one.

It's so much faster now. If it's slow for you, try a new circuit, sometimes you will get a slow one, but it is easy to just get a new one

item.title: What's Next for Nvidia?
item.description: 441 points, 559 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (steveblank.com)

→ HN comments  ·  441 points  ·  559 comments  ·  comments as of 20h

Top #1 — areoform:

What made Steve Jobs great was that he would rather have Apple cannibalize its successful product lines than fall prey to a competitor. You can see this pattern with the iPod. The iPod disrupted itself many, many times. The iPod Mini then the iPod Nano. Then the iPod shuffle as the answer to the race ot the bottom.

The biggest moment was partnering with Motorola as phones started becoming more capable and flash memory got cheaper to bring music to phones, which was then the prelude to the iPhone.

The iPhone killed the iPod. Most companies would have never created the product, because it would have killed their golden goose, but Jobs did.

Just like he went all in on the iPad which had the potential to kill the cheap student Mac.

If Nvidia's next CEO is smart, they'd buy up a bunch of these companies that "burn" weights to silicon, make the process better, and then sell that as a service. Let it cannibalize the sales of their products. It's better for them to do it to themselves than their competitors.

↳ reply 1 — CoolestBeans:

Jensen's strategy has been to stimulate demand and then own as big a chunk of it as you can. This is the strategy of GPGPUs and CUDA. Have developers go create new demand for your cards and then lock them in. And they did. Financially, the circular deals are similar. Getting into making ASIC inference chips, you don't own the demand and you're making a commodity so you can't lock people in.

Steve Jobs was completely unsentimental about obsoleting Apple's lineup with new products but that's because Steve Jobs's strategy was to be a ruthless fast follower. Just wait for the technology to catch up with a burgeoning product category and then come out with a product with way more polish and sensible UX than everyone else. That's great for consumer electronics but its not so great for Nvidia. There's a lot less value in "taste" and "polish" when it comes to a device that's going to sit in a data center for its whole life.

↳↳ reply — mike_hearn:

Is there? A lot of what made CUDA good beyond the basics was the polish.

↳↳↳ reply — torginus:

I am surprised nobody caught up to CUDA. Back in the early 10s I wrote my thesis in OpenCL, and I picked it on a whim, tooling seemed about equal.

Since then, OpenCL fell off completely while the CUDA of today doesn't seem all that different to my cursory inspection. Also, I'm not sure how high-level a language modern CUDA is, considering that back then it was common wisdom that every uArch was so different that you could easily lose more than half of the performance if you didn't optimize for it, which often meant swapping out entire algorithms or changing how the data is laid out. This applied to moving between vendors and moving to newer generations from the same vendor. So programming CUDA was much more about trying to coax the compiler into generating the right sort of assembly.

Besides, my impression is that the kernels that run LLMs are a relatively small-ish (thousands of lines). Even with awful tooling, you can get a couple engineers to port the code to your architecture of choice, or nowadays, you can get the agents themselves to do it for you.

↳ reply 2 — FuriouslyAdrift:

AMD got ahead of them and bought the main company that does that first.

https://www.forbes.com/sites/jonmarkman/2026/08/09/amd-buys-...

↳ reply 3 — pyrale:

> If Nvidia's next CEO is smart, they'd buy up a bunch of these companies that "burn" weights to silicon

I really don't get why people want model asics. Why would you want that, when MoEs are everywhere?

Top #2 — 01100011:

As the author mentions, the biggest threat is from customers becoming competitors. The problem space is stabilizing and this allows the biggest buyers of GPUs to work with companies like broadcom to make their own chips. Thanks to agents, they can also spin up their own abstraction layers and debug tools. CUDA is becoming less relevant, and the rate at which that is happening is about to go parabolic.

Surely Nvidia won’t stand still and will continue to compete, but the margins will collapse along with volumes.

AMD will probably suffer less, relatively speaking. Their failure to invest in software finally seems to be paying off now that LLMs can pick up their slack. But the growth currently priced in to their stock will never materialize and they’ll be seen as arriving just in time for the lights to go out.

↳ reply 1 — vannevar:

>As the author mentions, the biggest threat is from customers becoming competitors.

Maybe in the long term. The biggest threat in the short term is Nvidia's exposure to the data center bubble, which was already showing signs of popping before Jensen's departure. Given Nvidia's role as a key investment bank in the AI trade, making and brokering circular financing deals around data centers, his departure could hasten the data center collapse if the company starts backing away from its key financing role.

↳↳ reply — Certhas:

I feel like the article skipped over this: Right now Huang seems to have been reinventing nVidia as a bank. And the successor will have to decide whether to try to execute on that.

↳↳↳ reply — adrian_b:

Yesterday there was some news article where the interim CEO and CFO said that she is re-examining the financing agreements that NVIDIA has with a great number of companies for purchasing GPUs.

She did not explain what she means by this, but the implication was that she might want to diminish the exposure that NVIDIA currently has for those companies becoming unable to pay.

↳ reply 2 — psadri:

Apple's strategy here was to buy out the most advanced fab's capacity years in advance. I think NVDA was probably doing the same. Even if you can design a new chip, you can't get it built because all the cutting edge fab capacity is locked up. Ironically that sustains demand for your product, enabling you to continue this pattern! Maybe NVDA's circular investments were to ensure this "demand" is sustained whenever they hit a slow patch.

Top #3 — kristopolous:

JIC people don't know the site's author Steve Blank is this Steve Blank https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Blank

The Startup Owner's Manual and The Four Steps to the Epiphany are fine books ... Certainly somewhere in my top 40 startup books you should take the time to understand. Like Geoffrey Moore, Ries & Trout, Clayton Christensen, somewhere in that group.

You'll be in for a commitment though.

A lot of popular "must read" business books are just folksy fluff ... blank is the opposite.

↳ reply 1 — z3dd:

For not chronically online - JIC seems to be 'just in case'

↳ reply 2 — khoo:

You mentioned top 40, what other books do you have in your list?

item.title: VisualBasic.World: A gallery of Planet Source Code programs from 1997 to 2012
item.description: 200 points, 76 comments. See description for top comments.

→ Article (visualbasic.world)

→ HN comments  ·  200 points  ·  76 comments

Top #1 — robviren:

A lovely gaggle of whacky, strange, and absolutely diverse projects. Very of the era with some of them. Views like this being me joy because it shows a more raw view of people just playing with technology and figuring it out rather than everything having to be perfect.

With AI powered project cleanup it will be hard to land back into a phase like this. Feels like everything lands in sort of a safe median now. Mercifully my 8 year old son came home with an absolutely awful looking PowerPoint slide deck printed off the other day. And we made a terrible HTML site with random pokemon gifs and Marquee elements. Gotta keep the flame of creativity lit for as long as I can. Haha.

↳ reply 1 — FearNotDaniel:

> raw view of people just playing with technology and figuring it out

I’m willing to bet that 30 years from now we’ll have exactly the same nostalgic response to the vibe-coded Claude UIs that are changing the rules about how software gets built in an uncannily similar way to those glory days of VB.

↳↳ reply — robviren:

I'm positive I'll look like so old foggie shaking my fist at things. It's strange to me that in the context of something like the Holodeck in Startrek I never had these thoughts about the stolen labor from 3d artists, voice actors, and programmers when they would have "computer" vibe code a Shakespeare scene for them. Obviously a different context but it's interesting how different realized pushback to such a capable system is vs the idealized version. Much like the 90s hopes and dreams of a connected information system enriching everyone's lives turns into a terror filled lie machine.

IDK, I just like when a person or teams of people can reason about a system. Claude can do incredible things but we do lose some of the reasoning and honestly some of the whimsy, irregularity, and intent, which this gallery shows. I'm torn because it enables people to do things they may have otherwise not done, but also pulls everyone with an invisible hands towards the bell curve of what has been done. For a vast majority of things that's probably ok, for anything novel it's an intelligent convincing barrier whispering to you that you should be conventional.

↳↳↳ reply — mostlysimilar:

> It's strange to me that in the context of something like the Holodeck in Startrek I never had these thoughts about the stolen labor from 3d artists, voice actors, and programmers when they would have "computer" vibe code a Shakespeare scene for them.

item.title: Old Bitly links are being hijacked
item.description: 369 points, 195 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (ransomnews.com)

→ HN comments  ·  369 points  ·  195 comments  ·  comments as of 22h

Top #1 — xp84:

Link shorteners that are outsourced are in my humble opinion an order of magnitude worse for the internet than they would be if in-house.

The way they accrete URLs over time, and then time passes, and anything can happen (your account gets deactivated, shortener company goes out of business / experiences catastrophic data loss / etc) is just asking for permanently broken links which may be unfixable.

Especially when you consider how these services can, unless they're spammy enough to inject gross interstitial ad pages, make 0 revenue from you if you aren't currently paying for a premium service, it's easy to see how they can go under.

Note: Clearly with the kind of ephemeral crap these 2011 tweets were, I'm assuming the 'attacker' publicized "Hey guys look at these funny tweets" because obviously who cares about 15 year old McDonalds marketing messages. But in general it's sad to see these still being used. To be fair to bitly, they do offer the ability to use your own domain at least, but sadly, with a service targeted mainly at marketing departments, usually they don't have the ability to work with the in-house tech team(s) to even set up DNS.

↳ reply 1 — dijit:

Yeah, but the alternative is everyone having a short domain, which is unfortunately difficult due to the fundamental mathematical principle that a low amount of characters has a very small number of options available.

Everything with finite space is expensive, the more finite the more expensive.

So, while I am in favour of what you say, and I’m in favour of self-governance as much as possible, I understand the challenges.

↳↳ reply — citrin_ru:

> but the alternative is everyone having a short domain

a typical domain is not that long (but a typical URL is), one can have a short-url service in the same domain https://example.com/r/Yx9FH -> https://example.com/a-typically-long-url

↳↳↳ reply — xp84:

^agree. Yeah it’s not that important that the domain is shockingly short anymore. Just use something like go.(mycompany).com/slug

Your audience can type your whole domain name, it’ll be fine.

↳ reply 2 — OJFord:

I don't think it goes either way in general – it's just whether you're trust the stability of the company creating the link or the third-party (in one case) providing the link service more isn't it?

Bit.ly et al. (even some that have disappeared) must have outlived many a startup that used their services, leaving working links behind (that didn't necessarily go down with the startup if archived, on 'social media' rather than their own site, etc.).

↳ reply 3 — thephyber:

This comment is where the risk is.

Also, my company at the time saw an uptick in account takeovers when HotMail (a popular free email provider) changed their policy to allowing usernames to be recycled. Because email account ownership is basically equivalent to identity proof for most websites, HotMail's policy change effectively cost us a massive customer service workload. (I think the mass liquidity of virtual items out of accounts was more of the direct issue, not so much that users were still active on our site while being inactive on their email account for a year)

Top #2 — 101008:

Short anecdote: Famous author (with huge fanbase!) used a Bit.ly link in one of their books (the narrative needed a fake tweet with fake link). Editor didn't notice/care and never registered it. I noticed on release date, caught it and redirected it to a website that referenced the book, a few people tweet about it thinking the author used the link on purpose!

↳ reply — 4ggr0:

that's very kind of you! the wrong person noticing this could've done some really nasty stuff...

Top #3 — silisili:

I think the biggest surprise to me is that a URL shortener makes enough money to have a Trust and Safety team. I assumed it was just a side project a person or two ran.

↳ reply 1 — transcriptase:

My take is that any shortener without one would voluntarily close doors after being inundated with the most illegal, scammy, and horrid use-cases, and subsequent requests from law enforcement that would far outweigh any ROI.

↳↳ reply — supriyo-biswas:

As someone who was running such a service for a brief period of time, parent is 100% correct.

↳↳↳ reply — tgv:

While abuse of internet facilities does not come as a surprise, I wonder why they would want to shorten those urls? To hide them, probably, but from what? Do you have any insight?

↳ reply 2 — geor9e:

Google had a popular link-shortening service for a long time before trust and safety started consuming too much staff time, and they killed it. Considering how often link shorteners are used for scams and illegal stuff, you either need a trust and safety team or you're just waiting for the FBI to knock and do it for you.

item.title: Vulcan rocket fails during return-to-flight launch, 40 Amazon satellites lost

Top #1 — allenrb:

I’ve been a huge SpaceX fan since back when they were failing to reach orbit with Falcon 1. That said, we (the US, the planet) need more than one successful launch provider. Even Elon (of whom I’m not such a fan) has said things along these lines.

Top #1 — diverted247:

Here is the design https://dai.studio/ted/ex-baron that was used to generate the "baron" flight simulator.

Source: https://github.com/dai-studio/ex-baron (BSD 2-Clause)

Each typed element in the design describes detailed aspects of the game. This is the primary "Context" element. Just select an element to see it's schema/data.

"Baron is an arcade biplane game set in a WWI-inspired, cartoon world. The player builds their aircraft in the hangar, takes off from an airfield, flies over a procedurally generated landscape under procedurally generated clouds, and lands again. There is no combat. Pillars: (1) Flying feels great: quick to learn, satisfying to master. (2) A readable, cheerful cartoon look: toon shading, ink outlines, bold colours. (3) Every flight is different: a seed generates terrain, clouds and airfields. (4) Instant play: opens in a browser tab with no install."

Try pasting the raw diagram into an agent, here is the prompt...

"Build https://dai.studio/ted/ex-baron/raw"

You won't get the identical game but all the specified details will be there in the end result. If you swap out some key dependencies... Unreal Engine vs three.js, you will get some wild result. Have fun and post your results. :)

Top #2 — kqr:

I'm surprised how well this handled. I usually have large complaints on the flight dynamics in projects like these, and for this (in expert mode) they were not that large. Of course, it's no X-Plane, but I'm trying to keep in mind what sort of project it is. In a good blend of arcade and simulation, it should be a toy that is easy to get into, but someone who has simulator experience should also feel at home and not run into counter-intuitive dynamics.

I suppose I am a little surprised the biplane was able to loop on its own power from level flight.

Interaction-wise, I would have liked

- to be able to invert the Y axis on the mouse control! Nuts that this alternative is not included.

- a vertical speed gauge all the time, not just when the simulator thinks I'm about to land.

- go-arounds to be handled more gracefully, rather than as a very long landing.

- a trim control on the mouse wheel to set the airspeed. (And then the mouse control could keep returning to centre, at least in expert mode.)

- a toggle for opting out of metric units, and instead using more customary knots for speed, feet for altitude, feet per minute for vertical speed etc.

- pre-tuned navigation radios (or even just VFR charts) as an optional replacement for arrows in the sky.

With these changes (and possibly more I think of later) this could be a really fun way to get children into flight simulation, since it's so action packed.

↳ reply — diverted247:

The goal was a light, fun, open, introductory flight sim. My kids wanted to try a loop, so I added flaps and added 25% more power to biplane. Just enough.

Great list, I will add these in time.

Top #1 — breue:

The sad part is I was one of their first customers - I helped onboard over a 70 clients for them over the years.

↳ reply — weird-eye-issue:

So you allowed people to do card testing on your platform and never recognized it was happening? You have to keep on top of things like that especially if using Stripe Connect where users can withdraw money since you are facilitating theft and money laundering

> there was very little negligence on our side

Lol

> they nerfed the post

Nobody nerfed the post. It just isn't interesting since it's your fault. Lesson learned, hopefully!

↳↳ reply — matheusmoreira:

So the corporation doesn't care about a guy who generated 1.6 million dollars in fees and onboarded additional clients? Even when they post about their problem publicly on HN?

I suppose it's hopeless for the rest of us.

↳↳↳ reply — weird-eye-issue:

He misused their platform by failing to do proper verification of marketplace users and transactions and allowed criminals to extract several thousand dollars from victims of credit card theft. He's the one at fault here and his unverified claims about fees sounds like it's from a different project anyways so what exactly do you expect support to do? Roll out the red carpet and help him out with these fees related to the funds he helped launder? If he was negligent and didn't do the proper verifications of the buyers and sellers on his platform then he shouldn't have set it up in the first place. It's basic common sense and if he's really used Stripe so much he would know that. Instead of immediately blaming Stripe why don't you ask him if he followed all of the best practices for using Stripe Connect

It's a relatively risky thing to implement so you should only do it if you have all the checks in place and can accept a certain level of risk: https://docs.stripe.com/connect/risk-management

Top #2 — philsquared_:

This is as high risk as it comes... imagine a person bought a lemonade from you for $1 then later on you charged them $1500 because you saved their cc. That is all stripe sees.

You need to not charge the $1 at all first of all because technically that is a fraudulent transaction since the customer is expecting to pay $1500 not $1501. Stripes docs literally say this by the way... you can always run an auth but that isn't my recommendation...

You should be sending them payable invoices through stripes invoice system not manually charging a saved card. In this case you should have sent 3 $500 invoices.

Stripe is not wrong in this case. You made yourself look like a scammer.

↳ reply — josephcsible:

Stripe is wrong in this case. They'd only be right to leave you banned if you are a scammer. If you're not a scammer but just look like one, you should be able to get your ban overturned.

↳↳ reply — dannyw:

We still don’t know what OP’s business actually is. From the description, it sounds very similar to activities like an escort business.

I’m not saying that’s what OP does, but $1 + $1500 and being super vague about the commercial activity doesn’t help.

If OP wasn’t fully transparent and messaged stripe support explaining their business as “we connect homeowners with pre booked appointments” to Stripe then yeah, anyone who works in the field would’ve closed as unsupported business.

↳↳↳ reply — refulgentis:

Isn't it in the first line? "Pre-booked appointments with homeowners, sold to local contractors" is appointment setting for home-improvement contractors: you line up a homeowner who wants a roofer, HVAC tech, etc., and the contractor pays per appointment that actually happens. That's a common, boring industry.

It did put a smile on my face, realizing how easy it is to miscommunicate. I never would have imagined someone hearing that and thinking "Ah, escort service."

Top #3 — didgeoridoo:

Yeah unfortunately this charge pattern could not have looked MORE like merchant fraud. The right approach would have been to use https://docs.stripe.com/payments/setup-intents and set it for off-session usage.

You still might have gotten a payment hold on the first transaction until someone in risk could take a peek at your site to make sure you had all the right disclosures in place, but you probably would have kept the account.

China is following the "buy, build , bridge" strategy and wishes not to be prevented from following it:

1 Buy) To be able to buy or otherwise access latest GPUs/silicon for the training and development of their own models and strategic tasks they might want their models to assist them with.

2 Build) To be able to eventually design (with the help of 1) and manufacture their own world class GPUs/silicon, freeing themselves of geopolitical rivals interference in the supply chain.

3 Bridge) While they are working to get to (2), they want to sanctions-proof compute wherever they can get it. To this end they have Chinese owned and operated companies build and lease facilities outside of strict US export control geographies.

There are a whole bunch of other policies and measures and pressures brought to bear to make 1, 2, and 3 happen, but those are the big pillars.

item.title: Microsoft 365 outage leads to chlorine gas poisoning of 15 hotel guests
item.description: 615 points, 269 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (www1.wdr.de)

→ HN comments  ·  615 points  ·  269 comments  ·  comments as of 25h

Top #1 — amluto:

I personally operate a fairly advanced closed-loop chlorination system, and this is beyond screwed up.

These systems can easily fail, and they tend to fail in a way that causes them to measure low or zero chlorine and thus overdispense chlorine. More below on why.

First, this means that an operator must always ensure safety, both against excessive chlorine and against insufficient chlorine. In a commercial context, that means that a real human (or maybe a totally different sensor design, e.g. a colorimetric sensor) need to measure the pool chlorine level, preferably with a high quality titration (drop test) every day before opening the pool. They should probably record the result in pen on water resistant paper, but this part is icing on the cake.

Second, hoping that an email gets noticed is ridiculous. If you do not have positive confirmation that the pool is safe to open, don’t open it.

Third, the systems should be sized so that they cannot overdose quickly. The maximum dispensing rate should be such that hours of continuous operation would be required to reach an uncomfortable level, let alone a dangerous level. (Hot tubs are sort of an exception here.)

Fourth, everyone should be using a reasonable amount of CYA in their pool. Even at a lowish level of 30ppm CYA it takes a lot of chlorine to become dangerous unless the operator has also lost control of pH. I realize that some codes are confused about this.

Fifth, chlorine is smelly. Someone should have noticed, even just casually. Admittedly, lots of swimmers may be conditioned to stinky pools, and checking for safety isn’t their job. But the staff should notice.

Sixth, the systems I’ve seen beep when there’s an alert. It’s easy to add flashing lights, too. (In fact, the system I’m familiar with automatically shuts down if it feeds for more than X minutes without reaching the setpoint, and you cannot turn this feature off. You can, however, defeat it by switching the power to the whole controller.)

—- sensors —-

Actual free chlorine sensors intended for pools use an amperometric probe immersed in iodide solution or gel, separated from the pool water by a fancy membrane. Free chlorine oxidizes iodide to iodine, and the sensor measures the iodine concentration. If the membrane fails (or general wear and tear or excessive pressure swings) cause the iodide to be lost, then the chlorine can’t react and the sensor reads zero (or low if there’s tiny bit of iodide left).

Interestingly, these sensors are rather expensive devices that appear to mostly come from France and Germany. The Chinese vendors seem to be rebranding European parts (!), and the major US vendor is very clearly reselling a French company’s product.

There are some vendors who sell a cheap (or absurdly marked up) potentiometric ORP-based closed-loop system. In my considered opinion, these are worse than useless.

↳ reply 1 — jug:

Yep, my wife worked on a hotel in the past and they always tested for chlorine before opening, in person with equipment. It was simply part of cleaning services etc. And that was no big deal of a hotel either in a fairly small city, indicative of how commonplace this _should_ be and how much of a screwup this is.

If I were to guess, this is not the only problem that hotel has as it speaks of systemic issues.

↳ reply 2 — malfist:

> Fifth, chlorine is smelly.

Isn't it the chloramines that are smelly? Or at least non free chlorine. A strong chlorine smell is often a sign of a poorly cared for pool or spa

↳ reply 3 — wlonkly:

> reasonable amount of CYA in their pool. Even at a lowish level of 30ppm CYA

The pool in the article clearly needed more than 30 ppm, they definitely did not sufficiently cover their asses here.

Top #2 — N19PEDL2:

This is 100% fault of the hotel, not of Microsoft. It’s unacceptable that the communications regarding such a dangerous thing totally rely on email, without any backup or double check.

↳ reply 1 — DanHulton:

Decades of “root cause analysis” poisoning have ruined our ability to think about safety and reliability holistically.

There isn’t one root cause here or one person or entity at fault. Many things went wrong and bad choices were made by many people and entities to lead us to this point, and they ought to be all regarded seriously and addressed rigorously.

- Whomever at the hotel that approved this as the sole (or even primary) alert system is at fault. - The lack of training and experience this hotel employee had when in a position to make such a dangerous choice was at fault. - Ditto the alarm company - everyone involved in designing, approving, and implementing this system is at fault, as well as whatever process ensured that nobody had the experience or safety to be able to speak up about this dangerous design is at fault. - The regulatory system that allowed this design is at fault. - The health and safety inspection system that didn’t catch this risk is at fault.

I’m sure there’s more; I’m just spitballing here. But the point is that there’s no one person or thing to blame here, and no one fix. This should kick off a wave of personal and professional soul-searching and improvements.

↳↳ reply — delta_p_delta_x:

> Decades of “root cause analysis” poisoning have ruined our ability to think about safety and reliability holistically.

This is not the case in aviation. Even in the most egregiously obvious single-cause failures, there's always an analysis of issues in the wider system that allowed that single cause to become the single cause in the first place.

I agree with your points, though. In this case, Microsoft absolutely takes shared responsibility. It is only a matter of time until a similar outage in some other wider networked system with a so-called 'five/seven/nine nines uptime guarantee' goes out for a couple of days, and takes with it some critical life-sustaining system, and people die.

↳↳↳ reply — fransje26:

> This is not the case in aviation.

And yet, as late as yesterday, the idiots in charge have announced that there is absolutely "No Need To Investigate the FAA Ground Stop".

↳ reply 2 — toofy:

> This is 100% fault of the hotel, not of Microsoft.

- the hotel company for seemingly doing no dilligence at all. and just blindly listening to some salesman “connect everything”

- accountant types and their “we can save pennie’s if we cut all of these corners.” and the stupid corners they choose to cut.

- etc…

on a macro scale it’s amazing to me how many people are victims to slimey car salesman types leading to situations like this.

Top #3 — bketelsen:

I'm not even going to read the article. If your hotel depends on some cloud service to prevent chlorine gas poisoning you're doing something terribly wrong. Full stop. I don't know anything about the laws in Germany but this is dangerously close to libel in the US.

item.title: Crows make decisions faster than we can
item.description: 304 points, 202 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (nytimes.com)

→ HN comments  ·  304 points  ·  202 comments  ·  comments as of 26h

Top #1 — Animats:

Intelligence has evolved on Earth at least three times - mammals, corvids, and octopuses. All the mammals have roughly the same brain architecture. But the corvids are not on the same evolutionary branch, and have a different neuron design and a different brain architecture. "Such behavioral flexibility might seem unexpected because a layered cerebral cortex, the highest integration center in the mammalian brain, is not existant in birds."[1] So there's more than one way to do intelligence. Useful to know for AI purposes.

Octopuses have a much more distributed system than mammals, suggesting a quite different approach is possible.

[1] https://niederlab.org/Nieder%20(2017)%20COBS.pdf

↳ reply 1 — animal531:

"Roughly the same brain architecture" is true, but watching the processing speed in short term memory tests in chimps is quite impressive: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PNrWUS13th8

Humans can also be trained in tasks like these and we improve a lot over the course of training, but my ADD banana brain for one probably won't ever get past 50-60% of what the chimp can do.

↳↳ reply — imchillyb:

While that is impressive, the chimps will not lay awake at night due to existential dread from contemplating our reality sphere.

Speed is not necessarily always a good thing. Deep contemplation is usually much preferred over spotting the ripest banana first.

↳↳↳ reply — TedDoesntTalk:

> lay awake at night due to existential dread from contemplating our reality sphere ... Deep contemplation is usually much preferred"

Decades ago I would have agreed with you. Not anymore. What you describe is anxiety about things that haven't happened. Most of what I've worried about never came to pass, and I'm not alone. Deep contemplation and thinking is very often not helpful except in a work environment.

↳ reply 2 — Sharlin:

I don't think you can single out corvids from the rest of the avians and at the same time bunch all mammals together. I don't think there's evidence that their smarts or brain architecture are qualitatively different from other birds, some of which are plenty smart. If intelligence - for some definition of intelligence - evolved separately in mammals and birds, it's not implausible to me that the basic architecture developed before avian dinosaurs branched from other theropods, and some theropods might have been quite smart indeed.

↳ reply 3 — Vetch:

You left off Parrots, which are just about as intelligent as Corvids. For example, keas have a similar number of pallial neurons to ravens (or maybe slightly more). Parrots and songbirds generally have extremely high neural density but still lower raw neuron counts compared to primates, which makes their competitiveness in many cognitive tasks interesting.

Among parrots, everyone knows African Greys but cockatoos are also highly intelligent, with goffin's cockatoos the standouts in terms of cleverness.

Top #2 — taeric:

Speed of decision based on visual cues seems like it would have to be faster for anything that can fly? Would be neat to see them compared specifically to race drivers.

Similarly, I'd assume that any of the fast swimmers have a faster response time?

Is this not what people's priors would have been going into the idea?

Top #3 — WalterBright:

They might think faster because the brain is smaller - a shorter distance for connections.

For example, learning to play a piano is training the spine, not the brain. Because the feedback loop with the spine is shorter.

It's the same with dancing. One is trained to not look at one's feet, because the feedback loop is too slow.

↳ reply 1 — rob74:

Spine? I thought it was the cerebellum (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cerebellum)? Any kind of motion that you have learned so well as to be able to do it "subconsciously" (playing an instrument, riding a bicycle, walking etc.) is stored in the cerebellum. The moment I realized how important this is was back in driving school while learning to start a stick shift car from a full stop. This requires some coordination between releasing the clutch pedal and pressing the gas pedal, and my first attempts failed miserably, killing the engine. Next day it suddenly started working, because the cerebellum had taken over.

↳ reply 2 — jyounker:

That is going to be part of the answer, simply because birds have much smaller neurons that are more densely packed than in mammals. They are also much more energy efficient, using something like 1/3 of the energy. They also have a different neural architecture, which may also contribute.

Long time SRE/DevOps with 20 year of FinTech experience in banks/hedge funds/crypto and having seen many, many outages (some listed here [0]):

- There is almost always a standard operating procedure (SOP)

- Just b/c there is a SOP for releases etc, that doesn't mean that people always follow it

- This can be due to many reasons e.g. laziness, being distracted, pressure from higher ups ("just push it out there and I'll take the risk" ha!), tired from having a newborn etc etc

item.description: 204 points, 120 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (joshblais.com)

→ HN comments  ·  204 points  ·  120 comments  ·  comments as of 18h

Top #1 — kmstout:

Shameless plug time: About a year and a half ago, I wrote [1] about a way of squeezing more text onto the screen, using Emacs, that plays well with eww and does a reasonable job of preserving readability. Basically, it's a hack that builds on follow-mode to quickly convert a frame into a columnar display for long buffers, with interactive adjustment of the number of columns.

[1] https://www.reindeereffect.com/0002

↳ reply — marttt:

I used Emacs around 2010-2012 or so as a journalist, and I remember asking help on Stackoverflow regarding this exact same thing. I've lost my elisp multi-column-mode snippet; thanks for sharing yours. It was a really good way to edit a longer story; it's actually quite surprising that using something like this in a text editor is not that common. I later moved over to Plan9 Acme editor and IIRC implemented a similar solution there as well.

If you want to put the multi-column mode on massive steroids, check out an old Vim add-on called microViche for inspiration -- "text editing on an infinite pane": https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9YNiPUTGO28 and https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xkED6Mv_4bc

The addon itself, FWIW (no idea if it works on a current Vim): https://www.vim.org/scripts/script.php?script_id=4835

I remember trying to use this one as well, because the paradigm/concept is really cool and IMO unusual. I couldn't really get used to it, but it was a fun and inspirational way to make one's brain explode.

Top #2 — Arubis:

The most important part of this is toward the end, and whether you consider it a limitation or a feature is a matter of perspective: the modern commercial web does not play nice with this. So static HTML and blogs yes, Reddit and most anything commercial no.

You can actually get other close-to-browser experiences with stuff like xwidget and embedded WebKit (https://emacsdocs.org/docs/emacs/Embedded-WebKit-Widgets) but generally it’s not worth the fight for commercial sites these days; everything is vibed and only tested against Chrome, so if you’re lucky they’ll load in other Chromium browsers and _maybe_ Firefox.

↳ reply 1 — graemep:
