Quite a lot of sites work well with other browser engines too. I have tried PaleMoon, Netsurf. Users of Apple mobile devices seem to be fine with Safari.

Really light or unusual browsers might be a problem. Dillo, for example (its very fast though).

↳↳ reply — dunham:

The two things that I'm missing in Safari are auto dark mode (re-coloring pages) and toggling javascript per-site. Currently I'm using the "Quiche" browser (paid) for that, but github is suddenly hating it (requiring a login). I like that desktop chrome lets me toggle javascript per site out of the box.

It sounds like the dark mode thing is coming in the next Safari release.

↳ reply 2 — kkylin:

I think that's absolutely right: whether this works or not depends on what you do.

I tried xwidget-webkit as main browser briefly, but very quickly gave up. When a collaborator sends me a Google Doc, for example, I really still need a browser to work on it. I still use xwidget-webkit daily -- it's a great PDF viewer, and really nice to be able to have Jupyter notebooks open side by side with code buffers -- but for most tasks involving the web I'll switch to a browser.

The one thing above all that is urgently necessary is a content-addressable replacement for (or layer above) HTTP(S) which is genuinely ready to go and has adoption which is meaningful and moving in the right direction. Unfortunately we seem to be going in the wrong direction there right now. Cute browser setups and retro-chic web servers are fun and a nice gesture but they won't get us there.

item.title: All AI-generated code should be Open Source
item.description: 1166 points, 615 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (jakub.jankiewicz.org)

→ HN comments  ·  1166 points  ·  615 comments  ·  comments as of 18h

Top #1 — jrmg:

In the United States the Copyright Office actually has guidance on this that I feel most people aren’t aware of.

https://www.copyright.gov/ai/Copyright-and-Artificial-Intell...

An excerpt, with emphasis mine:

• Questions of copyrightability and AI can be resolved pursuant to existing law, without the need for legislative change.

• The use of AI tools to assist rather than stand in for human creativity does not affect the availability of copyright protection for the output.

• Copyright protects the original expression in a work created by a human author, even if the work also includes AI-generated material.

• Copyright does not extend to purely AI-generated material, or material where there is insufficient human control over the expressive elements.

• Whether human contributions to AI-generated outputs are sufficient to constitute authorship must be analyzed on a case-by-case basis.

• Based on the functioning of current generally available technology, prompts do not alone provide sufficient control.

• Human authors are entitled to copyright in their works of authorship that are perceptible in AI-generated outputs, as well as the creative selection, coordination, or arrangement of material in the outputs, or creative modifications of the outputs.

• The case has not been made for additional copyright or sui generis protection for AI- generated content.

I am sure there will be many more legal battles and probably legislation about this to come.

↳ reply 1 — timbritt:

This is why I keep a comprehensive and exhaustive record of infrastructural, architectural, business logic and code-level decisions in the form of tasks/issues for everything I build. It’s literally a real-time record of my personal involvement in the design of the system.

↳↳ reply — trinsic2:

Same here, but I do it to remind myself where I've been and where i am going.

↳ reply 2 — rixed:

It doesn't say much about the copyrights of the many authors whose work was in the model training data, or does it?

↳ reply 3 — Garlef:

So...

• What about non-ai code generators (such as https://heyapi.dev/)?

• And what about a code generator that is a hybrid? (So: Something like heyapi but with LLM/agents intertwined)

Top #2 — blagie:

I am the author of multiple AGPL systems, many in mainstream use. Early LLM models would spit out my code almost verbatim. Modern systems borrow heavily on the creative design of those systems.

One company first pirated my AGPL code (e.g. shipped it without my name, copyright notices, source availability, etc.). I sent them violation notices. After many months of fighting, they had an LLM clone the system. The LLM clone feels:

a) Buggy and bad compared to my code

b) Still, like it's basically my creative content

It's as if you asked an LLM to rewrite Harry Potter, with the same plot, but bad dialogue.

↳ reply 1 — thephyber:

> b) Still, like it's basically my creative content

Isn't this the crux of all IP theft issues?

There was a lawsuit against Katy Perry's _Dark Horse_ song based on a supposedly reused melody. The lawsuit succeeded, but there are music experts who break down the case on YouTube and it's not clear why the plaintiff won (except perhaps the plaintiff's expert was more convincing than the defendant's).

As applied to LLMs, we still don't have clear legal guidance about where the line between copying and "being inspired by", especially since we don't normally apply the verb "inspired by" to non-human things.

↳↳ reply — patentatt:

There is well-established precedent for clean-room design being a defense in copyright infringement of software. The question remains if LLM-assisted design is actually ‘clean’ or not, and it would be fascinating to see the experts debate it.

↳↳↳ reply — bayindirh:

The problem with these LLMs are they really emitted the same code, verbatim. One scientific library developer was able to emit his code from his repository by typing the beginning of the function name, and the "thing" completed the rest of it, as-is [0].

We can debate clean-room development all day long, and it's fair point, but the pain point is/was reproducing the repo as-is, sans its license and ownership information.

GitHub promised to build tools around its Copilot to find code provenance (e.g.: list of repos with similar code), but they silently dropped all the plans AFAIK, since it'll show how the sausage is made, and nobody wants you to know how that sausage is made.

I stand corrected: They added it, but I don't know at what capacity because I don't use LLM assisted code generation [1].

[0]: https://x.com/docsparse/status/1581461734665367554

[1]: https://github.blog/ai-and-ml/github-copilot/preview-referen...

↳ reply 2 — Aurornis:

> Early LLM models would spit out my code almost verbatim. Modern systems borrow heavily on the creative design of those systems.

Do you have some specific, actual examples you can share?

I’ve been hearing this exact claim for years, but every time I ask for a specific example, any example at all, I can’t seem to find anything more than a highly generic snippet of code or a coerced continuation.

Top #3 — viraptor:

Doe v. GitHub already decided (I'm simplifying, read the actual thing yourself) that LLM output is not automatically open source - or specifically it doesn't infringe on the open source training material and doesn't inherit the oss copyright notice.

Thaler v. Perlmutter (again simplified) showed 100% AI output can't be given any copyright.

The directions the current cases are going are very much opposed to that idea and I wouldn't expect things to change in the opposite direction.

↳ reply 1 — carllerche:

That is not the Thaler v. Perlmutter conclusion. That case was about whether the machine itself could be made an author under copyright law. That is very different than whether AI output can be protected by copyright law. I am not aware of any cases that test that question yet.

↳ reply 2 — WaitWaitWha:

They will just claim the code is trade secret and use Defend Trade Secrets Act (DTSA).

And, the DTSA has only two reqs:

derive independent economic value from not being generally known or readily ascertainable by others, and the "owner" takes reasonable measures to maintain their secrecy (e.g., coke secret sauce).

since trade secret law does not prevent independent development or lawful reverse engineering, there are still opportunities. also, if a someone independently devs the same functionality, trade secret generally does not give them original dev ownership of that functionality. so, win.

Artcraft will be a good test case if Adobe goes after Brandon Thomas.

Much to be developed.

(and, this is why we keep extensive commit and development records outside of our genAI - ie provenance tracking)

item.title: Things That Turbo Pascal Is Smaller Than (2011)
item.description: 236 points, 131 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (prog21.dadgum.com)

→ HN comments  ·  236 points  ·  131 comments  ·  comments as of 19h

Top #1 — jbellis:

Anders Heljsberg GOAT. Turbo Pascal, Delphi, C#, TypeScript, just a phenomenal career marked with better taste than any other language designer I can think of, certainly any designer whose work is so mainstream.

↳ reply 1 — tim333:

This video with him on the history is good https://youtu.be/uMqx8NNT4xY "The history of C# and TypeScript with Anders Hejlsberg | GitHub"

↳ reply 2 — pjmlp:

You are missing J++, several C# features were born in J++, e.g. P/Invoke was J/Direct.

Top #2 — hawkice:

Given development speed is way up, I'd be interested to see what a from-basic-principles simple and efficient OS and programming system might look like. Or people trying radically different versions of efficiency and simplicity, like an OS that uses an existing battle-tested sandboxed execution environment like v8 for userspace safety/isolation.

Fundamentally, many inefficiencies were justified for developer productivity, and I'm not sure that makes sense anymore, and the cost of larger projects with clear abstraction boundaries has plummetted.

↳ reply 1 — Isamu:

>Fundamentally, many inefficiencies were justified for developer productivity, and I'm not sure that makes sense anymore

Having lived through this period, I would disagree, quite the opposite we tended to develop in C and assembly specifically for runtime efficiency because we had to.

For developer productivity you could opt for Lisp or SmallTalk or some such, which ran much slower until high quality compilers for these became available, and even then your target machine might only have a C compiler.

↳↳ reply — SoftTalker:

I read GP's comment differently, that we ended up where we are today (bloated languages, IDEs and runtimes) due to chasing developer productivity at all costs.

Now, developer productivity is becoming less important as developers are factored out entirely.

↳↳↳ reply — LeFantome:

We will end up with something that is easier for AI to write, efficient to execute, and possible for people to audit.

Rust is becoming popular as LLM output. The resulting code is very efficient. The compiler helps keep the LLM on track and holds it to a minimum level of quality. Humans can read it if they want to. But it is not great to read.

Python is also a popular target. Easy to audit. LOTS of training data. The “one way to do it” philosophy of Python helps. But the resulting code is not very efficient.

I think we will end up with a new language that balances all these things better.

↳ reply 2 — userbinator:

I'd be interested to see what a from-basic-principles simple and efficient OS and programming system might look like.

UNIX. Seriously. Look at what it could do with 1970s era hardware, that was unmatched even when DOS came out in the early 80s.

Top #3 — jll29:

While some comparisons may look silly, the fact that the touch command's binary should exceed Turbo Pascal is insane: the command basically creates an empty file or updates the file change date if the file already exists, not more.

There's no reason (other than laziness) why that should take more than 2k.

On the other hand, a lot of boilerplace code is repeated in each and every command. When I first learned as a kid about UNIX commands being ordinary programs, I was intrigued (there is nothing "special" about them, you can also write your own!) but also shocked about the overhead compared to an architecture in which e.g. the shell contained all (at least core) commands compiled into a single binary, which could share all the error handing, startup code, command line parsing code and so on.

↳ reply 1 — lelanthran:

> There's no reason (other than laziness) why that should take more than 2k.

Well...

     $ touch --help | wc -c
     1580
Just the text for the help message compiled into `touch` is over 1.5kB.

It's not just laziness, it's also what the program needs to do, like (for example) print out all the options it supports (1.5kB), then parse those options, execute a different code path depending on what the user wants to do, etc.

If all you want to do is update the date or create a new empty file, I can write a very short program that does that, although the minimum program in C is around 16kB (hello world), so that's the minimum overhead needed to have a C program loaded by Linux.

↳ reply 2 — pron:

By "laziness", do you mean attention to costs? Because there's been a ~30,000x inflation in RAM between 1986 and today (probably much more, because we didn't have virtual memory, let alone fast SSDs), and what's silly is to ignore that 1GB of RAM has about the same impact on the machine as 20kB in 1986. Software back then (and even a decade later) was significantly more bloated than the "lazy" programs of today.

Of course we spent a lot of effort cramming as much as we could into every byte back then, but it wasn't because of laziness, but because there was no choice and the value of that work to the user was many, many times higher than it is today.

item.title: The MacBook Pro's OLED PWM problem
item.description: 482 points, 260 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (macanorak.com)

→ HN comments  ·  482 points  ·  260 comments  ·  comments as of 20h

Top #1 — explosion-s:

As someone who’s had a concussion, this is really interesting. For me this is how any screen was to me, not just bright OLED ones. Even more interestingly it’s essentially only screens— backlist posters at the mall (paper with a backlight) still affect it but less so. To me perhaps it’s focusing on something on a screen that does this, but it’s really interesting to see this affect the general population.

It’s also odd to think about lack of ability to concentrate, and I wonder if screens cause this optically somehow but to a less noticeable degree even when less intense than this new one? (Independent distracting contents)

I noticed that adding a severe red filter to all my screens helped me significantly with the concussion and am also curious about that, would that impact the intensity of a refresh perhaps? Is blue light specifically the problem? I’m unsure but have a plethora of subjective experience.

I’m glad for this to enter public consciousness a bit and would love to see more research on the screen itself impacting our brain.

↳ reply 1 — prmoustache:

> As someone who’s had a concussion,

I am pretty sure an awful lot of people have suffered concussions and have never been diagnosed as such because they never went to ER.

↳↳ reply — alexjplant:

I met the diagnostic criteria for a concussion and went to the ER only to be told that I didn't have one because I was wearing a helmet when the accident in question happened. Me feeling funny and having missing memories apparently didn't matter. They charged me $800 for the privilege of having my blood pressure taken and receiving some WebMD print-outs about banging one's head.

I guess next time I have one I'll just skip the doctor and hope I don't die or whatever.

↳↳↳ reply — ssl-3:

It's about the same treatment even if they do decide you've had a concussion. Vitals taken, printouts produced, giant bill provided, and out the door.

↳ reply 2 — Fnoord:

After I had a psychosis (it was still 'active' at the time, in hindsight, but not as severe) I couldn't use a monitor for long, especially not gaming. It gave me immediate motion sickness, or made the headache more severe. Hw was TFT 1080p LCD screen, GPU was probably AMD 7770 HD, since a few years afterwards I replaced that with a Nvidia GeForce GTX 960.

My matte MBP 2010 didn't yield me this issue, but I didn't game on it either; just watched movies/series. A lot of them.

I grew up with CRT monitors though, and these could cause severe headaches. Especially if resolution too high.

↳ reply 3 — jareklupinski:

curious; do you mean like a red plastic see-thru filter applied on top of the screen (filtering the backlight too, like those screen protectors), or a software screen effect that makes everything on screen appear red (which on an OLED screen would probably be the same thing)?

red/blue/green detectors (cones) in our eyes use different paths and have different "refresh rates" than luminous intensity sensors (rods), im wondering if filtering to a single color makes the rods take over for visual pattern processing

Top #2 — achr2:

I am shocked that Apple would release a screen with such a low PWM frequency. Here is a paper showing humans can perceive flicker at frequencies more than double their display’s rate: https://www.nature.com/articles/srep07861

↳ reply 1 — jeremyjh:

The change in that study was dramatically different: they had half the screen black and half white and were flipping which side was which at that rate. Yes, most people could perceive that. The study included 10 participants, all in their 20s. They didn't ask about headaches other observed effects afterward.

↳↳ reply — adrian_b:

The purpose of that study was to show that the traditional fusion frequency, which is in the range of 50 to 90 Hz for most people, is valid only for what it was initially measured, i.e. the threshold where a sequence of complete static images is perceived to consist of continuous movements.

But when some new display technology is based on showing various image fragments at moments shifted in time, expecting that the eye will integrate them over time to form complete images and continuous movements, that may require higher sampling frequencies, up to 10 times higher, due to the interaction with the fast subconscious eye movements.

The study results are not surprising at all, and this is an effect that should be kept in mind by anyone who designs displays.

↳ reply 2 — winrid:

It's not even about perception at all. For some (like me) it seems to be related to muscles in the eyes reacting all the time and fatiguing, it seems such muscles can react much faster than our "perception" of flicker, so something like a 10khz PWM driven display still causes fatigue, even though there's no way you can see it. People that get headaches are probably experiencing something different.

Top #3 — Zak:

I'm surprised by Apple putting out a laptop display with slow PWM. That's the kind of detail Apple has a reputation for paying attention to when other companies don't.

↳ reply 1 — cherioo:

Apple has been using low PWM screen for nearly a decade on iphone and ipad now. There’s just been limited demand to improve this in the market outside of china.

There’s also trade off to high pwm, usually worse color accuracy. But at least give us a toggle!

↳↳ reply — xp84:

Wait, why's there a difference in demand in the China market?

↳ reply 2 — layer8:

item.title: Understanding Positional Embeddings in Modern LLMs
item.description: 227 points, 27 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (magazine.sebastianraschka.com)

→ HN comments  ·  227 points  ·  27 comments  ·  comments as of 21h

Top #1 — programjames:

This article is only about understanding the implementation of positional embeddings, but to really understand positional embeddings you have to understand the theory. Positional embeddings are group representations. This is how you find them, and this is also how you parameterize them to make them differentiable/learnable. To give a few examples:

1. Rotary positional embeddings are representations of the translation group. The n-dimensional translation group ℝⁿ is abelian, so its irreducible representations are all one-dimensional ρ: ℝⁿ → ℂ, specified by a momentum vector m: ρₘ(x) = exp(i⟨m, x⟩). You can get a multi-dimensional representation by choosing several m, which are your learnable parameters.

2. If you wanted RoPE embeddings to also preserve rotation (perhaps you have scenes viewed at arbitrary angles), you are looking for representations of the special Euclidean group. The irreducible representations in four dimensions are your familiar particles: electrons, protons, etc., and in general are parameterized by a momentum vector and a discrete spin vector. You would have to do some kind of annealing process to train the spin vector (or you could just make it constant).

3. If you want to do attention on quadtrees, well, what is the group? Suppose every node in the quadtree has local coordinates scaled to [0, 1]. Moving up/down/to a neighbor in the quadtree requires an affine transformation of the local coordinates, which compose, so we can label every node by its affine transformation to the root (x, d): y → x + 2⁻ᵈy, where x is the node's translation in the image and d is its depth in the tree. The finite-dimensional irreducible representations are parameterized by momentum vectors m as well as a modulus M and basis vectors {e₁, e₂, ..., eₖ} where k = ord₂(M) and look like ρₘ,ₑ(x, d) = DPᵈ where D is the diagonal matrix with entries Dⱼⱼ = exp(2πi⟨2ʲm, x⟩ / M) and P permutes the basis vectors.

↳ reply 1 — nlitened:

As I understand, this is post-factum rationalization of what positional embedding is, not the actual theory used to build neural networks.

From what I usually see, ML researches just throw everything at the wall and see what sticks. Whatever approach turns out to work better, gets used more often, and sometimes theoretical background is developed for why it works. RoPE works not because it’s good math, just it turned out to work better than some other equally arbitrary approaches at some point, and then other approaches have also been developed that work better than RoPE.

↳↳ reply — Mabusto:

This is the most frustrating part of trying to understand machine learning. You can read a bunch of really great math books that rigorously build concepts from the ground up (calculus, linear algebra), then you start to get into the more hand wavey math (_some_ statistical concepts feel like this) and then you start getting into some of the theory behind machine learning systems and expecting the same amount of rigor and ability to understand _why_ something works and it’s always an unsatisfying explanation. I really wish there would be more disclosure like “this is what we tried and this seems to work, we think this is why” rather than present the method, give some mathematical formalization of the method, then go “it works great” and then move on. It leaves people like me wondering if there is something that I’m missing or some hole in my knowledge that is obvious to everyone else, OR does no one actually know why this works and just don’t want to say. Just give us a hint, make the shrug emoji or something, the more I learn about machine learning, the more I get that it really is more art than science.

↳↳↳ reply — programjames:

Most people who write ML papers are at the stage of alchemy—try a bunch of things and see if you can create gold out of lead. Usually their papers are not worth reading, because even if they do something right, they do not know what made it right, and it cannot lead to further or generalizable insights.

A few ML researchers do actually have a lot of this theoretical knowledge. You can see this in papers like Variational Diffusion Models, Continuous Normalizing Flows, <?> Delta Attention. These papers are usually also better written, because the authors understand why things work so they can deprioritize irrelevant details.

↳ reply 2 — tsimionescu:

> The irreducible representations in four dimensions are your familiar particles: electrons, protons, etc

Can you explain more what you mean here? What do electrons (elementary particles) have to do with protons (complex composite particles) and with general principles of four-dimensional spatial transformation? The electrical force is not a direct consequence of space-time geometry, and even less so the specific particles we happen to find in our universe.

↳ reply 3 — LudwigNagasena:

That seems to skip a few steps that explain why any of that is important for a positional encoding. I think the original author of RoPE explains the motivation behind it in his own blogpost quite well ( https://spaces.ac.cn/archives/8265 ). And it doesn’t seem to treat group theoretic understanding as something foundational. It mostly relies on engineering goals and geometrical intuition.

It's cool to see the Nintendo games are still being developed! I was 8yo when the NES came out and my mom saved up all her waitress money and bought me one that Christmas.

↳ reply — spicyjpeg:

Basically all 8- and 16-bit consoles, as well as some later ones (such as the Game Boy Advance, Nintendo DS and more recently the N64), have very active homebrew scenes at this point. There are even no-code options for some platforms [1] that have proven to be remarkably popular, to the point even McDonald's promotional game "Grimace's Birthday" was made in GB Studio and released in emulated form. The ease of manufacturing new PCBs and cartridges using modern parts has also led to a market for physical commercial homebrew releases, both through publishers and directly from developers.

Unfortunately, like many other hobby programming niches, most homebrew communities are currently dealing with the recent influx of low-effort vibe coded games that completely defeat the point of learning to work and be creative with limited hardware. Some started adopting strict no-AI stances, which is refreshing to see when seemingly every other community is going the other way; so far my own released work (mainly on the original PlayStation) is completely free of LLM contributions and I'd like to keep it that way for as long as I can.

[1] https://www.gbstudio.dev

↳↳ reply — ImJasonH:

I've wanted to get into NES homebrewing for years but found it difficult to get started. Eventually I vibe-coded a language specifically designed to build NES games, but then fell down the rabbithole of designing that language and the compiler, instead of building games. Typical.

I was able to produce a few (very) "low effort vibe-coded games that completely defeat the point of learning to work and be creative with limited hardware", but along the way I was still able to learn how to build a compiler to be creative with limited hardware for me. And that was fun.

I'll never make anything 1/1000th as impressive as the games passionate hobbyists have made over the years, and I don't think we're even building the same thing, conceptually. For me, vibe-coding the game (and the language, and the compiler) is the game itself.

https://github.com/imjasonh/playground/blob/main/nescript/RE...

My favorite thing to come out of it is https://imjasonh.github.io/playground/nes-player/?rom=subway which is a RCR clone set on the NYC subway, complete with realistic routes, schedules and transfers. There's no "point" to it really, just go from place to place punching dudes.

But that's the thing: the things made with genAI are mostly interesting to the prompter only. Everyone is making custom one-off software that has one developer and an install base of one.

I took a glance at your game and Kunio fighting endless Kunio clones looks boring to me. I guess the realistic NYC subway angle might be interesting but it's not obviously an interesting game mechanic.

Vibe all you want, but don't expect others to be as enthusiastic of your own vibe as you are yourself.

item.title: We're Asking an Appeals Court to Require a Warrant for ALPR Searches
item.description: 325 points, 108 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (eff.org)

→ HN comments  ·  325 points  ·  108 comments  ·  comments as of 19h

Top #1 — hedora:

I don't think they should be keeping data that's not involved in an active warrant.

However, if they do anyway, there should be strong victims' rights protections so that the data is actually used during investigations.

There was a string of burglaries in our area a few years ago, and panopticon N-1 (Google Map's auto recording of all phone GPS traces for marketing information) could have found the perpetrators pretty much instantly.

They hit rural outbuildings in the middle of the night on camera, so timestamps were precise, but faces were obscured. A reverse geofence warrant keyed on time of arrival / departure would have narrowed it down to just the crooks with extremely high probability, and other details in the videos would have corroborated the GPS traces.

None of the victims were politically connected, so the police couldn't (by policy) run the reverse GPS lookups. This is the worst of both worlds: Our data is recorded to be used against us later, but if ever it would be useful, we do not have access to it. The same is true for vehicle black boxes / cameras. They record a few seconds before airbag deploy, but you usually are not allowed to access them as part of an insurance dispute (even the ones from your own car).

↳ reply 1 — digitalPhonix:

> However, if they do anyway

They should face criminal penalties for violating people’s rights

> the data is actually used during investigations.

Absolutely no! All that data collected without due process (judicial warrant, paper trail, whatever is the norm in your neck of the woods) has to be treated as tainted.

↳↳ reply — hedora:

I wasn't arguing against warrants (and argued the datasets shouldn't exist).

Concretely, for my examples, due process already should give victims access to the data, but does not:

Any judge would write a warrant to pull the reverse geofence data. There's a timestamped video of the robbery, and police took photos of the aftermath.

For the car accidents: At least let me have access to my own camera recordings! No warrant needed. I can imagine the police getting a warrant to pull it off the car too if they wanted (they probably already can).

↳ reply 2 — rconti:

I don’t think they should be collecting data without a warrant or probable cause or _some_ level of legally actionable cause.

IMO this is no different from recording and storing everyone’s phone calls in case the data later proves to be useful.

↳ reply 3 — acoustics:

> A reverse geofence warrant keyed on time of arrival / departure would have narrowed it down to just the crooks with extremely high probability

It's an open question whether geofence warrants are constitutional at all. I know that at least in the Fifth Circuit, they are not.

Top #2 — petcat:

Flock and ALPR usage is solved in USA if every state adopts New Hampshire's law:

* Illegal to collect every plate for later analysis

* Illegal to collect anything except for license plates (no drivers, pedestrians, etc.)

* Must delete "non hit" plate images within 3 minutes

* Strict forbidden to upload "non hit" camera imagery off the device

I would add that it should also require a warrant to access the ALPR data, but it's a great start.

https://gc.nh.gov/rsa/html/XXI/261/261-75-b.htm

↳ reply 1 — briffle:

Don’t even need to make that law, just make them ‘public records’, and when people start following the police chief, mayor, etc, those policies will change very, very quickly.

↳↳ reply — captn3m0:

↳ reply 2 — purpleidea:

I agree this is all good but you're missing one important point: if someone breaks the rules, there need to be clear and obvious prison sentences for the manufacturer and/or police involved, and a large payout to everyone who's data is affected, and large whistleblower rewards if you report such a crime.

Top #3 — largbae:

This is a great step but it needs to go even farther. The ALPR tools should only be able to store hits on license plates that are under an active warrant.

It's a 3 way prisoners dilemma market where the prisoners have been caught explicitly colluding before. Now they do not need explicit colluding anymore as the pattern and outcome has been established already and the "jail" is as good as closed to new entrants. Clearly the expected "market" is not working in this niche, so something will have to be done about it.

↳ reply 1 — jeremyjh:

The reason there are only three is that other players in their industry have been wiped out by investing in new production capacity to meet demand that doesn’t exist by the time they come online. It is very much an open question whether HBM demand growth really continues as forecast - it could collapse dramatically for various different reasons.

↳↳ reply — londons_explore:

Isn't this what contracts for future delivery are for? Pass the risk on to the customer/financial markets.

↳↳↳ reply — jeremyjh:

You'd need years of contracts - at prices no can predict are going to be good - to pay off the investment. Do you think the companies who failed or left the industry did so because they didn't know what contracts or futures were?

↳ reply 2 — gpt5:

I honestly don’t understand how can anyone conclude that. All 3 players have their entire inventory sold + reliable reports that their entire next year’s inventory sold.

If you really are thinking from a game theory perspective, in order for it to be the prisoner dilemma, they each need to benefit from lowering prices individually (to cheat). But given that demand outstrips supply so much, they each just lose if they lower price, regardless of what the other players do.

Top #3 — lpghatguy:

A machine-drafted AI news website should not be eligible for submission here.

item.title: How did Woz write the Apple 1 BASIC before building the computer?
item.description: 271 points, 142 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (retrocomputing.stackexchange.com)

→ HN comments  ·  271 points  ·  142 comments  ·  comments as of 17h

Top #1 — femto:

What Woz did was the default way of writing assembly language programs for owners of 8-bit computers (mostly hobbyists). You didn't have money for a second machine, so you wrote your program on paper, you entered it then tested it in situ. Mostly you got it right, as doing it on paper was slow and meant you had the opportunity to put lots of thought into it. 8-bit instruction sets were simple enough that you eventually learned the most common instructions by heart. There was a point where I could mostly translate a Z80 program from assembly to machine code from (my) memory.

Maybe that is part of the nostalgia for the 8-bit days: the practice of "slow programming"? It was relaxing, sort of like those "slow tv" shows.

↳ reply 1 — dhosek:

I find it amusing that so many of the comments were surprised about hand-assembling 6502 code. When I came to the Apple ][, assemblers were relatively more accessible, but even at around $200, it was well beyond my financial means so I would write code longhand in spiral bound graph paper notebooks in four columns: Addresses, labels, hex codes (up to three bytes per opcode) and then the assembly code.

And that $200 being out of bounds went pretty low: for the first couple years of my programming life, floppy disks were beyond my means, so any code I wrote lived in its official version as hand-written code and would have to be retyped any time I wanted it.

↳↳ reply — JKCalhoun:

I'm working on a modern "The First Book of KIM" [1] and there are pages of assembly code for games, utilities. Alongside the assembly is the machine code (byte code).

As near as I can tell, the assembly is not formatted in a way that would actually assemble? Furthermore, there are missing labels, errors… My understanding is that the assembly is there more or less as documentation for the machine code—it was the hex that the person purchasing the book was expected to enter into KIM.

[1] https://archive.org/details/The_First_Book_of_KIM

A new game for the fifty-year-old KIM-1: https://engineersneedart.com/blog/yahtc/yahtc.html

↳ reply 2 — billforsternz:

Yes. My first serious program was done this way. At the start of the project (final year of EE degree, 1981) I didn't really understand what a program was, but I learned by studying the technical reference manual for the Intel 8085 CPU. It kind of seemed like magic, I can mold the functionality by storing codes in memory? Wow!

I figured out exactly what I wanted to do, wrote it out very carefully on paper, looked up all the hex codes, wrote those out very carefully, adjusted addresses etc. as needed. This took many hours spread over weeks. Then I entered the whole thing on the hex keyboard and display of a primitive development board each time I needed it, perhaps an hour or so each time (I think I only did it twice). It worked first time, because why wouldn't it if you were sufficiently meticulous about your work in a process that was very obviously very intolerant of the tiniest mistake?

I must admit my program (gather input information from some transducers, do some calculations, present some results) was likely somewhere between one and two orders of magnitude simpler than a complete Basic interpreter!

↳ reply 3 — semiquaver:

Amazing to think that it will not be long before people feel as nostalgic and impressed about the idea of writing high level code in C.

Top #2 — kamma4434:

For what it’s worth: when I used to do assembly on the commodore 64, after a while, your eyes are so used to seeing A9 close to LDA let you start knowing them by heart without even thinking. Of course this is possible on 6502 and will be way harder on modern CPUs. In the end of the number of common opcodes might have been 30-50, and you can always look up the rest from a one-page table.

I remember that was a book that went on to say that you should learn machine code (that is, raw opcodes), not assembly, to program the c-64. Not sure I would agree, but it’s definitely feasible.

The only thing that is strange in the Woz story is that you would usually start by creating a dirt-poor monitor/assembler so that you would have a sane environment to do further development in. That was the approach manuals from the era suggested for new hardware (eg Rodnay Zack’s)

↳ reply 1 — boomlinde:

> The only thing that is strange in the Woz story is that you would usually start by creating a dirt-poor monitor/assembler so that you would have a sane environment to do further development in.

He wrote a monitor as well, but the premise here is that he wrote the BASIC interpreter before there was a computer at all, so a monitor wouldn't have helped.

↳ reply 2 — LoganDark:

Like the Woz Monitor?

Top #3 — runjake:

I don’t know about other people, but back in the early 80s, I spent a lot of time writing code (mostly assembler, some BASIC and other dead languages) with pencil on paper for various reasons: sometimes I preferred it, sometimes I was writing code for computers I only had access to in labs or at school.

There were even pre-made paper forms for writing code, like the IBM COBOL program sheets and similar for assembler.

Even now, if I’m working on a tough issue, I still print out code sections on paper and hash it out with a pencil.

↳ reply 1 — joelshep:

Yup. All the way up to my second year of college ('85), I'd very carefully plan and write code by hand -- either in BASIC or 6502 assembly -- edit it and "test" it on paper, all so when I got a period at school or 15 minutes for $0.25 at the local library I could make the most of the time at the keyboard.

I will never forget the thrill of keying in a moderately-sized program I'd hand-coded -- a few hundred lines probably -- running it, fixing one or two typos, and then having the program just work. I'm sure they had bugs, but the fact was all that hand-coding effort paid off as programs that ran successfully on the first try.

↳ reply 2 — tonyedgecombe:

We did that at school. We would hand write Fortran code on sheets and send it off somewhere. A week to two later we would get the results back. I seem to remember most of the mistakes were when the operator entered the code.

item.title: SpaceX catches the Starship to end Flight 15
item.description: 1454 points, 980 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (spacex.com)

→ HN comments  ·  1454 points  ·  980 comments  ·  comments as of 18h

Top #1 — Zigurd:

I've been a frequent critic of starship. But the significance of this milestone is clear: it's the first demonstration of a reusable upper stage of a rocket system since the space shuttle.

Part of the importance is due to the fact that while the space shuttle was a technical success in terms of being able to build and operate a reusable upper stage, it was hella expensive. It required a lot of expensive refurbishment between missions. Launch cadence had a fairly low upper bound. And it wasn't safe enough.

The true believers will claim that catching a starship upper stage marks a new era. It marks the possibility of a new era. It proves it is plausible that a vertical landing upper stage could possibly be a better approach than a space plane. But it hasn't proven any of that. There are about a dozen major milestones between here and actually having a rocket system that meets all of its claimed specifications, both technical and financial. Here's just one big hairy example: to fly manned missions, starship either needs to be redesigned to accommodate an escape system, or it needs to show a level of reliability and safety never previously achieved by a rocket.

In my estimation, it will take at least another five years to know what starship really can do and what it will cost.

↳ reply 1 — izend:

I think it is obvious by now that Starship was not designed for manned missions and that it was designed to provide cheap launch capabilities for very large payload capacity.

Flight 13 launched 20 Starlink v3 sats for a total payload of 34,100 kg.

Flight 14 launched 26 Starlink v3 sats for a total payload of 44,330 kg.

The Space Shuttle's max payload capacity was only 22,780kg (https://i.redd.it/8t8j1n4032lh1.png)

↳ reply 2 — MattDamonSpace:

Idk imo the hard part is catching the giant rocket, everything else is “known”

↳ reply 3 — pfdietz:

> it's the first demonstration of a reusable upper stage of a rocket system since the space shuttle.

And even Space Shuttle wasn't a demonstration of that, since the propellant tankage (the largest volume of any stage) wasn't reusable.

SpaceX has pretty conclusively shown the Shuttle architecture (stage and a half, using LH2 at launch) was not the right choice.

Top #2 — ChuckMcM:

Huge congratulations to the engineering team on this one! It's been quite interesting to watch the evolution of Starship. Had they put another couple of tonnes of propellant and oxidizer on the Booster they might have caught both of them. It is still unclear to me what the final mass fraction to orbit will work out to be, but something that is 100% re-usable is better than something 60% reusable[1].

[1] Estimate of Falcon 9's booster + fairings being 60% (by cost, not by mass) of the launch package.

↳ reply 1 — vl:

It looks like they delivered 50 tons today. Even if it stays this way, it will still reduce price to orbit significantly.

↳↳ reply — cubefox:

Unfortunately the payload margins continue to be much lower than what they were aiming for at various points.

Originally they aimed for 150 tons of payload to LEO for Starship V1. Then they lowered that goal to 100 tons. But then Starship V1 only managed to achieve approximately 0 tons, which prompted them to target 100 tons for a larger, more powerful Starship V3 (and 200 tons for Starship V4). But now Starship V3 only achieves around 50 tons to LEO, based on the estimated weight of 26 Starlink V3 satellites.

I think the main issues were that Starship dry mass continued to be heavier than expected, and that the Raptor engines performed lower than they thought they would. Elon Musk recently said the Raptor V3 engines could only reliably achieve 230 tons of thrust per engine (a measure of force) instead of the originally projected 280.

↳↳↳ reply — fartfeatures:

I have every confidence they will work this out. I would hate it if people benchmarked my code whilst it was still in development and extrapolated the future performance from that.

↳ reply 2 — throwaway2037:

    > Had they put another couple of tonnes of propellant and oxidizer on the Booster they might have caught both of them.
Can you explain this part?

Top #3 — BiraIgnacio:

To everyone who works at SpaceX and read this. You are all amazing.

I hope other great minds at SpaceX are well remembered into the far future.

Top #1 — firefoxd:

I got one of those many years ago when I was in college. I desperately needed money, so I found a job listing on Craigslist, sent my resume, got a call back, we agreed on the in-person time and place, it was neat.

I show up at a building 2 blocks from school, a random tenant tells me to form a line by the door that was locked. I was confused because I was the only one there. A second person came in, joined the line. Then a third, fourth, fifth. We were a crowd, standing in front of a door, where I thought I'd interview for a entry level job in tech.

When the door opened and the person on the other side greeted us and a good number of people immediately left. More luck for me to get this job. But turns out, it was going to be a group interview. In fact, not exactly an interview. It was a pitch. And a few lucky ones would have the privilege to sell high tech knives. All we had to do was buy the first batch of knives for something like $300.

item.title: US IRS free online tax filing open source repo (2025)
item.description: 174 points, 106 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (github.com)

→ HN comments  ·  174 points  ·  106 comments  ·  comments as of 22h

★ Comments from: simonw

Top #1 — gouggoug:

I wanted to electronically file my own taxes last year instead of paying turbotax or an actual accountant.

While my situation isn't particularly complex (but complex enough that I did need help from an accountant the first times), none of the free filing services online (IRS FreeFile included) offered the more complex forms I need.

"Not a problem!" I thought. Except, even if I could download the forms from the IRS and do all the work myself, I could not for the life of me find a way to electronically submit (and had to hire my accountant again).

Is it possible in the US to electronically file your own taxes?

↳ reply 1 — glimshe:

Freetaxusa is pretty comprehensive. I've used them twice and my personal situation is fairly complex. It was free for federal and paid for state.

↳ reply 2 — shadytrees:

A few coworkers and I were able to point a combination of Fable and Astra at our statements and compute our federal and state taxes. They seem to understand W-2 income, K-1 partnership income, rental income, brokerage accounts, backdoor Roth rollovers, and late-payment penalties 100%? I even sanity-checked mine against an accountant's work this year and the numbers agreed; it even flagged that I was eligible for first-time penalty abatement, something my accountant did not. I don't think I'm going to pay for an accountant for taxes again unless my finances become substantially more complicated.

Once you're confident in the federal tax calculation, you can point Claude at Free Fillable Forms through Chrome's remote-debugging port and e-file your taxes that way. Most states (all states?) don't have an equivalent. Some of us did Claude + computer use + Turbotax Premier. Some of us did Claude + Chrome remote debugging port + FreeTaxUSA. It sometimes helps to do both Free Fillable Forms and shell out $20 for FreeTaxUSA just so another calculator can check your work. But, again, Fable/Astra's numbers were accurate. They certainly made errors along the way, but if you can handle the fatigue of reading LLM English and patiently answering every little question the models come up with (if I was good at skimming text before this year, I certainly am now), you can probably prompt them into doing your taxes.

At the very least it's good to run them on your previous taxes. Fable found a $1500 overpayment on last year's taxes. My accountant last year was terrible, and this was no shock. The true test will be whether the amendment I had Claude fill out will yield a real check from the IRS twelve months from now (paper filings take forever), and whether I get audited in future years when I'm no longer relying on an accountant.

↳ reply 3 — ksec:

>need help from an accountant

For those of us outside US and not filing tax in US. Can someone explain why there is ever a need for an accountant on the assumption you are just normal working class employee?

It feels so complicated every time I read about US IRS. In the UK most dont even have to file anything at all and is done and deducted automatically. Although I believe this is also not ideal but it prove it can be done.

Top #2 — ane:

When I read these and the related stories I am thankful I live in a country where you don't even need to file taxes. Virtually all income is reported to the tax authorities, so they will calculate a tax rate for you and you rarely need to make adjustments if your income is stable and regular.

Only when I need to make some surprise deductions (e.g. purchasing work-related literature, deductible by law here up to some sum) or for some reason the payer of income is not reported to the tax authorities. Or when the income falls short of what was projected for that year (e.g. unpaid leave, getting fired, changing to jobs to a lower salary (it happens) etc.), or there is a surprise bonus and so on. Normally I do not need to anything.

Let’s say I rent a spare bedroom my home to someone; who’s going to report that income if not me?

If your income is actually fully reported to the IRS (W-2 or various 1099) filing taxes is a breeze anyways. Use one of the several free (as in beer) software to take a picture of your forms and it generates the right form that you can submit electronically to the IRS.

↳↳ reply — throw0101d:

Basically everyone I know has at least some "peer to peer" income that involves no middleman or business.

Now on the other hand I have no idea how many of those people are properly reporting their income. Some definitely do but I suspect many don't.

Will not shed any tears if Turbotax doesn't make it.

item.title: A family tree of software job titles
item.description: 382 points, 189 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (zwischenzugs.com)

Top #1 — probably_wrong:

Recently I spoke to someone who wanted to know what they should call themselves seeing as they never learned software development, formally or otherwise, but that's not stopping them from releasing AI-powered Python projects in GitHub. I suggested Project Manager, but they took offense to that because (I think) they wanted to hear Software Engineer in order to apply to those jobs. My counter-argument was that, legal rules aside, a S.E. should be able to differentiate good code from bad, but my suggestion wasn't super well received.

The point being: I'm always amazed at the cross-purpose impulse of arguing "the title is not important" while, simultaneously, really wanting to use the title.

The titles between different levels don't seem to mean much because of the variation between companies. But I do see merit to differentiating between roles.

As an example, I moved from Software Engineering to IT Controls Analyst. The pay brackets are lower and there are way fewer job postings. Even this chart of software related job completely leaves out any compliance or audit function, illustrating just how little my own profession thinks of us.

↳ reply 3 — julianpye:

I think the role is that of a producer - similar to a music producer in the 70s and 80s integrating new synth and recording technology into ambitious outcomes where the goal was defined but the shape and detail unpredictable.

Top #2 — siva7:

Scrum and Agile seem to be dying. I had a Product Owner and Scrum Master cert for years on my resume but i've dropped it from my current. Feels now like the ancient webmaster title of the mid 90s. Made for another timeline which is not more relevant.

DevOps is another sad story as it was a saner approach to get people skilled for both dev and ops but turns out people don't like learning new skills as much as they claim. So its meaning differed from org to org and even within the same company.

↳ reply 1 — nkmnz:

- ship to production

- monitor and learn from production usage

You don't need "devopsy" skills to do that, rather organizational structures that allow for incremental change. FWIW, deployments could still be a 2005-like upload via FTP, and the benefits of DevOps could still be reaped.

> DevOps should be a guiding principle for the organization, not a dedicated role

The way I've always phrased it is that if a company has "DevOps" teams or titles, they're not doing DevOps by definition

↳↳↳ reply — sighansen:

I call it the reverse devops principle. The more a company speaks of doing DevOps, the less they are actually doing it.

↳ reply 2 — Aurornis:

> but turns out people don't like learning new skills as much as they claim. So its meaning differed from org to org and even within the same company.

Titles like these always mean something different from company to company.

Even “product manager” has had different meanings at my different employers, some times with major consequences for people who got hired into those roles expecting to do one type of work and then being evaluated on different expectations.

For DevOps, there were a lot of unrealistic expectations from everyone who saw the word and assumed they knew what it meant. I saw a lot of engineering leaders come up with completely different expectations for DevOps roles, but when the chaos arrived most of them reduced the DevOps people into the responsible-for-everything people, which just burned people out.

Top #3 — rester324:

I need to point out that these titles are very much culture specific. For example in the japanese work culture regardless of whatever experience, skills and certificates you have, you are just a software engineer, an idiot who is treated like a low IQ moron and paid in peanuts (OK, I am strongly exaggerating, but not that much in reality sadly :/)

item.title: Lovable apps expose passport details and more than 200K private messages
item.description: 937 points, 358 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (crissyfield.de)

→ HN comments  ·  937 points  ·  358 comments  ·  comments as of 22h

Top #1 — yakkomajuri:

I don't know how so many people bought into the row-level security stuff with the frontend talking directly to the Supabase backend. Always seemed like a minefield to me. I've used Supabase a time or two but always as a standard Postgres that I'd connect to from my backend. They will send you a million emails though about how your DB is insecure because you don't have RLS configured.

In this case we're talking about vibe coders, who don't know about the implementation details. But we've gotten here in the first place because a lot of developers adopted this Supabase RLS serverless model. I always found it surprising that this model stuck.

↳ reply 1 — jappgar:

The whole premise of RLS is that you only have to think about data permissions in one place.

If you're up for maintaining that, and if you're willing to suffer the serious performance hits it inevitably entails, it can be a very convenient and secure option.

The problem is that most engineers (let alone vibe coders) are decidedly terrible at db design. The outcome here is entirely predictable.

↳↳ reply — yakkomajuri:

Agreed. Nothing inherently bad about RLS itself, but the way it was pushed forward in the Supabase model was always bound to be dangerous. Because like you say, it requires proper DB design, whereas the selling points of the Supabase model are simplicity and speed, so there's a bit of a mismatch here.

↳ reply 2 — skeeter2020:

RLS can be a dangerous point for secure implementations. Even if you use single tenant you might need to filter for departmental or individual permissions and you're often a single missed join from sharing data you shouldn't. In the past year or so I've adopted the strategy DBs that only contain the data the audience is allowed to see using DuckDB - specifically for scenarios where the end users can write their own queries (a growing approach with AI), so there's nothing to leak. You still need to be careful with security but it's analogous of pushing a runtime bug to compile time. Most people don't really have big data; small data for the win!

Top #2 — neathack:

Hi, I’m the author of this blog post. I submitted it to HN two weeks ago, but it didn’t gain much traction, so I’m glad to see it resubmitted. Happy to answer any questions, though I think the situation is fairly self-explanatory.

Top #3 — SOLAR_FIELDS:

The part people are ignoring is Supabase's culpability in this matter: https://github.com/orgs/supabase/discussions/4547

This was supposedly fixed on October 30, but there are reports floating around that for existing projects, the defaults still apply.

Lovable deserves some heat for using this, but this was a choice that was made by Supabase many years ago to support making it easier to onboard potential customers, a deliberate tradeoff of less onboarding pain for less security.

↳ reply 1 — yard2010:

> I've realised that the supabaseKey needed for creating the client on the frontend also grants users access to the database by default.

I can't believe someone actually made this by design

↳↳ reply — weird-eye-issue:

There is nothing wrong with this. It's no different from unauthenticated API routes to get public information. The issue is when somebody doesn't use RLS correctly.

↳↳↳ reply — skeeter2020:

>> The issue is when somebody doesn't use RLS correctly.

True, but I've seen staff+ level developers get bit by this. What hope do vibe coders have?

↳ reply 2 — fudged71:

This 5 year old issue was only just fixed this October? Got a link to where it was fixed?

item.title: Formalizing US Tax Code (Using Lean)
item.description: 145 points, 95 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (lexifina.com)

→ HN comments  ·  145 points  ·  95 comments  ·  comments as of 17h

Top #1 — patrickmay:

I worked for a company pre-LLMs that analyzed laws and regulations in order to answer questions about financial transaction legality and reporting requirements. One problem that came up frequently is that the rules governments make don't have to be consistent. There are conflicts, some quite significant. The best we could do was make them visible and escalate to a human.

It would be interesting to require laws to be compilable. Charles Stross wrote a couple of books that include that idea.

↳ reply 1 — AnthonyMouse:

In theory "impossibility" is a defense to most crimes.

In practice you usually get screwed in one of the following ways: a) the law makes it impossible to do X without breaking the law, even though X is a normal thing and neither law was supposed to be a total ban on X, but you could comply by not doing X at all, b) the inconsistent laws are imposed by different jurisdictions and then they each insist you follow theirs, often a special case of the first one where X is "be in two different jurisdictions" but sometimes the even stupider one where a jurisdiction demands that you follow its laws even when you're not in it, c) it's impossible for you to follow both laws at once so you followed only one of them and then they decide after the fact that you should have followed only the other one.

↳↳ reply — jaza:

Re: imposed by different jurisdictions. I don't know the letter of the law in the US, but here in Australia at least, most such differences are easily resolved by section 109 of our constitution (note: Commonwealth == Federal):

"When a law of a State is inconsistent with a law of the Commonwealth, the latter shall prevail, and the former shall, to the extent of the inconsistency, be invalid."

Hmmm, just googled, and it would seem that Article VI Clause 2 of the US constitution, aka the Supremacy Clause, is basically equivalent.

↳↳↳ reply — Georgelemental:

In the US, the Supremacy Clause only holds insofar as federal law doesn't overstep the restrictions on federal power outlined elsewhere in the Constitution. The wording is "the Laws of the United States which shall be made in Pursuance [of the Constitution]".

If you follow federal law over state law, but then a federal judge holds that the federal law you followed was an unconstitutional overstep in a domain that the Constitution reserves to the states, you are SOL

↳ reply 2 — serioussecurity:

My understanding is that consistency is explicitly not a goal of the American legal system.

Laws are designed to give law enforcement latitude to pursue the charges they seem fit, subject to the taste of a judge.

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I_know_it_when_I_see_it

Top #2 — rancar2:

Wow, if I'm reading this correctly, the Big Beautiful Bill introduced a pretty large gap that punishes married couples filing jointly: a couple making about $300K each can lose up to $15K in write-offs compared with filing separately, pretty much everywhere except the nine states with no broad income tax (Alaska, Florida, Nevada, New Hampshire, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Washington, and Wyoming), where few couples pay the $25K in state and local taxes needed to trigger it. I think most tax software will assume the $5K cap each, but the regulation here is inconsistent. Here’s the take-away quote from the article:

“A married couple can deduct more state and local tax by filing separately. The deduction for state and local taxes (SALT) is capped, and the cap shrinks as income rises: by 30 cents for each dollar over $500,000 on a joint return. On a separate return, the law halves the cap after shrinking it, so it shrinks by only 15 cents a dollar. A couple earning $300,000 each can deduct up to $25,000 on two separate returns, but only $10,000 on one joint return.”

This is non-trivial impact to joint returns if this is true, and I won’t be surprised if there are multiple appeals for refunds and more people filling separately going towards.

↳ reply 1 — jghn:

> punishes married couples filing jointly: a couple making about $300K each

The number of married couples where each partner is making $300K each is a very, very small percentage of the population. Not sure this is a big deal to be concerned about in the grand scheme of things. For instance, only a few %age of households have an income over 300K in the first place, much less coming from 2 earners of that amount.

↳↳ reply — jedberg:

It might be a few people nationwide, but it's a whole lot of families in the Bay Area, New York, Los Angeles, and a few other major cities.

The law was specifically designed to punish these people. Remember, at first they wanted to drop the SALT deduction completely to punish blue states.

Edit: It seems that people are assuming I'm against removing the SALT deduction. Far from it. I am glad they got it done despite being a political third rail for a long time. And despite being a huge beneficiary of the SALT deductions myself.

I don't think people choosing to live in high tax states should get to save on their federal income taxes.

↳↳↳ reply — Auracle:

Don’t tax the rich (and yes, 600k for a couple per year is absolutely rich territory)? “They need to pay their fair share!” Tax the rich? “They’re targeting people in blue cities!”

The SALT deduction is nonsense. Why should high tax states effectively be able to take money from the federal government?

↳ reply 2 — AnthonyMouse:

The tax code has significantly punished dual-income married couples for quite a while. It presumably started some time in the 20th century as some sexists not wanting women in the workplace and then continued because changing it to have them pay the same taxes as they would if they were unmarried would result in a significant reduction in government revenue.

Top #3 — jedberg:

It's important to remember that the loopholes are often intentional. They are left there so that rich people who can afford CPAs can take advantage of them, while middle income and poor people cannot afford to.

They are also left there so there is wiggle room for interpretation if it comes in front of an auditor or a judge.

And also, it's important to remember that in tax matters, the final arbiter of interpretation is a judge. Judges are humans, not machines. You can't "Trick" them by saying "well technically this is allowed!". Because they rule on the sprit of the law, not as it was written. Judges aren't amused when you try to be cute with how you interpret a law. And some Judges have biases, where you get a different ruling depending on if you play at their golf club or not.

Laws aren't computer code. They are vague on purpose.

↳ reply 1 — rendaw:

I've heard this repeated a couple times here on HN. Do you have any citations for laws being vague on purpose? The whole point of laws, and the formal structure they take, is to reduce vagueness. Is this rock on person A's land or person B's land? When it turns out, despite best efforts, that a law is vague we even have a second system to step in and reduce the vagueness further: case law. I have no doubt that people are trying to exploit vagueness on both sides, but naysaying here is nonsense. And almost nobody wants law to be vague either.

↳↳ reply — DannyBee:

Lawyer here (but I don't make any money from it and absolutely have no dog in this fight). I agree. Law is vague for two reasons - first it is often as a compromise between two positions that people were okay having decided on a case by case basis instead of fighting to the death over what to write down. It also is vague sometimes to intentionally capture the spirit of what it is trying to do. While I won't claim vagueness is never left to benefit someone ( I'm sure it happens), I would claim it is rare.

Law is basically a representation of societal judgement. While criminal law is intended to be clear enough to know when you've violated it, that is not the same as beimg logical or consistent. Civil law is even less logical and consistent. Formalizing it into logic generally does not make sense overall - it isn't really broken in most cases because it was never intended to be totally consistent. There are certainly areas that could use cleaner rewriting but courts are generally well equipped to figure out what it means. Congress and the states can always overturn interpretations of law, but the rate at which they rewrite laws because they thought courts interpreted it wrong is very, very low.

↳ reply 2 — djoldman:

> And also, it's important to remember that in tax matters, the final arbiter of interpretation is a judge. Judges are humans, not machines. You can't "Trick" them by saying "well technically this is allowed!". Because they rule on the sprit of the law, not as it was written. Judges aren't amused when you try to be cute with how you interpret a law. And some Judges have biases, where you get a different ruling depending on if you play at their golf club or not.

> Laws aren't computer code. They are vague on purpose.

Yes... but. Tax law is a bit different because it is similar to an equation: you put in your inputs and you get your outputs.

There have been famous cases where the courts have said in essence, "yes you completely and exactly and precisely followed the law, but we're not going to allow you to do that anyway." Those rulings have become less frequent.

item.title: PyPI's redesigned project pages with clearer security signals are now live
item.description: 239 points, 100 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (blog.pypi.org)

→ HN comments  ·  239 points  ·  100 comments  ·  comments as of 17h

Top #1 — time4tea:

Not very keen that the whole story of trust is basically centralisation - requiring "big cloud" and essentially promoting lock-in.

Did I get that right? Seems a bit anti-pythonic.

↳ reply 1 — rtpg:

I believe you got that wrong.

Here's some extra context [0]: https://github.com/pypi/warehouse/issues/20927. Loooots of links to click in.

the point here being small service providers are _also_ able to get into this system, but I think there's an expectation of success.

The bar for trusted publishers is very high though. I don't think it's high "on purpose" to leave out certain platforms for being too small, but in effect if (for example) your provider doesn't have a security contact point then that's going to rule them out here.

↳↳ reply — kapilvt:

I’d like to see support for trusted publisher signing and manual upload. Think of it as two step auth for artifact publishing. Pipeline generated artifacts and human upload of those verifiable artifacts. The current reality of trusted publishing, is devoid of trust, except it was triggered by a pipeline that pypi trusted. That pypi is now able to call out such trust is great btw, but as a project that currently does this two step generation, it feels like we are penalized for trying to introduce additional steps out of abundance of caution… separately, what mechanism does a client installer have to verify a pkg install was cryptographically attested to wrt to production?

sans client verification of signatures by default, install is still roulette, and I’m glad package managers have introduced package publication date based cool off options now.

↳↳↳ reply — rtpg:

Yeah that's not the worst idea, since in theory signing is about tamper prevention.

(Personally I think that we just shouldn't have automated releases via CI, full stop. There should "always" be a person pressing a button to release things. So I'm in a bit of a big tent with manual upload support. At least some second factor for releases!)

I think generally though the idea is that trusted publisher signing + upload is about simplifying .... something. But given how attacks have been happening in the past 24 months I fear that this might not help as much as we want.

↳ reply 2 — sublimefire:

For example MSFT (not a small player i know) is having its slightly different approach to those signals and they cannot be used here (search scitt). I mean different type signature envelopes, different roots of trust. But in the spirit it is the same. This approach is partially a territorial grab by google (first npm, then pypi, next golang). But importantly I think these security improvements are marginal and you are at the mercy of the dependency developer anyway. Just look at npm, they had some nasty vectors and similar “improvements” were close to useless in those cases.

↳ reply 3 — bbor:

It's anti lots of things, but I don't think it's anti-Pythonic. Python is about pragmatism & empathy if it's about anything -- bitcoin and such don't factor into it. See: Astral/OpenAI, Anaconda, most of the PSF board historically being employees of big corporate users of python, NVidia's relation to the ecosystem in general, etc.

As a passionate anarchosyndicalist, I, for one, am thrilled about it. Decentralization is a tool in our toolbox for identifying and dismantling unjust hierarchies, but it is not a panacea, and can be quite damaging when taken to the extreme. See: cryptocurrency speedrunning 200y of bank regulations in 20y.

To put my trust for Python in more concrete terms: they support GitLab. As a passionate GitLab shill, I really couldn't be more impressed! It continues to shock me how infrequently the second most popular forge is acknowledged, much less supported. This shows they're not just, IDK, bowing to Microsoft's demands.

Top #2 — djoldman:

Some examples:

dlt (no provenance): https://pypi.org/project/dlt/#files

datasette (yes provenance): https://pypi.org/project/datasette/#files

↳ reply — MeteorMarc:

The source distributions have icons while the wheels have not. Strange and confusing.

↳↳ reply — Latty:

I see the icon for both, but in different places (below the name for the wheel, alongside for the source).

Top #3 — mhils:

Very cool to see PyPI put more emphasis towards exposing provenance info. It would be even cooler if trusted publishing would finally support reusable workflows (https://github.com/pypi/warehouse/issues/11096).

↳ reply — pdonis:

It would be even nicer if there were a way to have an attestation without publishing with a workflow controlled by one of the tech giants. There's no way for me, someone who has had a PyPI account for many years and has used it for all that time to upload packages, to attach my own public key to my PyPI account and then sign uploaded distributions with my private key so the signature can be verified and count as an attestation.

↳↳ reply — angry_octet:

I think the problem is this type of attestation is hard to weigh as a trust signal, vs the cloud CI version.

Inherently, if someone steals your key, or gains access to a box that can use that key for signing, they are indistinguishable from you. Hand PGP signing also lacks time-bound signing, any ratchet mechanism, CT log, consistent key hierarchy, or standard to bind signer name and project identity.

↳↳↳ reply — pdonis:

> this type of attestation is hard to weigh as a trust signal, vs the cloud CI version

In the sense that I'm not a large corporation and nobody else is auditing my personal computer, yes, that's true. Note, though, that large corporations are also subject to nefarious actors misusing their infrastructure. What if a rogue employee hacks their internal system? Or Russia or China manages to get a backdoor into it?

In any case, all this doesn't make the method I described impossible. It just means that attestations produced by an individual workflow need to be clearly labeled to distinguish them from attestations produced using a tech forge's workflow, so people will understand what, specifically, is being attested to. Then people could weigh each trust signal as they choose.

> Hand PGP signing

To be clear, I wasn't talking specifically about this method of signing with a personal key. I agree there are lots of issues with PGP as an overall system. I was only talking about the general idea of having some way for individuals to independently generate an attestation without having to go through a tech forge's workflow.

Top #3 — joebarbere:

Thanks for this! I've been trying to get local training working on Fedora with ROCm for a while now, and this is the first project that ran end-to-end on my RX 7600 XT 16GB.

The whole reason for me buying the card was to play around with deep learning and models, so it's awesome to have a stepping off point now!

No CUDA meant ROCm surprisingly just worked with JAX.

Gotchas for anyone with a 7600 XT: it needed two env vars, HSA_OVERRIDE_GFX_VERSION=11.0.0 because JAX's plugin rejects gfx1102, and XLA_FLAGS=--xla_gpu_enable_triton_gemm=false to stop a GPU hang.

I'm on Fedora 45 with the in-kernel amdgpu driver, rootless podman and AMD's rocm/jax image (ROCm 10.1, JAX 0.11.1). Nothing ROCm is installed on the host, which is nice.

Container setup is in a PR if it helps anyone: https://github.com/Vaibhaav-Tiwari/deepseek-v3-jax/pull/1

↳ reply — DaSHacka:

By "Entered for the first time", I assume you mean after a fresh boot? If so, that means the phone is Before First Unlock (BFU), where the user data is actually encrypted. The "Lock Screen is just a UI" applies to After First Unlock where its just a UI element. BFU and AFU are essentially the core two states in the mobile device security world. Not sure why it would take a long time on Samsung devices though, it's usually almost instant on most handsets.

item.title: Show HN: A terminal-native idle factory game, written in Rust with ratatui
item.description: 155 points, 39 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (gitlab.com)

→ HN comments  ·  155 points  ·  39 comments  ·  comments as of 19h

Top #1 — brian-armstrong:

I'm still surprised people are not writing their own READMEs. It's the first impression anyone gets on your project, and having it be full of Claudeisms shows you just don't really care. It's also a pretty good indicator that the entire thing is slopware, so I guess it's a useful signal there.

Top #2 — Joker_vD:

> It is made to sit in a split next to your AI agents. They can send you short messages that show up in the game, so you can play while they work.

> Agent messages

> Your AI agents can message you inside the game. A message costs the agent only the words in it, and nothing prints on success. Messages wait while the game is closed.

It's kinda amazing how the ancient "local mail" technology keeps getting reinvented, you know, and reintegrated inside the gameplay? NetHack had its its "mail demon" since... (googles) version 1.0.2, in April 1985 — the creature would spawn in the game, deliver you a scroll of mail, and vanish. And apparently, it's still in use nowadays? "On public servers such as nethack.alt.org, a user may observe other users' games and communicate with them by sending mail."

↳ reply — neuronexmachina:

I guess it's a variation on jwz's old aphorism:

> Every program attempts to expand until it can read mail. Those programs which cannot so expand are replaced by ones which can.

Top #3 — ivanjermakov:

Why every factory game is about mining/smelting iron and copper? Aren't there more intersting industrial processes?

↳ reply — felixg3:

I’m currently vibe-coding a game for myself inspired by prison architect + workers & resources - it’s about a fictional 1940s-1980s Soviet plutonium production complex where you have to manage… workers, resources, political goodwill, quotas, and accidents. Modelled are Alpha, Beta, gamma and Neutron radiation, effects on workers like in rimworld.

Will be gpl 3.0 and I plan to release a playable 0.1 on GitHub. I care mostly about historical accuracy of radiation incidents and factory issues at the intersection of nuclear engineering & political issues akin to Paper’s please.

I’m afraid to publish it because I despise the amount of AI slop out there. I just want to tickle my need for a historical plutonium production management simulator.
